# Keyslam

> Keyslam (the Mac keyboard sound app, not the game studio) is a macOS menu-bar app that plays real mechanical keyboard and typewriter recordings as you type. On Apple silicon MacBooks with a motion sensor it measures how hard each key is struck and picks a real strike from that board's soft, medium, hard or slam band. $3.99 one-time (lifetime license), 7-day free trial, macOS 13 Ventura or later. Status: available to download.

## Key facts

- Price: $3.99 USD, one-time payment, lifetime license; free updates
- Free trial: 7 days, everything unlocked, no account or card
- Sounds: 15 packs, each cut from a real recording: MX Blue (Clicky), MX Brown (Tactile), MX Red (Linear), MX Black (Linear), Gateron Red (Linear), Topre (Electro-capacitive), Leopold (Tactile), WhiteFox (Tactile), Rainy 75 (Mechanical), Unicomp (Buckling spring), Model F (Buckling spring), Vintage Technics (Linear, modded), Laptop (Butterfly), Selectric (Typewriter), Olivetti (Typewriter)
- Each pack: cut from one real typing recording; every strike is detected and sorted by natural loudness into four strength bands (soft, medium, hard, and slam = the hardest ~8%), each band leveled. Keyboard packs pair each strike with its key-up and have separate takes for Space/Return/Delete; the typewriter packs have no key-up sounds and play a bell from a second CC0 recording on Return
- Force sensing: reads the MacBook accelerometer about 800 times a second; supported on MacBook Pro with M1 Pro/M1 Max or later and MacBooks with M2 or later
- Works on any Mac with macOS 13 Ventura or later (Apple silicon or Intel); without the motion sensor you pick the strength
- Privacy: the app has no analytics or telemetry and makes no network connections at all; the website uses Google Analytics (cookieless by default in Europe); the license key is Ed25519-signed and verified offline; uses only which key went down to choose a sound; never stores or sends what you type
- Buying: Stripe Checkout in your browser (seller: Venture Deals, Co.); personal license for all the Macs you own; 14-day refund
- Recordings: all source recordings are CC0 (public domain) on Freesound, credited on the site
- Website: https://keyslam.com

# Keyslam: verified facts

Single source of truth for anything we publish, pitch or post. If a claim isn't here
(or in a source linked here), don't make it. Update this file first when facts change.

_Last verified: 2026-11-02_

## Product

- **Keyslam** is a native macOS menu-bar app that plays real mechanical keyboard
  recordings as you type, in every app.
- **Force sensing:** on Apple silicon MacBooks with the motion sensor (MacBook Pro with
  M1 Pro/M1 Max and later; MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later) it reads the
  built-in accelerometer about 800 times a second, compares each keystroke's jolt with
  how you usually type, and picks and blends real strikes from four strength bands:
  soft, medium, hard, slam. Verified on an M5 Pro MacBook Pro; other models are based on
  public hardware information.
- **How the strength bands are made (say it exactly like this):** each pack is cut from
  one real typing recording. Every strike is detected and paired with its key-up; the
  strikes are sorted by natural loudness into four bands (soft ≈ 8th–30th percentile,
  medium ≈ 38th–62nd, hard ≈ 70th–88th, slam = the hardest ~8%), and each band is
  leveled to a consistent target. Never say "recorded at four strengths" or "a separate
  slam recording"; say "real strikes sorted into four strength bands".
- On other Macs (desktops, Intel, M1 Air/13" M1 Pro) every sound works at a strength the
  user picks.
- **Sounds (15 packs since 1.0.1, all real recordings, CC0 sources on Freesound):** MX Blue
  (clicky), MX Brown (tactile), MX Red (linear), MX Black (linear; Cherry MX Black on a
  Leopold FC980M PD), Gateron Red (linear; Gateron Red on a GMMK TKL), Topre (HHKB),
  Leopold (FC660M, MX Brown, PBT), WhiteFox (Hako Violet), Rainy 75 (mechanical; a Rainy 75,
  switches not stated), Unicomp (buckling spring; a Unicomp keyboard, model not stated),
  Model F (buckling spring; an early-1980s IBM Model F XT), Vintage Technics (modded,
  Gateron Yellow), Laptop (2018 MacBook Pro butterfly keys), IBM Selectric II typewriter,
  Olivetti Lettera 22 typewriter. That is 13 keyboards and 2 typewriters.
  - Kinds shown in the app: Clicky, Tactile, Linear (MX Red, MX Black, Gateron Red;
    Vintage Technics is "Linear, modded"), Electro-capacitive (Topre), Mechanical
    (Rainy 75), Buckling spring (Unicomp, Model F), Butterfly (Laptop), Typewriter.
  - Version 1.0.0 had 10 packs; 1.0.1 added Unicomp, Model F, Gateron Red, MX Black and
    Rainy 75. Sources (Freesound, CC0 1.0): Unicomp "Typing on a keyboard" by SamsterBirdies
    (#489423), Model F "IBM Model F keyboard typing" by Fractal_ (#500430), Gateron Red
    "Typing on a mechanical keyboard" by IRF1010N (#583085), MX Black "leopold fc980m pd
    cherry mx black.flac" by ujonathan (#628325), Rainy 75 "Typing on a rainy 75" by
    Techrul (#815614). Uploaders' words: "Unicomp buckling spring keyboard"; "IBM Model F XT
    buckling spring keyboard from the early 1980s"; "GMMK TKL keyboard with Gateron Red
    switches"; "my leopold fc980mpd with cherry mx black"; "my Rainy 75 keyboard" (tags
    include creamy and thocky). Checked 2026-11-02.
- Each pack: four strength bands, every pack leveled to the same loudness (-28 LUFS).
  The 13 keyboard packs also have separate takes for regular keys and for
  Space/Return/Delete, and key-up sounds. The 2 typewriter packs have no key-up sounds,
  use their letter strikes for Space and Delete, and play a bell from a second CC0
  recording on Return: "Typewriter bell & carriage reset" by knufds (#345955, Selectric)
  and "Typewriter ding_near_mono.wav" by _stubb (#406243, Olivetti) (Resources/Recipes,
  `enterSources` and `noReleases`).
- Stereo placement by key position; each key keeps its own take and pitch.
- Native Swift app with a C real-time audio core; audio buffer about 5 ms.
- Audio and motion sensor switch off after 3 idle minutes.
- Custom packs: WAV/AIFF/FLAC + `pack.json` in the Packs folder.
- Requires macOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel.
- App: about 16 MB installed (universal Apple silicon + Intel, all 15 packs; measured on the
  1.0.1 release build); the DMG download is 10.9 MB. (1.0.0 with 10 packs: 12 MB / 8.1 MB.)
- **Measured (2026-11-02, M5 Pro MacBook Pro, `Keyslam --selftest`):** audio engine, key
  tap, one loaded pack (Leopold, 43 takes, 1.5 MB of audio) and the motion sensor running
  together used about 11 MB peak memory footprint and 0.04 s of CPU time over 1.75 s; the
  motion sensor delivered ~1,300 reports in that window (≈800 per second). Say "in our
  self-test"; it isn't a steady-state typing benchmark.
- **Turn sounds on/off from anywhere:** global shortcut ⌃⌥⌘K by default (menu: "Turn
  sounds on/off with", can be switched off or changed to ⌃⌥⌘S, ⌃⌥⌘M or ⌃⌥⌘T). No extra
  permission. If another app already owns the shortcut, the menu says so.
- **Quiet during calls** (on by default): while any app is using the microphone, sounds
  pause automatically and come back when the mic is released. Keyslam doesn't record or
  access the microphone (no microphone permission); it only reads whether the input
  device is in use.

## Price and buying

- **$3.99 one-time, lifetime license**, free updates, all current and future packs.
- **7-day free trial**, everything unlocked, no account, no card.
- Sold through Stripe Checkout (merchant of record: Venture Deals, Co.). After paying,
  the browser shows the license key and an "Activate Keyslam" button
  (keyslam://activate). The key is Ed25519-signed and verified offline on the Mac.
- **License:** personal license, use it on all the Macs you own. Nothing counts or
  limits activations ("Remove License From This Mac" only deletes it locally).
- **Refunds:** full refund within 14 days if it doesn't work for you — reply to the
  Stripe receipt or use the contact form.
- Direct download, not the Mac App Store. Wording allowed: "None of the 42 Mac App
  Store keyboard-sound apps we checked offers force sensing." Never say the App Store
  sandbox makes it impossible (not verified).
- Release: **version 1.0.1** is built, Developer ID-signed (Venture Deals, Co.),
  notarized by Apple and stapled (2026-11-02): universal DMG (Apple silicon + Intel),
  10.9 MB, **live at https://keyslam.com/download/Keyslam.dmg** (1.0.0 went live the same day)
  (sha256 in /download/Keyslam.dmg.sha256). Status: **launched** — say "download it",
  never "launching soon". Buying is live (Stripe Payment Link).
- **Version 1.0.1** (dated 2026-11-02): five new packs (15 in all), the menu's Sound grid
  fits all 15, and each pack's credits name every source recording once. No built-in
  updater: 1.0.0 owners download the new version from /download/ and keep the same
  license, at no cost.

## Privacy

- No analytics, telemetry or tracking **in the app**. The **website** uses Google Analytics 4
  (G-BM5WT1XXDH, since 2026-11-02) with Consent Mode v2: ad storage always denied; analytics
  storage denied by default in the EEA, UK and Switzerland until the visitor clicks Allow;
  events: begin_checkout, file_download, select_content (sound pack), purchase (/thanks/).
  Never say the website has no analytics or sets no cookies; say "the app has no analytics".
- **The app makes no network connections at all** (verified in code: no URLSession or
  any networking in Sources/). License checks run offline; the trial date is kept in
  the Mac's Keychain. Buying happens in your browser on Stripe's checkout page, and the
  /thanks/ page fetches the key from our license Worker (Cloudflare) using the Stripe
  session id.
- Uses Input Monitoring only to know which key went down; never stores or sends what
  you type. macOS doesn't deliver keystrokes from password fields to any app.
- Website forms (notify me / contact) store the email you type on our Cloudflare Worker
  only to reply or send the launch link. Google Analytics is the website's only third-party script.

# Keyboard Sound App for Mac That Feels How Hard You Type
URL: https://keyslam.com/
Updated: 2026-11-02

$3.99Once, for life · 15 real keyboards and typewriters

## Keyboard sound app for Mac Hit harder. Hear harder.

Each pack is cut from a real recording into four bands of real strikes, soft to slam. On MacBooks with the motion sensor, Keyslam picks from them on every keystroke, so a light tap stays light and a hard hit lands hard.

Get Keyslam
Hear it right here →

Free 7-day trial, no account or card · $3.99 once · macOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel

Short answer: Keyslam is a keyboard sound app for Mac. It plays real recordings of 13 keyboards and 2 typewriters on every key you press, in any app, so you get mechanical keyboard sounds on your Mac without changing keyboards. On Apple silicon MacBooks with the motion sensor, it feels how hard each key lands and plays a softer or harder real strike to match. It costs $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial, makes no network connections, and is available to download.

$3.99once, lifetime license
7 daysfree trial, no card
15real keyboards and typewriters
~16 MBthe whole app, every pack included
~5 msaudio buffer in the C audio core
0network connections from the app

Force sensing

### Your MacBook already feels how hard you type.

MacBooks with an M1 Pro, M1 Max, M2 or later chip have a motion sensor inside the case. Keyslam reads it about 800 times a second and compares each keystroke's jolt with how you usually type. Then it picks real strikes from that board's soft, medium, hard and slam bands and crossfades between the two closest.

The sound starts as soon as the key goes down, usually at your typical strength, and settles on the measured strength within about 16 ms. You hear one keystroke, not two. Read how these keyboard sounds that react to how hard you type are measured.

~800 Hzmotion sensor readings

4strength bands per board

16 msto settle on your force

Impact

1.0× a typical keystroke · Medium 100%

Drag Impact and press Strike. The curves show how much of each band you hear at that force.

The recordings
### Real strikes, sorted soft to slam

Every pack starts as one real typing recording, released as CC0 on Freesound; the two typewriters add a recorded bell for Return. Keyslam's slicer finds each strike and drops clipped or overlapping hits. On the keyboards it also pairs each strike with its key-up and keeps Space, Return and Delete apart (they ring longer). Then it sorts the strikes by natural loudness into four bands.

- Band | Strikes it takes from the recording | Level target vs. medium | Where it sits on a MacBook |
- Soft | 8th to 30th percentile | 0.55× | about 0.4× your usual keystroke |
- Medium | 38th to 62nd percentile | 1× (the reference) | your usual keystroke |
- Hard | 70th to 88th percentile | 1.45× | about 2.2× |
- Slam | 92nd to 100th percentile, the hardest ~8% | 2× | about 4× and up |

Slam isn't a separate recording. It's the hardest ~8% of strikes from someone typing normally. Strikes that fall between two bands are skipped, so neighboring bands sound clearly different. Each band is then nudged toward its own level target, and every pack is matched to the same loudness (-28 LUFS), so switching boards doesn't jump in volume.

MX BlueClickyMX BrownTactileMX RedLinearMX BlackLinearGateron RedLinearTopreElectro-capacitiveLeopoldTactileWhiteFoxTactileRainy 75MechanicalUnicompBuckling springModel FBuckling springVintage TechnicsLinear, moddedLaptopButterflySelectricTypewriterOlivettiTypewriter

### Works on any Mac with macOS 13 or later

#### Feels your force

MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, and MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later. These have the motion sensor. Tested on an M5 Pro MacBook Pro; the other models are based on public hardware information.

#### Plays at the strength you pick

Intel Macs, iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, the M1 MacBook Air and the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro. Every sound works; choose Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam in the menu bar.

#### External keyboards

Keys on an external keyboard play sounds too. The sensor feels the MacBook's own case, so when it feels no jolt, as with a separate keyboard, the key plays at your usual strength.

Details: which MacBooks have the motion sensor, what the MacBook typing sound app does on each Air and Pro, and keyboard sounds on Intel Macs and desktops.

### Keyslam next to Haptyk, TapNoise and Klack

Prices and features from each app's own site or Mac App Store page, checked November 2, 2026. Looking for the best keyboard sound app for Mac? All the apps we checked are compared there, with sources.

Haptyk also reads the MacBook motion sensor, and its trial runs 3 days; Keyslam's runs 7 (more in Keyslam as a Haptyk alternative). If you'd rather buy through the Mac App Store, Klack is $4.99 there; the Klack alternative page sets out how the two differ. If you need it free and open source, Mechvibes or KeyEcho may suit you better; see free keyboard sound apps for Mac.

Keyslam is sold directly, not on the Mac App Store. None of the 42 Mac App Store keyboard-sound apps we checked offers force sensing.

Privacy
### An app with no network connections, no analytics and no account.

#### Hears keys, not words

Input Monitoring tells Keyslam which key went down. It never stores or sends what you type, and macOS keeps password fields hidden from all apps.

#### Checks your license offline

Your key is Ed25519-signed and verified on your Mac. The app never contacts a server, not even to check the license.

#### Trial date in your Keychain

The trial start date and your license live in your Mac's Keychain. There's no account to make.

#### Buy in your browser

Checkout runs on Stripe's page in your browser. The app only opens the link.

Read the privacy policy or what Input Monitoring lets an app see.

### Small, native and light on your Mac

#### About 16 MB

That's the whole app, all 15 packs included. Native Swift, no Electron.

#### A 5 ms audio buffer

A C audio core holds every take in memory with an audio buffer of about 5 ms, so a key press only starts a sound.

#### Every key its own

Each key keeps its own take and pitch, like a real board, so fast typing doesn't sound like one sample on repeat.

#### Stereo by position

Q sits a little left and P a little right, like the keyboard in front of you. One checkbox turns it off.

#### Key-up sounds

Real keys sound on the way back up too. On the keyboard packs, Keyslam plays a recorded release, quieter after a soft press. The typewriter packs have no key-up sound.

#### Rests when you do

After 3 minutes without typing, the audio and the motion sensor switch off until your next key press.

#### Bring your own pack

Drop WAV, AIFF or FLAC recordings with a small pack.json into the Packs folder from the menu bar.

#### Open at login

Tick one box and the sounds are there after every restart, from the menu bar.

### Questions people ask first

Does the Keyslam app connect to the internet?
No. The app makes no network connections at all. Your license key is Ed25519-signed and checked offline on your Mac, and the trial start date lives in your Mac's Keychain. You only go online in your browser, to download Keyslam or to pay on Stripe's checkout page.

Is Keyslam a native Mac app?
Yes. It's written in Swift with a C real-time audio core, not Electron or a web wrapper. The whole app, with all 15 packs, is about 16 MB, the audio buffer is about 5 ms, and after 3 idle minutes it switches its audio and the motion sensor off.

Which apps does Keyslam play sounds in?
Any app you type in. It listens to the keyboard system-wide, with the Input Monitoring permission, instead of inside one app. Password fields are the exception: macOS hides those keystrokes from all apps, so nothing plays there.

Can I try Keyslam before I buy it?
Yes. The Mac app is free for 7 days with everything unlocked, and the board on this page plays the same 15 recordings in your browser.

### Mechanical keyboard sound effects on every keystroke

A good keyboard sound effect has to keep up with fast typing and never sound like the same sample on a loop. Here is what Keyslam does in the few milliseconds after you press a key:

- macOS reports the key. With the Input Monitoring permission, Keyslam learns only which key went down. It can't change or block what you type, and it never stores or sends it.

- It picks that key's take. Letters use one set of takes; on the keyboard packs, Space, Return and Delete share a separate set of darker, longer-ringing strikes. Every key keeps its own take and pitch, the way each key on a real board sounds slightly different.

- It picks the strength. On MacBooks with the motion sensor, Keyslam reads the accelerometer about 800 times a second, compares the jolt with how you usually type, and blends real strikes from the soft to slam bands. On other Macs you pick the strength.

- It places and plays the sound left or right by key position, through a C audio core with an audio buffer of about 5 ms, on your speakers or headphones.

- The key comes back up and the board's key-up sound plays; with force sensing on, it's softer after a soft press.

Read how the strength step works on keyboard sounds that react to how hard you type.
If you're after audio files for a video rather than live sound, see free keyboard typing sound effects to download.

### Mechanical keyboard sounds on Mac: questions

Is there a clicky keyboard sound app for Mac?
Yes. Keyslam is a clicky keyboard sound app for Mac when you pick the MX Blue board: every press plays a real Cherry MX Blue click, and the key-up click plays as the key returns. For the buckling-spring click of an IBM-style board, pick Unicomp or Model F. Pick MX Brown or Topre if you want the mechanical sound without the click.

Is it just a fake mechanical keyboard sound?
It's a fake mechanical keyboard sound in one sense: your keyboard stays the same, and the sound comes from your speakers or headphones. But nothing is synthesized. Each of the 15 boards is cut from a real recording of that keyboard or typewriter, credited to the person who made it.

How do I get mechanical keyboard sounds on my Mac?
Install Keyslam (step-by-step in how to make your MacBook sound like a mechanical keyboard), allow Input Monitoring when macOS asks, and pick a board from the menu bar. Every key you press then plays that board, in any app, until you switch it off from the same menu.

Can I use it with headphones or AirPods?
Yes. Sound follows your current output, including when you switch to headphones or AirPods. With headphones on, people on a call usually won't hear it. Bluetooth adds its own lag: why AirPods sound late, and how to test it.

Will it slow down my Mac?
It's built to stay light. Every recording is already in memory, so a key press only starts a sound, and the audio and motion sensor switch off after 3 minutes without typing. In our self-test on an M5 Pro MacBook Pro, the audio engine, key tap, one loaded pack and the motion sensor together peaked at about 11 MB of memory. The app is about 16 MB installed.

### Real recordings, not synthesized

Nothing here is generated. Each board is cut from one real typing recording that its author released as CC0 (public domain) on Freesound;
the typewriters add a second CC0 recording for the bell on Return.
Keyslam finds every strike, pairs it with its key-up where the recording has one, and sorts the strikes by natural loudness into four bands:
soft (about the 8th to 30th percentile), medium (38th to 62nd), hard (70th to 88th) and slam, the hardest ~8%. Each band is then leveled to a consistent target,
and every board to the same overall loudness (-28 LUFS on a standard typing passage), so switching boards doesn't jump in volume. The table shows what that left for each key group.

- Board | Recording | Regular keys (soft / medium / hard / slam) | Space, Return, Delete | Key-up sounds | Return |
- MX Blue | Mechanical Keyboard 'Cherry Blue Switches' by EricsSoundschmiede | 6 / 6 / 6 / 6 | Their own set, shared by all three (16 takes across the bands) | 6 takes | Same takes as Space and Delete |
- MX Brown | Mechanical Keyboard Cherry MX Brown by majod | 6 / 6 / 6 / 6 | Their own set, shared by all three (14 takes across the bands) | 4 takes | Same takes as Space and Delete |
- MX Red | Keyboard clicking typing Cherry Red Mechanical by handygaber | 6 / 6 / 6 / 6 | Their own set, shared by all three (16 takes across the bands) | 6 takes | Same takes as Space and Delete |
- MX Black | leopold fc980m pd cherry mx black.flac by ujonathan | 6 / 6 / 6 / 6 | Their own set, shared by all three (15 takes across the bands) | 4 takes | Same takes as Space and Delete |
- Gateron Red | Typing on a mechanical keyboard by IRF1010N | 6 / 6 / 6 / 6 | Their own set, shared by all three (12 takes across the bands) | 6 takes | Same takes as Space and Delete |
- Topre | Keyboard Typing 2 (HHKB, Topre) by grcekh | 6 / 6 / 6 / 6 | Their own set, shared by all three (3 takes across the bands) | 3 takes | Same takes as Space and Delete |

Counted from the sound files this page loads, November 2, 2026. A count of 1 means the band had one usable strike. When a band is empty, this page borrows the nearest band and adjusts its level.

### How the simulator works, and its limits

- Same takes as the Mac app. The browser loads each board as one losslessly compressed file of the same strikes the app plays, then cuts them apart in memory.

- You choose the strength here. Natural varies each press a little around medium, the way ordinary typing does, with Space and Return landing a bit harder. In the app, MacBooks with Apple's motion sensor pick the strength from how hard you actually hit, read about 800 times a second.

- Each key keeps its own take and a small fixed pitch offset, so a fast run of letters doesn't sound like one sample on repeat. Keys on the left sit slightly left in stereo, keys on the right slightly right.

- Browser audio adds delay that depends on your browser and device. The Keyslam keyboard sound app for Mac uses a C audio core with an audio buffer of about 5 ms.

- Only this tab hears you. Shortcuts with Cmd or Ctrl don't play here, and macOS usually keeps some keys, like Fn and the media keys, to itself.

- Phones often don't say which key you pressed, so the type box plays a sound for each character instead.

- Nothing leaves your device. The sounds play in your browser; what you type here isn't sent anywhere.

More on where the recordings come from and how the packs are built is on the Keyslam about page.

### Keyboard simulator questions

Is the keyboard simulator free?
Yes. It runs in your browser with no account, no download and no time limit.

Can I use this as a keyboard tester?
Partly. When the browser receives a key that is on the on-screen layout, that key lights up and stays outlined, so it is a quick way to check that the main keys on a keyboard register. The layout has no Esc or function row. It can't measure rollover, ghosting or key chatter, and keys macOS handles itself (Fn, brightness, media keys, Touch ID) usually don't reach a web page. Use a dedicated hardware tester for those.

Can I share a board and strength with someone?
Yes. Pick a board and a strength, then press Copy a link to this sound. The link adds the board and strength to the address, for example ?board=selectric&strength=hard, and opens the simulator with that sound selected.

How close is the browser simulator to the Mac app?
It plays the same recorded strikes and key-up sounds, and each key keeps its own take, as in the app. The differences: here you choose the strength, browser audio adds some delay, and sounds only play in this tab. The Keyslam app plays them for every key you press in any app on your Mac, and on supported MacBooks it reads how hard you type.

Does the on-screen keyboard work on a phone or tablet?
Yes. Tap keys on the on-screen keyboard, or tap the type box and use your phone's own keyboard. Several fingers at once work too.

# Keyboard Sound Test: A/B 15 Real Boards, Measured

## Keyboard sound test: compare 15 real switches and typewriters

Play two boards back to back with the same phrase, the same rhythm and matched loudness, then try a blind round. Below that: measured loudness and brightness for every board, quietest to loudest.
Start the A/B test ↓Get Keyslam for Mac
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: at medium strength the 15 boards measure within 2.2 LU of each other (-28.7 to -26.5 LUFS), because every pack is leveled to the same loudness. The differences show when you hit hard: Topre and Unicomp stay the quietest at slam (-23.1 and -22.9 LUFS), and Vintage Technics and Olivetti get the loudest (-20.5 and -20.0 LUFS). Use headphones and the A/B player below to hear the rest: the click, the thock and how long each key rings.

- | Typewriter | -27.8 | -8.0 | -20.0 | 13.3 |

Measured by us on November 2, 2026 from the sound files this page plays, at 100% volume. LUFS is perceived loudness (closer to zero is louder);
dBTP is the highest true peak; LU is the gap in loudness between the soft and slam bands. Method below.

### What makes each board sound different

Laptop, Rainy 75 and Topre keep the most energy below 200 Hz, the low thump people call thock. Olivetti, Unicomp and Model F keep the most above 2 kHz, where clicks and typewriter strikes live.

- Board | Below 200 Hz | Above 2 kHz | Brightness (centroid) | In a sentence |
- | 90% | 2% | 253 Hz | A 2018 MacBook Pro's butterfly keys, close-miked: soft and subtle. |
- | 90% | 4% | 264 Hz | A Rainy 75 keyboard (switches unstated): a dark, creamy thock. |
- | 33% | 6% | 803 Hz | Cherry MX Brown switches: a soft bump and a muted clack. |
- | 67% | 11% | 819 Hz | A Happy Hacking Keyboard with Topre switches: deep, rounded thock. |
- | 21% | 9% | 1,152 Hz | An old Technics board with waxed Gateron Yellows: chunky and old-school. |
- | 6% | 20% | 1,238 Hz | Gateron Red switches on a GMMK TKL: dark, smooth and a little hollow. |
- | 33% | 16% | 1,338 Hz | Cherry MX Black switches on a Leopold FC980M PD: heavy, smooth and full-bodied. |
- | 55% | 29% | 1,474 Hz | Leopold FC660M, MX Browns and PBT caps, close-miked: crisp and detailed. |
- | 26% | 25% | 1,492 Hz | A WhiteFox board with Hako Violet switches: punchy, with a long ring. |
- | 13% | 28% | 1,650 Hz | Cherry MX Red switches on a Corsair K95: smooth, light and quick. |
- | 20% | 46% | 1,876 Hz | Cherry MX Blue switches: a crisp click on every press. |
- | 22% | 50% | 2,704 Hz | An early-1980s IBM Model F XT: buckling springs with a loud, deep clack. |
- | 5% | 32% | 3,447 Hz | IBM Selectric II: the electric typeball strike, with a bell on Return. |
- | 8% | 61% | 3,507 Hz | A Unicomp buckling-spring keyboard, the Model M design: a big, springy click-clack. |
- | 5% | 82% | 5,017 Hz | Olivetti Lettera 22: a manual portable's snappy typebars and a bell. |

Sorted from deepest to brightest. Shares are of each strike's energy, and brightness is its spectral centroid: the higher the number, the brighter the strike. Each board's own page lists its decay and peak range.
For the vocabulary, see thocky vs clacky, explained.

### Membrane / laptop vs mechanical keyboard sound test

Most people asking this want to know what they'd gain by moving from a flat laptop or membrane keyboard to a mechanical one.
The closest thing to a membrane board here is the Laptop pack: a 2018 MacBook Pro butterfly keyboard, close-miked, with short travel, thin caps and no mechanical switch.
The mechanical side is a Cherry MX Brown, a tactile switch with no click, which keeps the comparison about the switch and not about a loud click jacket.

The numbers agree with your ears. The laptop strike keeps 90% of its energy below 200 Hz and 2% above 2 kHz; the MX Brown keeps 33% and 6%. At slam the laptop measures -20.8 LUFS and the MX Brown -21.6 LUFS, so what you hear between them is mostly character, not volume.
Listen for three things: the laptop has a short, dull tap with almost no top end; the MX Brown adds a plastic clack as the cap bottoms out;
and the MX Brown rings a little longer. To hear the laptop recording key by key, open the MacBook keyboard sound test.

### How to run a fair switch sound test

- Use headphones and set the volume once. Changing it between boards makes the louder one sound "better".

- Keep the strength the same. The A/B player locks it. The Play buttons in the tables vary each press a little, like normal typing, so use the A/B player for a strict comparison.

- Listen for one thing at a time: the click before bottom-out (only clicky switches have it), the pitch of the bottom-out, the ring after the key, and the sound on the way back up.

- Go blind. Pick two close boards, like two tactile ones, and play X ten times. If you score around 5 of 10, you probably can't hear a difference, and that's useful to know before you buy a keyboard.

### How we measured

On November 2, 2026 we rendered the same 40-key passage from each board's soft, medium, hard and slam strikes: the letters of “the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog”, repeated to 40 keys,
one every 150 ms (about 80 words per minute) with its key-up 80 ms later, at 100% volume, the way this page plays them, minus its small random variations. Each passage was read with ffmpeg's EBU R128 meter for integrated loudness and true peak.
The frequency numbers come from the first 85 ms of every medium and hard strike, median across strikes. All 15 boards were measured the same way on the same day.

The packs in the Keyslam keyboard sound app for Mac are cut from one real typing recording each (the typewriters add a bell recording for Return). Keyslam sorts the strikes by natural loudness into soft, medium, hard and slam (the hardest ~8%)
and levels each band, and every pack's standard typing passage is leveled to the same loudness (-28 LUFS). That is why the medium column is so even.
More on the recordings is on the Keyslam about page.

### Keyboard sound test questions

Which keyboard sound is the quietest?
At medium strength the 15 boards measure within 2.2 LU of each other (-28.7 to -26.5 LUFS), because every pack is leveled to the same loudness. The differences show when you hit hard: Topre and Unicomp stay the quietest at slam (-23.1 and -22.9 LUFS), and Vintage Technics and Olivetti get the loudest (-20.5 and -20.0 LUFS).

Why are the boards matched at medium but not at slam?
Because the leveling targets medium. Keyslam sets every pack so a standard medium-strength typing passage measures -28 LUFS, which is why the medium column sits within 2.2 LU. Within each band, every take is moved most of the way, not all the way, toward the band's level target, so part of each recording's natural spread survives, and that spread shows in the slam column. At medium, this is a test of character: click, thock, ring and the key-up sound.

What do LUFS, LU and dBTP mean?
LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale) measures perceived loudness, with numbers closer to zero being louder. A difference of 1 LU equals 1 dB. dBTP is the true peak, the highest point of the waveform, where 0 is the top before clipping.

Is a laptop keyboard sound test useful if I already own a MacBook?
Yes. The Laptop pack is a recording of a real 2018 MacBook Pro butterfly keyboard, so it shows what a gentle "just confirm the press" sound is like next to a mechanical board, at the same loudness.

### MacBook questions

Why doesn't my MacBook keyboard click?
MacBook keys are built to be quiet: short travel and no click mechanism in the switch, so most of what you hear is a soft tap. Keyslam adds a real recorded click, clack or thock through your speakers or headphones. For what macOS itself offers (and doesn't), see how to turn Mac keyboard click sounds on or off.

Does Keyslam work on a MacBook Air?
Yes, on every MacBook Air that runs macOS 13 Ventura or later. On MacBook Air models with M2, M3, M4 or M5 it also feels how hard you type. The M1 MacBook Air (2020) has no motion sensor, so you pick the strength; see keyboard sounds on the M1 MacBook Air and Intel Macs.

Does force sensing still work with my MacBook on my lap?
It's designed to. Keyslam judges each keystroke against your own recent typing, the median of your last 96 felt keystrokes, so it re-learns what “medium” means when you move from a desk to your lap or a sofa. Give it about a hundred keystrokes to settle.

Which pack sounds most like a MacBook keyboard?
The Laptop pack. It is cut from a close-miked recording of a 2018 MacBook Pro's butterfly keyboard, so it sounds like a MacBook. Newer MacBooks use scissor keys, so it may not match yours exactly. Hear the MacBook keyboard sound test.

# Typewriter Sound for Mac: Real Selectric and Olivetti Keys

Typewriter sounds for Mac
## Typewriter sounds for your Mac keyboard

Two real typewriters, cut strike by strike from CC0 recordings: an IBM Selectric II electric and an Olivetti Lettera 22 manual portable. Keyslam plays them on every key you press, in all your apps, and Return rings the bell.

Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: yes, you can make your Mac keyboard sound like a typewriter. Keyslam is a typewriter keyboard app for Mac: choose its Selectric or Olivetti pack in the menu bar and every key you press plays a real typewriter strike, in any app, from Pages to your browser. Return plays a bell. On MacBooks with Apple's motion sensor, harder presses play harder strikes. Keyslam costs $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial.

### Type a line, then press Return

Pick a machine and type in the box. Press Return at the end of a line to hear the bell.

Type here

### The two machines, side by side

- | IBM Selectric II | Olivetti Lettera 22 |
- Kind | Electric office typewriter | Manual portable typewriter |
- Introduced | 1971 (the first Selectric was 1961) | 1950 |
- How a key strikes | A motor rotates and tilts a golf-ball-sized typeball into the paper | Your finger swings a typebar into the platen |
- What that means for the sound | The motor sets the force, so strikes vary less than on a manual | Strikes follow your finger, so they vary a lot |
- Main recording | “Typewriter, IBM Selectric II” by secretmojo | “typewriter-olivetti-lettra-22.wav” by keithpeter |
- Return sound | A separate CC0 recording of an antique typewriter's bell and carriage return: “Typewriter bell & carriage reset” by knufds (2.5 s) | A separate CC0 recording of a typewriter bell: “Typewriter ding_near_mono.wav” by _stubb (1.0 s) |
- Takes in the pack | 20 | 25 |
- Strikes per band (soft · medium · hard · slam) | 6 · 1 · 6 · 6 | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 |
- Key-up sounds | None: every hit in the recording is treated as a press | None: every hit in the recording is treated as a press |
- Soft to slam (measured) | 12.4 dB | 14.3 dB |

Recordings: the Freesound pages linked above, all CC0. Soft to slam is the median level of each strike's first 40 ms, slam band minus soft band, measured November 2, 2026. The Selectric recording gave only one clean strike in its medium band, so medium presses blend it with the soft and hard strikes around it.

### How the bell and Return work

On a real typewriter the margin bell rings a few characters before the end of the line, as a warning, and then you throw the carriage return. A Mac has no margin, so Keyslam rings on Return (and the keypad Enter key), the moment a line actually ends.

- Selectric: Return plays 2.5 s of an antique typewriter's bell and carriage return, from “Typewriter bell & carriage reset” by knufds. The Selectric in the main recording had a broken bell.

- Olivetti: Return plays a bell, 1.0 s long, from “Typewriter ding_near_mono.wav” by _stubb.

- Every Return rings. It's the same bell recording each time; pressing harder plays it louder, not differently. There's no setting to ring it after a set number of characters.

- Space and Delete use the same strikes as the letter keys.

- No key-up sounds. A typewriter key makes its noise on the way down, so both packs stay silent when you let go.

### Selectric or Olivetti?

Pick the Selectric if you want an office electric. The motor does the striking, so its strikes vary less than the Olivetti's, and Return plays a bell followed by a carriage return.

Pick the Olivetti if you want the feel of a manual. Its strikes vary the most: the slam band plays 14.3 dB above the soft band, the widest range of the boards we measured. On a MacBook with the motion sensor, a light tap and a hard hit sound like two different keystrokes.

### Typewriter sounds while you type, in any app

A typewriter sound effect file plays once. A typewriter app plays a strike for every key you press. Keyslam does that system-wide: in Pages, Word, Google Docs, Notes, Mail, a code editor or a chat window. It's how to make your keyboard sound like a typewriter without touching the keyboard.

- Install Keyslam from the download page, and open it from the menu bar.
- Allow Input Monitoring in System Settings › Privacy & Security. Keyslam only uses which key went down; it never stores or sends what you type.
- Choose Selectric or Olivetti in the Sound grid.
- Set the strength. On MacBooks with the motion sensor, keep “Feel how hard you type” on. On other Macs, pick Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam.
- Type. Press Return at the end of a line for the bell.

The two typewriters come with every other board in Keyslam, a keyboard sound app for Mac that runs on macOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel. It makes no network connections and plays through your speakers or headphones.

### Other ways to get a typewriter sound

- In your browser, free: both machines are in our online typewriter and keyboard simulator, no download.

- As files for video editing: see keyboard and typewriter sound effects.

- Other Mac apps: prices and features of the other apps we checked are in keyboard sound apps for Mac, compared.

- For recordings and streams: ASMR keyboard and typewriter sounds.
- A vintage computer keyboard instead: the Model F pack is an early-1980s IBM Model F XT, a buckling-spring keyboard from the company behind the Selectric.

### Why writers like it

Many writers find that the strike, strike, ding of a typewriter makes progress audible, the way it did on paper. With headphones on, nobody else has to hear the draft being written.

### Typewriter sounds: questions

Can I make my Mac keyboard sound like a typewriter?
Yes. Choose Selectric or Olivetti in Keyslam and every key you press plays a real typewriter strike in any app, with a bell on Return. It works with the built-in keyboard and with external keyboards.

Does the typewriter bell ring at the end of every line?
It rings every time you press Return, because that's where a line ends on a Mac. Unlike a real margin bell, it doesn't count characters or warn you before the margin.

Do the typewriter keys make a sound when I let go?
No. A typewriter's noise is the strike on the way down, so the Selectric and Olivetti packs have no key-up sounds. The keyboard packs do.

Does it work in Pages, Word and Google Docs?
Yes. Keyslam plays on every key you press, whichever app is in front. macOS keeps password fields private, so those stay silent.

# Keyboard Sounds That React to How Hard You Type | Keyslam
URL: https://keyslam.com/force-sensing/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Force sensing
## Keyboard sounds that react to how hard you type

Keyslam uses the motion sensor hidden inside newer MacBooks to feel each keystroke, then plays a real soft, medium, hard or slam strike to match. Velocity-sensitive keyboard sounds, without any extra hardware.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: on Apple silicon MacBooks with the built-in motion sensor, Keyslam, the keyboard sound app for Mac, reads the accelerometer about 800 times a second,
compares each keystroke's jolt with how you usually type, and plays real strikes from one of four strength bands (soft, medium, hard or slam), blending
the two nearest. The bands are real strikes from one typing recording, sorted by how loud they naturally were. A light tap plays a light strike; a hard hit plays a hard one.

It works on MacBook Pro models with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, and MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models with M2 and later. We test it on a 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro; the other models are based on public hardware information.
See which MacBooks have the accelerometer, model by model.

### Hear how the bands blend

Drag the impact slider and press Strike. The curves show how much of each band plays at each strength. Between two band centers, Keyslam crossfades
the two nearest bands with an equal-power curve, so the sound changes smoothly instead of jumping.

The scale is your typical keystroke, which the app learns as you type. 1× is how you usually type; slam sits at about 4× that jolt.

Impact

1.0× a typical keystroke · Medium 100%

### One key, six strengths

Pick a board, then press each strength. The page uses the same band centers and blend as the Mac app; on a MacBook the app chooses the strength from the sensor instead.

### What happens in the 16 ms after you press a key

The sound never waits for the sensor. It starts the moment macOS reports the key, then Keyslam keeps measuring and adjusts the sound that is already playing.
You hear one keystroke, not two.

- Time from key-down | What Keyslam does |
- −12 ms | The window it searches for the keystroke's jolt opens a little before the key event, in case the jolt arrives first. |
- 0 ms | macOS reports the key and the sound starts at once. If the jolt is already in the buffer and at least 0.6× your typical keystroke, it starts at that strength. Otherwise it starts at your typical strength. |
- +4 ms | First re-measure. The playing sound crossfades toward the band that matches the jolt so far. |
- +10 ms | Second re-measure and crossfade. |
- +14 ms | The search window closes. |
- +16 ms | Final measurement. The strength is fixed and, if the sensor felt the keystroke, it is added to your calibration. |

### Velocity-sensitive keyboard sounds: a different strike, not only a louder one

On a real keyboard, a hard press usually doesn't just get louder; the strike itself sounds different. Turning one sample up only changes its volume.
So Keyslam changes which strike plays. A soft-band take is a strike that really was soft when it was recorded. A slam-band take is one
of the hardest strikes in the recording, so it keeps whatever character that harder hit had.

Levels are adjusted too, and it's fair to say so. Each band is leveled toward its own target, and slam's target is twice the level of medium. Keystrokes lighter than the
soft band's center (0.4×) play quieter, down to 0.45×, and keystrokes past slam's center (4×) play up to 1.25× louder.

### How the four strength bands are made

- One real recording. Each pack starts as one recording of someone typing on a real keyboard or typewriter, released as CC0 on Freesound. The typewriter packs add a separate bell recording for Return.

- Every strike is found. The slicer detects each keystroke, pairs it with the quieter key-up that follows, and sets the darkest, longest-ringing strikes (up to about 14% on keyboards) aside for Space, Return and Delete.

- Bad takes are dropped. Clipped strikes, and strikes that overlap the previous key's ring, are thrown out.

- Strikes are sorted by natural loudness into the four bands below, with gaps between them so neighboring bands stay distinct. The quietest 8% aren't used.

- Each band is leveled. Every take moves 70% of the way (in decibels) toward its band's target, so some of its natural variation stays.

- Band | Strikes it uses (by natural loudness) | Leveling target | Plays when the jolt is about |
- Soft | 8th to 30th percentile | 0.55× medium | 0.4× your typical keystroke |
- Medium | 38th to 62nd percentile | 1× (the reference) | 1×, how you usually type |
- Hard | 70th to 88th percentile | 1.45× medium | 2.2× |
- Slam | 92nd to 100th percentile (the hardest ~8%) | 2.0× medium | 4× |

Slam is the hardest ~8% of strikes in that same recording; there is no separate session for it. Each pack keeps up to 6 takes per band for regular keys
and up to 4 for Space, Return and Delete, plus separate key-up sounds on the keyboards that have them. All 15 built-in packs are made this way.

### Calibration: what "medium" means for you

Keyslam starts with a typical keystroke of 0.02 g. Once it has felt 12 keystrokes it switches to the median jolt of your last 96, kept between a quarter and four times
that default. Move from a desk to your lap and the reference follows within about a hundred keystrokes. Because the limits are fixed, a real slam still takes a real hit.

### The signal chain

- Sensor: the undocumented accelerometer inside the MacBook case, run by the chip's Sensor Processing Unit and read through IOKit HID (AppleSPUHIDDevice, vendor usage page 0xFF00, usage 3).

- Rate: Keyslam asks for a reading every millisecond and receives about 800 a second, only while sounds and force sensing are on.

- Filter: a high-pass filter with a time constant of about 25 ms removes gravity and slow tilting, so only the sharp jolt of a keystroke counts.

- Background: the app tracks the desk's background vibration from quiet moments, and a keystroke must stand 3 times above it.

- Memory: the last 4,096 readings, about 5 seconds, are kept in memory to time each keystroke. Nothing is written to disk or sent anywhere; the app makes no network connections.

- Permissions: no root, admin password, driver or kernel extension. Keyslam asks for one permission, Input Monitoring, for the key presses.

- Power: the sensor and the audio device switch off after 3 minutes without typing, or when you switch sounds off.

### Other apps that react to typing force

Keyslam isn't the only one. Haptyk ($8 one-time, 3-day trial) also reads the MacBook accelerometer, and TapNoise advertises soft and hard responses (both checked November 2, 2026).
If you already use one of them and like it, force sensing alone isn't a reason to switch. Keyslam's case is the price ($3.99 once), the
7-day trial with no account, and real strikes sorted from named, credited recordings. The details, with sources, are on
Keyslam as a Haptyk alternative and Keyslam as a TapNoise alternative.
See every Mac keyboard sound app compared, with prices and sources.

### Force sensing: questions

Why can keyboard sounds sound repetitive?
When the same short sample plays for every press, you hear the repeat. Real typing doesn't repeat exactly: each key sounds a little different, and no two presses land with the same force. Keyslam gives every key its own take and a fixed pitch offset of up to about 1.2%. With force sensing on, it also varies each press by up to 6% in level and 0.4% in pitch and changes which band of real strikes plays as your force changes. Without it, each press leans a little toward a neighboring band.

Can I adjust how hard a slam is?
Yes. With force sensing on, the menu bar has a Sensitivity slider that scales every measured jolt from about 0.35× to 2.8×. Slide it up and hard and slam come with less effort; slide it down and you have to hit harder to reach them.

Why does a light tap sometimes play at medium?
If the sensor can't feel a key, the app doesn't guess. A jolt has to be at least 3 times the background vibration, and at least 0.0015 g, to count. Feather-light taps and keys on an external keyboard fall below that, so they play at your typical strength and don't skew your calibration.

Can I turn force sensing off?
Yes. Switch off Feel how hard you type in the menu bar and pick Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam instead. Keyslam still gives each key its own take and blends each press a little toward the neighboring bands, so it doesn't repeat one sample.

Does force sensing work on Intel or desktop Macs?
No. It needs the motion sensor inside newer Apple silicon MacBooks. On Intel Macs, iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, the M1 MacBook Air and the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, every sound still works and you choose the strength. See keyboard sounds on Macs without the sensor.

- Olivetti | Typewriter | Olivetti Lettera 22 | keithpeter | 25 | |
Takes are the single keystrokes in each pack, counted from the app's own pack files. Each pack has its own page with the recording details, measurements and a sound test.

### Pick by sound

- Clicky: MX Blue, a crisp click on every press.
- Buckling springs: Unicomp, a big, springy click-clack from a Model M-style board; Model F, a loud, deep clack from capacitive buckling springs.
- Tactile: MX Brown, a soft bump and a muted clack; Leopold, close-miked, crisp and detailed; WhiteFox, punchy and even from soft to hard.
- Linear: MX Red, smooth, light and quick; MX Black, heavy, smooth and full-bodied; Gateron Red, dark and smooth, with a hollow note under each key; Vintage Technics, lubed Gateron Yellows, short and muted.
- Topre (electro-capacitive): Topre, a deep, rounded thock.
- Mechanical, switches not named: Rainy 75, a dark, even, creamy thock from an aluminum 75% board.
- Laptop: Laptop, a short, flat tap.
- Typewriters: Selectric, a steady electric strike, with a bell and carriage return on Return; Olivetti, snappy manual typebars, with a ding on Return.
Not sure? Play them all with the same phrase in the side-by-side keyboard sound test.

### How the packs are made

Nobody typed softly, then hard, then as hard as they could for these packs. Each one starts as a normal typing session, and the four strengths are sorted out of it afterwards. Keyslam's pack builder does this for every pack:

- Find every keystroke. It looks for sharp rises in a high-passed energy envelope, then pairs each press with the quieter key-up that follows 30–250 ms later.

- Set aside the wide keys. The darkest, longest-ringing presses of decent strength, up to about 14% of them, become Space, Return and Delete. Typewriters skip this step.

- Throw out the messy ones. Clipped hits, hits that start inside the previous key's ring and takes with a second keystroke in the tail are dropped.

- Sort by natural loudness. Soft is the 8th–30th percentile of strikes, medium the 38th–62nd, hard the 70th–88th and slam the hardest ~8%. The strikes between bands aren't used, which keeps the bands distinct.

- Pick the takes. Up to six per band for regular keys, four for wide keys and six key-ups, spread across each band. By default takes are capped at 230 ms (380 ms for wide keys, 120 ms for key-ups) and faded out.

- Level them. Each take moves 70% of the way, in dB, toward its band's target: soft 0.55×, medium 1×, hard 1.45× and slam 2× the medium level. Then the whole pack is set so a standard medium-strength typing passage measures −28 LUFS.

So the bands are real strikes from one recording, kept in order of their natural loudness, then pulled toward four set levels. The typewriters add a second recording for the bell on Return. In the app, each key keeps its own take and a fixed pitch offset of up to about 1.2%, so fast typing doesn't sound like one sample on repeat.

### Make your own pack

A Keyslam pack is a folder of audio files plus a pack.json that says which file plays for which key and strength. Put the folder in ~/Library/Application Support/Keyslam/Packs (choose Packs Folder… at the bottom of the Keyslam menu to open it), then open the menu again. Keyslam rescans the folder every time the menu opens.

- Start with recordings you're allowed to use. Your own keyboard, or CC0 recordings from Freesound.

- Cut one keystroke per file. Start each file just before the strike: the sound starts when the key goes down, so leading silence sounds like lag.

- Sort the strikes into soft, medium, hard and slam. The built-in packs use up to six takes per band for regular keys and up to four for Space, Return and Delete. One band is enough to start.

- Write pack.json next to the files, drop the folder into Packs and pick your pack from the menu.

{
"formatVersion": 1,
"id": "my-board",
"name": "My Board",
"kind": "Tactile",
"summary": "Hand-cut takes from my own keyboard.",
"author": "Your name",
"license": "CC0 1.0",
"groups": {
"alpha": {
"down": {
"soft": ["key-soft-1.wav", "key-soft-2.wav"],
"medium": ["key-medium-1.wav", "key-medium-2.wav"],
"hard": ["key-hard-1.wav", "key-hard-2.wav"],
"slam": ["key-slam-1.wav"]
},
"up": ["up-1.wav", "up-2.wav"]
},
"space": {
"down": { "medium": ["space-1.wav"], "hard": ["space-2.wav"] }
}
}
}

#### Fields

- Field | Required | What it does |
- formatVersion | Yes | Use 1. |
- id | Yes | A unique id. A pack you add with the same id as a built-in pack replaces it. |
- name | Yes | The name in the menu. |
- kind | Yes | The short label under the name, such as “Tactile”. |
- summary | No | The tooltip when you hover the pack in the menu. |
- author, license | No | Credit lines kept with the pack. The built-in packs name the Freesound recordist and link the CC0 source here. |
- groups | Yes | Key groups, each with “down” (bands to files) and an optional “up” list of key-up files. |

#### Key groups

- Group | Keys |
- alpha | Letters, numbers, punctuation, arrows, function keys and every key not listed below |
- space | Space bar |
- enter | Return and keypad Enter |
- backspace | Delete and Forward Delete |
- modifier | Shift, Control, Option, Command, Caps Lock, Tab and Fn |

#### Rules worth knowing

- Fallbacks. A group you leave out uses alpha. A band you leave out uses the nearest band you did provide, scaled 1.6× per step (about 4 dB), so soft still sounds softer. A group without “up” uses alpha's key-up sounds; if alpha has none either, those keys are silent on release.

- Files. WAV, AIFF or FLAC work best, and anything Core Audio can read loads, including CAF, M4A and MP3. Mono or stereo, any sample rate: Keyslam converts to 48 kHz stereo when it loads the pack.

- Paths. File names are relative to the pack folder. Subfolders are fine; names containing “..” or starting with “/” are rejected.

- Size. A pack can decode to at most 96 MB, about four minutes of 48 kHz stereo audio. Single keystrokes are tiny, so this only matters if you include long files.

- Consistent keys. Each key always picks the same position in a band's list, so bands with the same number of takes keep every key's character steady as strength changes.

- Loudness. Keyslam plays your files at the level you give them. To switch between your pack and the built-in ones without a jump, aim for about the same level as the built-in medium takes.

- Mechvibes packs (a config.json plus audio) don't load directly. Convert them by exporting each key's sound to its own file and listing the files in a pack.json.

### Sound pack questions

Can I import Mechvibes sound packs?
Not directly. Keyslam doesn't read Mechvibes' config.json. To bring a pack over, export each key's sound to its own file, list the files in a pack.json and check the pack's license first. For a wider look at the two apps, see how Keyslam compares with Mechvibes.

Where is the Keyslam Packs folder?
In ~/Library/Application Support/Keyslam/Packs. Choose Packs Folder… at the bottom of the menu to open it; Keyslam creates it if needed and rescans it each time you open the menu.

Why do all the built-in packs play at the same volume?
Each one is leveled so the same medium-strength typing passage, played through the real engine, measures −28 LUFS. Switching packs changes the tone, not the loudness. Packs you add play at the level of your files.

Can I share a pack I made?
Only if you have the rights to the recordings. CC0 recordings from Freesound are a safe start; put the recordist and source in the pack's author and license fields, the way the built-in packs do.

## Cherry MX Blue sound test

A Cherry keyboard with MX Blue switches, recorded by EricsSoundschmiede and released as CC0 on Freesound. Press a band below to hear the click from a light tap up to the hardest strikes in the session.

Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Cherry MX Blue sounds like a sharp, high click on every press, a lighter click as the key comes back up, and the plastic clack of the keycap bottoming out underneath. This page plays a real recording of a Cherry board with Blue switches, cut into 46 takes across four strength bands.

“You are hearing a Cherry Keyboard with Blue Switches. You also can use this as some sort of typewriter soundeffect.” — EricsSoundschmiede, on the Freesound page (checked November 2, 2026)

### How a Blue makes its click

Cherry, the German company behind the MX switch since the 1980s, makes the Blue as its clicky switch. Around the stem sits a separate plastic collar called the click jacket. About 2 mm into the 4 mm of travel, the jacket snaps down against the housing. That snap is the click, and it happens before the keycap reaches the bottom.

On the way up the jacket is pulled back into place, which makes a second, quieter click. So a Blue makes three sounds per keystroke: the click, the bottom-out and the return. The tactile peak is around 60 g, a little heavier than a Red or a Brown.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Cherry MX Blue pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 12.0 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 4 | −16.4 dBFS | 68 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −10.2 dBFS | 58 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 4 | −5.6 dBFS | 55 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 4 | −4.4 dBFS | 69 ms |

soft −16.4 dBFS peak · 68 ms
medium −10.2 dBFS peak · 58 ms
hard −5.6 dBFS peak · 55 ms
slam −4.4 dBFS peak · 69 msCherry MX Blue: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### What this recording adds

EricsSoundschmiede uploaded 2 minutes 21 seconds of steady typing in February 2017 as a 24-bit stereo WAV. The page names the switch and the maker but not the model, case or keycaps, so we don't either. The uploader's own note says it could double as a typewriter sound effect, which tells you how present the click is.

Keyslam kept 6 key-up takes from the session. They play when you let go of a key, a little softer after a soft press, so you hear the Blue's second click too. Regular keys have six takes per band, and the wider Space, Return and Delete keys have 4 of their own.

### MX Blue next to MX Brown and the Selectric

Two neighbours worth hearing back to back. Play each a few times; the numbers below come from the pack files.
- MX Brown: the same switch family without the click jacket. What's missing is the high click before the bottom-out.
- Selectric: a real office typewriter, for anyone who took the uploader's typewriter comment literally. It's heavier and has no key-up sound.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- MX Blue | Clicky | EricsSoundschmiede | 12.0 dB | 58 ms | |
- MX Brown | Tactile | majod | 11.1 dB | 75 ms | |
- Selectric | Typewriter | secretmojo | 12.6 dB | 99 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick MX Blue if you want to hear every keystroke land, or if you learned to type on a clicky board and miss it. The click is easy to hear under music.

Pick something else if you share a room or take calls on speakers. MX Brown keeps a tactile character without the click, and the Laptop pack is a short, soft tap.

### Cherry MX Blue: questions

Do MX Blues click on the way up too?
Usually, yes. The click jacket resets as the key returns, which makes a quieter second click. This pack keeps 6 key-up takes from the recording and plays one when you release a key.

Which Cherry keyboard is in this recording?
The uploader doesn't say. The Freesound page describes it only as “a Cherry Keyboard with Blue Switches”, so we don't name a model.

Does the click get louder when you press harder?
A little. The click happens at the same point whatever your force, but a hard press adds a louder bottom-out. In this pack the slam band peaks 12.0 dB above the soft band, the 10th widest of the 15 packs.

# Cherry MX Brown Sound Test: Hear Real Brown Switches

One minute of typing on Cherry MX Brown switches, recorded by majod and released as CC0. Hear it in four strength bands, then compare it with the same switch on a Leopold board.

Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Cherry MX Brown sounds like a rounded, mid-pitched clack with no click. The bump you feel makes almost no noise of its own; what you hear is the keycap bottoming out and springing back. This pack is cut from a CC0 recording by majod on Freesound, 42 takes in four strength bands.

### Cherry MX Brown sound test

Each button plays real strikes from one strength band of this recording. Natural mix lets every key vary, like normal typing. Headphones help.

### How a Brown makes its sound

The Brown is Cherry's tactile switch. The legs of its stem have a small bump that pushes past the metal contact leaf about 2 mm down, so you feel the moment the key registers. There is no click jacket, so that bump is nearly silent.

That leaves two sounds: the stem hitting the bottom of the housing and the stem returning to the top. The tactile peak is around 55 g. Many people treat Browns as the middle ground between a clicky Blue and a smooth Red, and they're a common pick for office and programming boards.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Cherry MX Brown pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 11.1 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 4 | −15.3 dBFS | 73 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −11.4 dBFS | 75 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 4 | −6.8 dBFS | 80 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 2 | −4.3 dBFS | 63 ms |

soft −15.3 dBFS peak · 73 ms
medium −11.4 dBFS peak · 75 ms
hard −6.8 dBFS peak · 80 ms
slam −4.3 dBFS peak · 63 msCherry MX Brown: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### What this recording adds

The file is a 16-bit, 48 kHz stereo FLAC from August 2017, just over a minute long. The uploader describes it in one line and doesn't name the keyboard or keycaps. Even so, a minute of steady typing gave the slicer enough clean strikes to fill every band with six regular-key takes, plus 2–4 takes per band for Space, Return and Delete.

The same switch appears in our Leopold pack, recorded on a different board with different keycaps and a microphone between the hands. Together they are a useful A/B of how much the keyboard, not the switch, shapes the sound.

### Same switch, two boards: MX Brown vs Leopold

Play these one after the other. The switch is the same in the first two; everything else differs.
- Leopold: a Leopold FC660M with MX Browns, close-miked from a wrist rest, with a mix of enjoyPBT and GMK keycaps. Brighter and more forward.
- MX Red: Cherry's linear switch. No bump at all, so the press is smoother and the sound is almost all bottom-out.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- MX Brown | Tactile | majod | 11.1 dB | 75 ms | |
- Leopold | Tactile | stu556 | 12.3 dB | 67 ms | |
- MX Red | Linear | handygaber | 12.7 dB | 78 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick MX Brown for writing, coding and office typing, or if Blues feel too sharp and Reds too plain.

Pick something else if you want more detail in each keystroke (Leopold) or a softer, deeper sound (Topre).

### Cherry MX Brown: questions

How quiet is the MX Brown pack next to MX Blue?
In Keyslam they play at the same loudness: every pack is leveled so a standard medium-strength typing passage measures −28 LUFS. The difference is tone. Brown has no high click, so it sounds less sharp at the same volume. Turn the volume down if you need it quieter.

Why does MX Brown sound different on the Leopold page?
Same switch, different keyboard, keycaps and microphone. The Leopold recording has enjoyPBT and GMK keycaps and a recorder on a wrist rest right in front of the space bar, and its uploader calls it the “more trebley” of their two takes.

Which keyboard and microphone were used for this MX Brown recording?
The uploader doesn't name either. The Freesound page is tagged “zoom” and “h1”, which suggests a Zoom H1 recorder, but that's a reading of the tags, not a stated fact. The switch is the one thing the description confirms.

Short answer: Cherry MX Red is a linear switch, so there is no click and no bump. You hear a smooth, light press, a low clack when the keycap bottoms out, and a quick tap as it springs back. This pack is cut from a CC0 recording of a Corsair K95 gaming keyboard with Red switches.

### Why a Red sounds the way it does

A Red has a straight-sided stem and a light spring, around 45 g, and it registers about 2 mm down. With no bump and no click jacket, almost all of its sound is the stem hitting the bottom of the housing and the top on the way back, plus whatever the case and plate add.

That's why linear switches are often described by their bottom-out: a clack on a hard plate, a duller thud on a softer one. Gamers like Reds because the press is light and feels the same all the way down.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Cherry MX Red pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 12.7 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 4 | −15.2 dBFS | 66 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −10.4 dBFS | 78 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 4 | −8.3 dBFS | 82 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 4 | −2.5 dBFS | 47 ms |

soft −15.2 dBFS peak · 66 ms
medium −10.4 dBFS peak · 78 ms
hard −8.3 dBFS peak · 82 ms
slam −2.5 dBFS peak · 47 msCherry MX Red: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### A gaming board, recorded in mono

The Corsair K95 is a full-size gaming keyboard. handygaber recorded it raw at 24-bit, 96 kHz, the highest sample rate of any source recording behind Keyslam's packs (the app's takes are all 48 kHz). The recording is mono, so all the left-to-right spread you hear in the app comes from Keyslam placing each key by its position on the keyboard (you can switch that off with Stereo by key position).

The session runs 1 minute 51 seconds. It gave six takes per band for regular keys, 4 per band for Space, Return and Delete, and 6 key-up takes, the full set the slicer aims for.

### MX Red vs Gateron Yellow and Topre

Two other smooth-feeling switches with very different sounds.
- Vintage Technics: another linear, with lubed, black-bottom Gateron Yellows in a vintage case. Its medium takes fall 30 dB below their peak in 49 ms, against 78 ms here.
- Topre: a rubber dome over a spring. The bump is soft and the bottom-out is cushioned, so it sounds lower and rounder.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- MX Red | Linear | handygaber | 12.7 dB | 78 ms | |
- Vintage Technics | Linear, modded | zrrion | 13.2 dB | 49 ms | |
- Topre | Electro-capacitive | grcekh | 9.4 dB | 63 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick MX Red if you type fast, game, or want a mechanical sound without a click or a scratchy bump.

Pick something else if you like feeling each key register (MX Brown) or want something warmer and more damped (Gateron Yellow).

### Cherry MX Red: questions

Is this recording from a gaming keyboard?
Yes, a Corsair K95 with Cherry MX Red switches, per the uploader. The original is a 24-bit, 96 kHz mono WAV, 1 minute 51 seconds long.

Why does MX Red sound stereo in Keyslam if the recording is mono?
Keyslam places each key left or right by where it sits on the keyboard, so Q sounds a little left and P a little right. Turn off Stereo by key position in the menu to hear it centered.

How does a red switch sound next to a Gateron Yellow?
Both are linear. The Yellows in our Vintage Technics pack are lubed and sit in an old case, and their takes decay faster: at medium strength they fall 30 dB below their peak in 49 ms, against 78 ms for this Red.

# Cherry MX Black Sound Test: Heavy Linear vs MX Red
URL: https://keyslam.com/sounds/mx-black/

Linear · sound test

Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Cherry MX Black is a heavy linear switch: no click, no bump, and a 60 cN spring where the MX Red has 45 cN. On this Leopold FC980M PD it sounds smooth and full-bodied, a solid bottom-out on every key, then a tap as the key comes back up. The pack is cut from ujonathan's CC0 recording on Freesound into 43 takes across four strength bands.

Each button plays real strikes from one strength band of this recording. Natural mix lets every key vary, like normal typing. Headphones help.

MicrophoneNot stated
LicenseCC0 1.0 (public domain)
In Keyslam43 takes, 4 of them key-up
“this is a recorder of the fantastic sound of my leopold fc980mpd with cherry mx black” — ujonathan, on the Freesound page (checked November 2, 2026)

### MX Black vs MX Red: same stem, heavier spring

Cherry lists the MX Black as a linear switch without a click: 60 cN of force at the point where the key registers, 2 mm into 4 mm of travel. The MX Red has the same stem, the same 2 mm and the same 4 mm, with a 45 cN spring. So on paper the two differ in the spring, while the stem and housing, whose impacts make most of the noise, are the same. In both, the stem strikes the floor of the housing at the bottom and snaps back against the top on release.

Choosing a heavy linear is about feel first. Sixty centinewtons makes it harder for resting fingers to press a key by accident, and it asks for a firmer stroke before the key bottoms out. Some typists like that resistance; others prefer a lighter spring for long sessions. For how linear, tactile and clicky switches differ by ear, see the three kinds of mechanical keyboard sound.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Cherry MX Black pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 14.5 dB. How the bands are made.

- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 4 | −16.9 dBFS | 91 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −12.0 dBFS | 76 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 4 | −7.7 dBFS | 81 ms |

### The Leopold FC980M PD

Leopold, which also made the FC660M in another Keyslam pack, builds the FC980M as a compact board that keeps its number pad: 98 keys, with the numpad pulled in against the arrow keys so the whole board is narrower than a full-size layout. In Leopold's model names, PD stands for PBT double-shot keycaps, thick caps with their legends moulded in from a second shot of plastic.

The uploader doesn't say whether this board still wears its original caps, or whether anything inside has been changed. So the about box lists keycaps as not stated, and this page treats the sound as one FC980M PD as recorded, not a reference for every MX Black board.

### 35 seconds of quick typing, in stereo

ujonathan uploaded the session in April 2022 as a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz stereo FLAC and called it “the fantastic sound” of their FC980M PD. The page is tagged mechanical-keyboard, field-recording and soundcheck, and carries a map pin in Montefalcone Appennino, Italy. No microphone is named.

The typing is quick, with the strokes close together. The slicer keeps only presses whose tails are free of the next keystroke, and the session still filled every regular-key band with six takes. Space, Return and Delete have 3–4 per band, and four key-up takes play on release. The slam band is a take short, since a recording this brief holds only so many of the dark, long-ringing strikes the builder reads as wide keys. From soft to slam the peaks rise 14.5 dB, the 3rd widest of the 15 packs. The MX Red pack spans 12.7 dB, so this one leaves more room between a light touch and a hard one.

### MX Black next to MX Red and MX Brown

MX Black's lighter linear sibling, and a tactile pack that measures close to it in our spectrum comparisons.
- MX Red: the same Cherry stem and travel with a 45 cN spring, in a Corsair K95 recorded raw in mono. Play both and listen for how much of the gap is the board, not the spring.
- MX Brown: a tactile switch, yet one of the packs nearest to MX Black in our spectrum comparisons. Its bump makes little noise of its own, which may be why the two measure closer than the names suggest.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- MX Black | Linear | ujonathan | 14.5 dB | 76 ms | |
- MX Red | Linear | handygaber | 12.7 dB | 78 ms | |
- MX Brown | Tactile | majod | 11.1 dB | 75 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick MX Black if you want a linear with weight behind it: no click, no bump, a full bottom-out on every key. Its soft-to-slam range is the 3rd widest of the 15 packs, which suits force sensing on a MacBook.

Pick something else if you'd rather have a lighter, quicker linear (MX Red), a bump under your fingers (MX Brown) or a softer, rounder landing (Topre).

### Cherry MX Black: questions

How heavy is a Cherry MX Black switch?
Cherry rates it at 60 cN where the key registers, 2 mm into 4 mm of travel; that's roughly 60 g. The MX Red needs 45 cN at the same point. Both are linear, with no bump and no click.

MX Black vs MX Red: what changes in the sound?
The two switches share their stem and travel, so the noise comes from the same two impacts: bottom-out and return. In Keyslam both packs also play at the same loudness. What separates these two packs is most likely the board and the recording: a Leopold FC980M PD recorded in stereo here, a Corsair K95 recorded in mono by someone else for the Red. From soft to slam this pack spans 14.5 dB and the Red pack 12.7 dB.

Is this the same Leopold as Keyslam's Leopold pack?
No. That pack is an FC660M, a compact 66-key board with MX Browns and a mix of enjoyPBT and GMK caps, from a different uploader. This one is an FC980M PD with MX Blacks. Same maker, different layout, switches and recording.

What does a heavy linear switch sound like?
Like any linear: a smooth stroke with no click or bump, then the bottom-out and the return. The heavier spring is mostly something you feel; the board, the keycaps and how hard you type shape most of the tone. On this Leopold it comes out smooth and full-bodied, and the medium takes stay within 30 dB of their peak for 76 ms.

# Gateron Red Sound Test (GMMK TKL) vs Cherry MX Red

On this GMMK TKL the bottom-out is dark and a little hollow, with a short, boxy note under every key that most likely comes from the case. The pack is cut from a CC0 recording by IRF1010N on Freesound into 42 takes across four strength bands.

### Gateron Red: the MX Red recipe from another maker

Gateron builds its Red to the same numbers Cherry uses for the MX Red: a straight-sided MX-style stem, roughly 45 g of force where the key registers, 2 mm of travel to that point and 4 mm to the bottom. There's no click jacket and no tactile leg, so the switch adds almost nothing of its own between the top and the bottom of the stroke.

That leaves two impacts per keystroke. The stem lands on the housing floor, then on release the spring throws it back against the top housing. Everything else you hear, the pitch, the body and any hollowness, is the keycap, the plate, the case, the room and the microphone. Builders often say Gateron linears feel smoother in travel than Cherry's; that's a feel, and no recording can show it. Our guide to clicky, tactile and linear sounds puts the Red family in context.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Gateron Red pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 14.0 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 2 | −17.9 dBFS | 66 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −11.2 dBFS | 79 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 4 | −6.9 dBFS | 63 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 2 | −3.8 dBFS | 59 ms |
