medium −11.2 dBFS peak · 79 ms
hard −6.9 dBFS peak · 63 ms
slam −3.8 dBFS peak · 59 msGateron Red: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### The GMMK TKL and its hollow note

The GMMK is Glorious's modular board: its sockets are hot-swappable, so switches pull out and push in without soldering. The TKL size drops the number pad and keeps the arrows and the navigation block. The uploader names the board, the switches and the microphone, and nothing else, so keycaps, plate and any mods stay unknown.

Listen under the bottom-out and you'll hear a short, pitched “tok”. When we measured this pack's regular-key takes, the energy near 320 Hz stood about 20 dB above the frequencies on either side, and it fades within the first few tens of milliseconds of each press, so it reads as hollow rather than ringing. The MX Red takes have no such peak. Because the two switches share a spec, the case and plate are the likely source, not the Red itself. Keyslam's only filter on these takes is a 45 Hz high-pass, so the note stays as recorded.

### 41 seconds through a USB mic

IRF1010N uploaded this in August 2021: a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz mono WAV, 41 seconds long. Keyslam starts cutting 2 seconds in. Being mono, it has no left or right of its own; the spread you hear in the app comes from Keyslam panning each key to match its place on the keyboard.

The gaps between strokes are close to silent, so the takes end cleanly. Every regular-key band holds six takes, and six key-up takes cover the release. Space, Return and Delete have 2–4 per band. The soft and slam ends have fewer: a session this short gives the builder only so many of the dark, long-ringing strikes it reads as wide keys, even with this pack's recipe letting it set aside up to 26% of presses for them (the default is 14%). From soft to slam the peaks climb 14.0 dB, the 4th widest of the 15 packs. That's more than the 12.7 dB of the MX Red pack, so light and heavy typing sit further apart here.

### Gateron Red vs Cherry MX Red and Gateron Yellow

Two linears to play against this one: Cherry's Red, built to the same spec, and Gateron's own Yellow.
- MX Red: Cherry's Red, the same nominal weight and travel, in a Corsair K95 recorded raw at 96 kHz. Brighter and plainer, with no boxy note under the press.
- Vintage Technics: Gateron's Yellow, the slightly heavier linear, here lubed and fitted with MX tops in an old Technics-branded board. At medium strength it is 30 dB down after 49 ms, where these Reds take 79 ms, so it stops sooner and sounds more muted.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- Gateron Red | Linear | IRF1010N | 14.0 dB | 79 ms | |
- MX Red | Linear | handygaber | 12.7 dB | 78 ms | |
- Vintage Technics | Linear, modded | zrrion | 13.2 dB | 49 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick Gateron Red if you like a darker linear with some body behind each press, and you don't mind hearing the case as well as the switch. Its soft-to-slam range is the 4th widest of the 15 packs, so on a MacBook with force sensing a light touch and a hard one sound clearly apart.

Pick something else if the hollow note bothers you: MX Red is the brighter, plainer linear, and the Gateron Yellows in Vintage Technics are shorter and more muted.

### Gateron Red: questions

Gateron Red vs Cherry MX Red: do they sound the same?
Not in these recordings. On paper the switches are close: both linear, about 45 g, 2 mm to actuation and 4 mm of travel. But these are different boards, recorded by different people, and the Gateron pack is darker, with a boxy note near 320 Hz that the Cherry pack doesn't have. From soft to slam the Gateron pack spans 14.0 dB and the Cherry pack 12.7 dB; at medium strength their takes stay within 30 dB of the peak for 79 ms and 78 ms.

What is the GMMK TKL in this recording?
The tenkeyless version of Glorious's GMMK: no number pad, and hot-swap sockets so the switches can be changed without soldering. The uploader names the board and the Gateron Red switches; keycaps, plate and mods aren't listed.

Why does this Gateron Red pack sound hollow?
Each press carries a short, pitched note in the low mids, near 320 Hz in our measurement of the takes. It fades within a few tens of milliseconds, which is why it sounds hollow rather than ringing. It's part of the recording, most likely from the board's case, and the pack keeps it.

What microphone was used?
The uploader lists a “TAWAPYZ USB Kit”, a USB microphone. The original is a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz mono WAV, 41 seconds long, uploaded in August 2021.

### How a Topre switch works

A Topre switch is a rubber dome with a conical spring inside it. There are no metal contacts: the board senses the spring compressing as a change in capacitance, which is why Topre is called electro-capacitive. The dome gives a rounded bump at the top of the press, and the rubber softens the landing at the bottom.

Topre Corporation in Japan makes the switches. They're best known from the HHKB, a compact 60-key layout with Control where most keyboards put Caps Lock, and from Topre's own Realforce boards. If you want to know why this counts as “thocky”, see what makes a keyboard sound thocky or clacky.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Topre (HHKB) pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 9.4 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 0 | −15.3 dBFS | 55 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 1 | −9.2 dBFS | 63 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 1 | −8.8 dBFS | 67 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 1 | −5.9 dBFS | 64 ms |

soft −15.3 dBFS peak · 55 ms
medium −9.2 dBFS peak · 63 ms
hard −8.8 dBFS peak · 67 ms
slam −5.9 dBFS peak · 64 msTopre (HHKB): the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### What this recording adds

grcekh typed 50-word tests on typings.gg for 3 minutes 17 seconds, with no post-production. The board is stock, so this is what an HHKB sounds like out of the box, picked up by a USB desk microphone rather than a studio setup. Space, Return and Delete have one take per band and no soft take: few of the strikes the slicer marked as wide keys passed its clean-take checks, so for soft those keys play the medium take turned down about 4 dB.

### Silenced vs unsilenced Topre

Silenced Topre boards exist too, such as PFU's HHKB Type-S and Topre's silent Realforce models, with dampened switches that are quieter again. The uploader lists a standard Professional Hybrid, not a Type-S, so this is the unsilenced Topre sound.

### Realforce sound

Realforce keyboards use the same Topre switch family, usually in larger cases and with other key weights. They sound closely related but not identical, because the case, plate and keycaps change the tone. Treat this pack as an HHKB, not a Realforce recording.

### Topre vs Cherry MX

Hear the rubber dome against two Cherry switches, then against a board from the same recordist.
- MX Red: the linear Cherry switch, with a harder bottom-out and nothing to cushion it.
- MX Brown: the tactile Cherry switch, with a bump like Topre's but felt through plastic, and a sharper clack.
- WhiteFox: recorded by grcekh too, with the same microphone and the same typing test, so the board is the main difference.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- Topre | Electro-capacitive | grcekh | 9.4 dB | 63 ms | |
- MX Red | Linear | handygaber | 12.7 dB | 78 ms | |
- MX Brown | Tactile | majod | 11.1 dB | 75 ms | |
- WhiteFox | Tactile | grcekh | 6.1 dB | 60 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick Topre for long writing sessions and anyone who wants a deep, soft sound instead of a click. It's also our first pick for slow ASMR keyboard sounds on a Mac.

Pick something else if you want a crisp, bright keystroke (MX Blue, Leopold) or the hard strike of a typewriter.

### Topre (HHKB): questions

Is the HHKB in this recording modded?
No. The uploader calls it an unmodded HHKB Professional Hybrid with 45 g Topre switches, typed with no post-production.

Is Topre quieter than Cherry MX?
Usually lower in pitch and softer at the bottom, though a heavy typist can be loud on either. In Keyslam every pack plays at the same loudness (−28 LUFS for a standard typing passage), so the difference you hear is tone, not volume.

Why do Space, Return and Delete have fewer takes here?
The slicer drops takes that are clipped, cut short by the next keystroke or have another sound in their tail, and few of this recording's wide-key strikes passed. Those keys have one take per band and none for soft; for soft they reuse the medium take about 4 dB quieter. Letters and modifiers have six takes per band.

### The board

Leopold is a South Korean keyboard maker known for plain, solidly built boards. The FC660M is a compact 66-key layout that keeps a dedicated arrow cluster, sold with Cherry MX switches. This one has MX Browns, Cherry's tactile switch.

The keycaps are a mix: enjoyPBT, a dye-sublimated PBT set, and GMK, which makes thick doubleshot ABS caps. Keycap material and thickness change the pitch of each keystroke, which is one reason this pack sounds different from our other MX Brown recording.

- MX Brown: the same Cherry MX Brown switch on an unnamed board, recorded from further away. Less attack, rounder.

### Who it suits

Pick Leopold if you like hearing the detail of each keystroke: the attack, the bump, the full clack of thick caps.

Pick something else if you want the switch a little further away (MX Brown) or a deeper, cushioned sound (Topre).

### Leopold FC660M: questions

Are the keycaps on this Leopold PBT?
Partly. The uploader lists “enjoypbt and gmk caps”, so it's a mix of PBT (enjoyPBT) and thick ABS (GMK) keycaps, not a pure PBT set.

Why is this called the treble version?
stu556 recorded two takes on the same keyboard and labeled this one the brighter of the two. It's the one Keyslam uses.

Leopold or MX Brown: which pack should I pick?
Same switch on different boards, keycaps and microphones. Leopold is close-miked and detailed; MX Brown is a little softer around the edges. Play both on this page before you choose.

This one ends with individual keys typed back to back. With the mic, typist and typing test the same, the biggest difference between the two packs is the keyboard.

From soft to slam this pack's peaks rise 6.1 dB, the narrowest of the 15 packs, so a light tap and a hard hit sit closer together than on most boards. Every band has six regular-key takes, 4 per band for the wide keys and 5 key-up takes.

- Topre: same recordist, mic and typing test, different board. Rubber domes against plastic tactiles.

Who makes Hako Violet switches?
Kailh, as part of the Hako line it made for Input Club. Input Club also sold the WhiteFox.

Less than most. Its slam band peaks 6.1 dB above its soft band, the narrowest of the 15 packs. On a MacBook with force sensing, you'll hear the change, but it's subtler than on the Laptop or Olivetti packs.

# Rainy 75 Sound Test: The Creamy Thock, Real Recording

Short answer: The Rainy 75 sounds like a dark, creamy thock: a low, rounded bottom-out with little high click or rattle, and very little change in character from key to key. This pack is a real Rainy 75 recorded by Techrul and released as CC0, cut into 42 takes in four strength bands. The uploader doesn't name the switches.

### Why a Rainy 75 thocks

The Rainy 75 comes from Wobkey. It's a 75% layout with 81 keys in a CNC-machined aluminum case, and Wobkey lists its weight at 1.8 to 2 kg. The plate is gasket-mounted: it sits between soft gaskets instead of being screwed to the case, so it can give a little under each keystroke. Wobkey sells Lite, Standard and Pro versions; the Pro has a different plate and different stock switches from the other two. Every version has hot-swap sockets, so owners can change switches without soldering.

Enthusiasts credit that kind of build for the sound people call thock. The usual explanation: a heavy metal case leaves less room for hollow ring, the gasket takes the sharp edge off the bottom-out, and what reaches your ears is mostly the low, rounded part of the keystroke. There's more on the vocabulary in thocky vs clacky keyboards.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Rainy 75 pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 12.4 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 4 | −13.2 dBFS | 64 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −7.8 dBFS | 73 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 3 | −4.8 dBFS | 53 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 2 | −0.8 dBFS | 44 ms |

medium −7.8 dBFS peak · 73 ms
hard −4.8 dBFS peak · 53 ms
slam −0.8 dBFS peak · 44 msRainy 75: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### What people mean by a creamy keyboard sound

“Creamy” is enthusiast shorthand, not a measurement. It describes a keystroke that sounds smooth and muted: a soft attack with no scratch, ping or rattle. People reach for it with well-damped boards of every kind, so on its own the word says nothing about which switches are inside.

Here it's the uploader's own word, in the recording's tags. In the app, medium-strength takes stay within 30 dB of their peak for 73 ms, the 7th shortest of the 15 packs, and from soft to slam the peaks rise 12.4 dB, the 8th widest of the 15 packs. Both sit in the middle of the lineup, so the thock isn't unusually short or unusually dynamic; what sets it apart is how dark and alike the strikes are.

### What this recording adds

Techrul posted 58 seconds of typing in July 2025, the newest recording behind any Keyslam pack, as a 48 kHz stereo MP3 with a one-line description and no microphone, keycap or switch details. The file is stereo, but in the takes the left and right channels match almost exactly. The left-right placement you hear in the app is Keyslam's own, set by where each key sits, and the Stereo by key position switch in the menu turns it off.

Every band of regular keys has six takes, Space, Return and Delete have 2–4 per band, and there are 5 key-up takes. The strikes in this recording resemble each other more than in most of the sessions behind Keyslam's packs, and every take is still a different strike, so you hear an even, steady thock rather than a mix of different-sounding keys. Try the Space bar button too: those takes have a small second tick just after the hit, most likely the stabilizer.

### Rainy 75 vs MX Brown and the MacBook keyboard

No pack in the lineup is a close match; these two come nearest in our spectrum measurements. Play each one right after the Rainy 75.
- MX Brown: Cherry's tactile switch on a board its uploader doesn't name, with no mods listed. A plain, rounded clack to set against this board's thock.
- Laptop: the 2018 MacBook Pro's butterfly keys, also low and dull rather than bright, but a shorter, lighter tap where the Rainy 75 gives a full keystroke.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |

- MX Brown | Tactile | majod | 11.1 dB | 75 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick Rainy 75 if you like the deep, muted sound of a modern enthusiast board and want it steady from key to key, for long writing sessions or late typing with the volume low.

Pick something else if you want a click you can hear across the room (MX Blue, Unicomp), more variety between keystrokes, or the rubber-cushioned kind of thock (Topre).

### Rainy 75: questions

Which switches are in this Rainy 75?
The uploader doesn't say. The whole Freesound description is “I just typed on my Rainy 75 keyboard.” The Pro version ships with different stock switches from the Lite and Standard, and every version has hot-swap sockets, so the board alone doesn't tell you, and we don't guess.

Who makes the Rainy 75?
Wobkey. Its spec sheet lists a 75% layout with 81 keys, a CNC-machined aluminum case, a gasket mount and a weight of 1.8 to 2 kg, in Lite, Standard and Pro versions.

Why do the Rainy 75 keys sound so alike?
Because the recording does. Its strikes are unusually similar to each other, and Keyslam keeps that: every press take is a different strike from the session, picked across each strength band, not one sample repeated. If you want more variety between keys, a pack like MX Brown or the Unicomp changes more from key to key.

Is the Rainy 75 thockier than Topre?
They thock differently. The Rainy 75's sound comes from a heavy aluminum case and a gasket-mounted plate; Topre's comes from a rubber dome over a spring that cushions the bottom of the press. Play the Topre pack and this one back to back; Keyslam levels both packs to −28 LUFS, so any difference you notice is tone.

### How a buckling spring makes its sound

Each key sits on a coil spring standing upright in a plastic barrel. The spring is held between the keycap and a small pivoting hammer. As you press, the spring first squashes evenly, then gives way sideways all at once. That buckle is the snap you feel in your finger, and it tips the hammer down so the key registers. On the Model M design that Unicomp builds, the hammer strikes contacts on a plastic membrane sheet. On IBM's older Model F, the hammer works over a capacitive circuit board instead.

So one keystroke stacks up several sounds: the snap of the buckle, the clack of the keycap reaching the bottom, and the spring straightening as the key rises. The coil can also ring faintly inside its barrel. Owners call that “spring ping”, and some lube their springs to quiet it. IBM's buckling-spring patents go back to the 1970s, with the cheaper membrane version following in the 1980s, and it's still the sound many people picture when they hear “clicky keyboard”.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Unicomp buckling spring pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 10.4 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |

- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −11.5 dBFS | 78 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 4 | −10.0 dBFS | 67 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 4 | −5.5 dBFS | 67 ms |

### Unicomp and the IBM Model M sound

IBM started making the Model M in 1985. In 1991 its keyboard production went to the newly formed Lexmark, and when Lexmark stopped making keyboards in 1996, a group of its employees bought part of the keyboard manufacturing assets and started Unicomp, based in Lexington, Kentucky. Unicomp kept building keyboards on the tooling it took over from Lexmark until 2020, when it replaced that worn tooling and shipped a board it sells as the New Model M.

So a Unicomp shares the Model M's membrane buckling-spring switch and its basic construction. It is still not a vintage IBM, and this uploader doesn't say which Unicomp they typed on, so we treat the pack as a buckling-spring sound from the Model M family, not as a recording of any particular IBM keyboard. For the capacitive branch of the family, play the Model F pack.

### What this recording adds

SamsterBirdies uploaded 2 minutes 16 seconds of typing in October 2019, saved as a 24-bit, 44.1 kHz stereo FLAC file. In the takes, though, its two channels come out effectively identical, so any width you hear in the app is added by Keyslam, which pans each key toward its side of the keyboard. The description names the maker, the switch and the microphone. The page's tags add “ibm”, “old” and “vintage”, but nothing on it gives a model or a year, so the pack is named after the maker.

A session that long gave the slicer plenty of clean strikes: six regular-key takes per band, 4 per band for Space, Return and Delete, and 6 key-up takes, 46 in all, the most the pack builder keeps by default. The original has a little steady hiss between strokes. Each take is short and faded out, so in the app the click-clack covers it.

### Unicomp vs MX Blue and the Model F

Start with Cherry's clicky switch, then the other buckling spring. The figures in the table are read from each pack's own files.
- MX Blue: Cherry's clicky switch, which gets its click from a plastic jacket rather than a spring. The two spectra are fairly close, so the giveaway is the ring: at medium strength this pack's takes stay within 30 dB of their peak for 78 ms, against 58 ms for the Blue.
- Model F: IBM's earlier buckling spring, read through a capacitive board instead of a membrane, on a keyboard from the early 1980s. Someone else recorded it and doesn't say with what microphone, so listen for the shape of each strike rather than its exact tone.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- Unicomp | Buckling spring | SamsterBirdies | 10.4 dB | 78 ms | |
- MX Blue | Clicky | EricsSoundschmiede | 12.0 dB | 58 ms | |
- Model F | Buckling spring | Fractal_ | 9.3 dB | 73 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick Unicomp if you learned to type on an old IBM-style keyboard and miss it, or want a keystroke with real weight and spring behind it.

Pick something else if other people can hear your desk: buckling springs are about as attention-grabbing as keyboards get. Topre and the Laptop pack are much gentler, and the Model F gives you a buckling spring with a different edge.

### Unicomp buckling spring: questions

Is this an IBM Model M?
Not as far as the source says. The uploader describes “a Unicomp buckling spring keyboard” and names no model. Unicomp makes its keyboards on IBM's Model M design, with the same kind of membrane buckling-spring switch, so the sound belongs to the Model M family, but we don't claim the board is an IBM Model M.

Model M vs Model F: how do they sound different?
Both use buckling springs. The Model M, and Unicomp's boards after it, register a key when the hammer strikes a membrane; the earlier Model F reads it through a capacitive circuit board. Collectors usually describe the Model F as crisper and louder. Keyslam's Model F pack is a separate recording by another uploader, so the A/B on this page sets one real keyboard against another; it isn't a lab test of the two switch designs.

Does pressing harder change a buckling spring's sound?
Less than in most of Keyslam’s packs. However hard you push, the spring gives way at the same point, so extra force mostly shows up in the clack at the bottom. Here the slam takes peak 10.4 dB higher than the soft ones, a soft-to-slam gap that is the 12th widest of the 15 packs, and the soft takes sound mostly like quieter versions of the slams rather than a different kind of strike.

Why is this pack called Unicomp and not Buckling Spring?
Because Keyslam has two buckling-spring packs, this one and the Model F. Each is named for what its uploader says it is: “a Unicomp buckling spring keyboard” here and “an IBM Model F XT” on the other.

This pack is an early-1980s Model F XT recorded by Fractal_ and released as CC0 on Freesound, cut into 39 takes in four strength bands.

### Capacitive buckling springs: how a Model F reads a key

Under every key of a Model F stands a coil spring in a barrel, pressing on a small pivoting hammer that Model F owners usually call a flipper. Push the key and the spring compresses, then buckles sideways in one snap, and the buckle swings the hammer. What the hammer does next is the Model F's trick. There's no membrane and no metal contact to close: the hammer's movement changes the capacitance between a pair of pads on the circuit board, and the keyboard reads that change as a keypress.

The mechanism is Richard Harris's “buckling spring torsional snap actuator”, patented for IBM in 1978. The Model F first appeared with the IBM System/23 Datamaster and was made mainly from 1981 to 1985. Its best-known form is the 83-key keyboard that came with the original IBM PC in 1981, known to collectors as the Model F XT.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the IBM Model F pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 9.3 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 2 | −13.4 dBFS | 67 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 4 | −10.1 dBFS | 73 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 3 | −5.8 dBFS | 69 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 5 | 2 | −4.1 dBFS | 69 ms |

soft −13.4 dBFS peak · 67 ms
medium −10.1 dBFS peak · 73 ms
hard −5.8 dBFS peak · 69 ms
slam −4.1 dBFS peak · 69 msIBM Model F: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### Model F vs Model M

From 1985 IBM moved to the Model M. The spring stayed and the capacitive board went: in a Model M the hammer strikes a plastic membrane sheet to close a circuit, and IBM's 1985 patent for that design put its cost at approximately half that of the capacitive mechanism. The Model M's hammer is also smaller and its springs have fewer coils, so the two don't feel quite the same.

Collectors generally rate the Model F as crisper to type on and louder and sharper to hear. Keyslam has one board from each branch: this Model F XT, and a Unicomp built on the Model M design. They come from two different uploaders, and this one doesn't name a microphone, so hear the comparison below as one real keyboard against another, not a controlled test of the two designs.

### What this recording adds

The upload is a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz stereo WAV file, 16 seconds long, the shortest typing recording behind any Keyslam pack, posted by Fractal_ in December 2019. Its one-line description, quoted above, is all the page says about the board: no microphone, keycaps or modifications are listed.

A burst that short limits how many clean strikes the slicer can choose from. This pack has 5–6 regular-key takes per band, 2–4 per band for Space, Return and Delete, and 5 key-up takes, 39 in all. The slicer gives Space, Return and Delete the darkest, longest-ringing strikes it can find, but this burst has no clearly darker group of strikes to give them, so the big keys sound much like the regular ones. Like the Unicomp, it sits in the narrower half of the soft-to-slam ranking: the slam band peaks 9.3 dB above soft, the 14th widest of the 15 packs.

The stereo is unusually wide: its left and right channels correlate at only 0.09, where 1.00 would mean identical, the least alike of the 15 packs. Headphones show it best. On laptop speakers, which sit close together, the two channels partly cancel in the treble, so the pack can sound a little duller and quieter than it does on headphones.

### Model F vs Unicomp and MX Blue

Start with the Model M-family buckling spring, then Cherry's clicky switch, and listen for the shape of each keystroke.
- Unicomp: a Unicomp board on the Model M design, where the hammer lands on a membrane instead of capacitive pads. It comes from a much longer session, recorded with a clip-on microphone.
- MX Blue: a modern clicky switch for scale. Its click comes from a plastic collar snapping inside the switch, not a spring buckling.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- Model F | Buckling spring | Fractal_ | 9.3 dB | 73 ms | |
- Unicomp | Buckling spring | SamsterBirdies | 10.4 dB | 78 ms | |
- MX Blue | Clicky | EricsSoundschmiede | 12.0 dB | 58 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick Model F if you want the sound of an early IBM PC keyboard, crisp and loud, and you mostly listen on headphones, where the wide stereo comes through.

Pick something else if you mostly listen on MacBook speakers or want more variety between keys: the Unicomp is a buckling spring with no stereo width to lose and more takes. For a quieter desk, try Topre.

### IBM Model F: questions

Is the Model F XT the keyboard that came with the original IBM PC?
Yes. The 83-key Model F known as the XT keyboard was released in 1981 with the original IBM PC and also came with the PC XT that followed. The uploader dates this one to the early 1980s and gives no exact year or part number.

Model F or Model M: which is louder?
Collectors usually call the capacitive Model F the louder and crisper of the two. Keyslam, though, levels every pack to one target, −28 LUFS over a medium-strength typing passage, so when you switch between this pack and the Unicomp, what changes is the shape of the keystroke, not its volume.

What does capacitive mean on a buckling-spring keyboard?
That no contact closes when you press a key. The buckling spring pivots a hammer above pads on the circuit board, and the keyboard reads the change in capacitance between them as a keypress. The membrane Model M uses the same kind of spring, but its hammer presses the layers of a plastic membrane together to close a circuit.

Why does the Model F pack have fewer takes than most?
Because the source runs only 16 seconds. Every strike has to be clean to become a take, with nothing clipped and no second key landing in its tail, and a short, busy recording offers fewer of those. It still fills each band, with 5–6 regular-key takes per band and 5 key-up takes.

### What Gateron Yellows sound like

Gateron is a Chinese maker of MX-compatible switches, popular with people who build their own keyboards. The Yellow is a linear switch, slightly heavier than a Cherry MX Red, and a popular budget choice. Like any linear, it has no bump or click, so its sound is the stem bottoming out and returning.

“Black bottom” means Yellows with black bottom housings, a variant some builders seek out for its sound. Swapping on Cherry MX top housings and lubing the sliders are common mods. Lube smooths the travel and takes away scratch, which is why modded linears like these are often described as muted or “creamy”.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Gateron Yellow (Vintage Technics) pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 13.2 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |

### About the board

The uploader describes it as a “Hengyu Computer Equipment Factory” Technics keyboard and lists the model as unidentified. They also wrote that its layout is terrible, and that they're “kinda mad at how nice it sounds.” The recording is 51 seconds of typing, saved as stereo Ogg Vorbis.

Short as it is, it filled every band with six regular-key takes, plus 2–4 per band for the wide keys and 6 key-up takes. In the app this pack is listed as Vintage Technics.

### Gateron Yellow vs Cherry MX Red

Two linears, played back to back. The Reds are in a gaming board with no mods listed; the Yellows are modded in an old case.
- MX Red: Cherry MX Reds in a Corsair K95, with a longer-ringing bottom-out.
- Topre: not a linear, but the other “soft” favourite. Compare the damped Yellow with Topre's rubber cushion.

### Who it suits

Pick Gateron Yellow if you like the sound of a lubed custom board: smooth, low and short, with little ring.

Pick something else if you want a crisp, bright linear (MX Red) or a click (MX Blue).

### Gateron Yellow (Vintage Technics): questions

Are these real Gateron Yellow switches?
Yes, per the uploader: “black bottom gat yellows with MX tops swapped on”. The bottom housings are Gateron Yellow and the top housings were swapped for MX tops, and the sliders are lubed, so a stock Yellow may sound a little different.

What does lubing do to the sound?
It smooths the stem's travel and damps scratch and ring. These sliders were wax-lubed and lubed with Krytox 205g0. In this pack the medium takes fall 30 dB below their peak in 49 ms, the shortest of the 15 packs.

Why is the pack called Vintage Technics?
Because the keyboard is the starting point: an old Technics-branded board the uploader couldn't identify. The Gateron Yellows are a mod inside it, which is why this page leads with the switch.

### The butterfly keyboard

Apple introduced the butterfly mechanism in the 12-inch MacBook in 2015 and used it in MacBook Pro and MacBook Air models until 2019 and 2020, when it went back to scissor switches under the name Magic Keyboard. Butterfly keys move far less than a mechanical switch, so there's no long travel to make noise, just the cap tapping down onto the frame.

The 2018 MacBook Pro has the third generation, which Apple described as quieter than earlier butterfly keyboards; a thin membrane sits under each key. That is what you hear here: a short, damped tap. For a membrane-vs-mechanical A/B, the keyboard sound test page compares this pack with MX Brown.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the MacBook butterfly keyboard pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 16.6 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Return, Delete | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | 2 | −17.0 dBFS | 65 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | 3 | −10.5 dBFS | 55 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | 3 | −7.1 dBFS | 64 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | 2 | −0.4 dBFS | 39 ms |

medium −10.5 dBFS peak · 55 ms
hard −7.1 dBFS peak · 64 ms

### Butterfly or scissor: which MacBook keyboard do you have?

If your MacBook is on the butterfly list, this pack is the same kind of keyboard as yours, recorded close up. If it's on the scissor list, your keys travel further, so they won't sound quite like this.

- MacBook | Keyboard |

- All Apple silicon MacBooks | Scissor (Magic Keyboard) |

### What this recording adds

The uploader recorded “various typings” close up: multiple keystrokes and single clicks at different speeds, 53 seconds as a 24-bit, 48 kHz mono WAV. A shotgun microphone this close turns a quiet keyboard into a clear, usable sound. Keyslam kept six regular-key takes per band, 2–3 per band for Space, Return and Delete, and 5 key-up takes.

Because the source is mono, the stereo spread in the app comes from Keyslam placing each key by its position.

### MacBook keys vs Topre and MX Brown

Two keyboard switches to hear next to the laptop keys.
- Topre: a soft, rounded switch sound, but deeper than a butterfly tap.
- MX Brown: a typical mechanical tactile switch, for the laptop-vs-mechanical contrast.

### Who it suits

Pick Laptop for shared rooms and late nights (with the volume down), or if you want gentle confirmation of each keystroke without pretending to have a different keyboard.

Pick something else if you want your MacBook to sound mechanical: MX Brown for a classic tactile, Topre for something soft but deep.

### MacBook butterfly keyboard: questions

Is this the sound of a current MacBook keyboard?
No, it's the 2018 butterfly keyboard. Apple silicon MacBooks use scissor keys (Apple's Magic Keyboard), which travel further, so they sound different. Keyslam doesn't have a scissor-key pack.

Was this recorded with the MacBook's own microphone?
No. khenshom used an external Sennheiser MKE600 shotgun microphone on a Zoom H5 recorder, close up, per the Freesound page.

Why add a laptop keyboard sound to a laptop?
Built-in keys are quiet, and some people type more confidently with audible feedback. This pack adds it without sounding like a different keyboard. In the app it plays at the same loudness as every other pack, so set the volume low if you want it subtle.

Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: an IBM Selectric sounds like a steady, solid strike on every key, because a motor drives the typeball and each character lands with similar force. This pack is a Correcting Selectric II recorded by secretmojo (CC0). Return plays “Typewriter bell & carriage reset” by knufds, since the uploader's Selectric bell was broken.

### What does an IBM Selectric sound like?

A firm, even thunk on every key, with less variation than a manual. There's no typebar swinging up and no carriage sliding along the page, so the rhythm is steady and the strikes sound alike. The uploader says this machine weighs about 80 pounds and calls it “the ‘quieter’ Selectric at the time”, and it still sounds solid.

In this pack the regular keys have 6 soft, 1 medium, 6 hard and 6 slam takes. Only one strike from the medium band passed the slicer's clean-take checks, so at a fixed medium strength the keys share it; with force sensing, keys blend between neighbouring bands.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the IBM Selectric II pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 12.6 dB. How the bands are made.

- Band | Percentile of strikes | Regular-key takes | Space, Delete (Return: bell) | Median peak | Audible length |
- Soft | 8th–30th | 6 | uses regular takes | −15.6 dBFS | 60 ms |
- Medium | 38th–62nd | 1 | uses regular takes | −9.9 dBFS | 99 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | uses regular takes | −8.6 dBFS | 81 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | uses regular takes | −3.0 dBFS | 83 ms |

soft −15.6 dBFS peak · 60 ms
medium −9.9 dBFS peak · 99 ms
hard −8.6 dBFS peak · 81 ms
slam −3.0 dBFS peak · 83 msIBM Selectric II: the middle take of each band, first 260 ms, same scale. Read from the app's own pack files.

### How a Selectric types

IBM introduced the Selectric in 1961. Instead of typebars it uses a golf-ball-sized typing element that tilts and rotates to put the right character in front of the paper. The paper stays in place while the element moves along the line, so a Selectric has no moving carriage to slam back. The Selectric II followed in 1971, and the Correcting Selectric II added a lift-off correction tape.

Because the motor, not your finger, sets the strike force, a real Selectric barely changes with how hard you press. Keyslam's bands for this pack come from the natural variation between strikes in the recording, leveled into four steps. If you want the real Selectric evenness on a MacBook, switch off Feel how hard you type and pick one strength.

### The bell on Return

The uploader notes that this Selectric's carriage return bell is broken. So Return plays “Typewriter bell & carriage reset” by knufds, described as an “antique typewriter margin bell and carriage return”, trimmed to 2.5 seconds. It comes from a different, antique typewriter, so it won't match a working Selectric's own return exactly. Space and Delete use the regular strikes, and like the Olivetti pack there are no key-up sounds.

From the 2:03 recording, Keyslam uses seconds 14 to 114. The uploader describes rolling paper in at the start and out at the end.

### Selectric vs the Olivetti and MX Blue

An electric typewriter, a manual one and a clicky keyboard switch.
- Olivetti: a manual portable. Your finger drives each typebar, so strikes vary more and Return is a short ding.
- MX Blue: the uploader of that recording suggested it could pass as a typewriter. Hear whether you agree.

- Pack | Type | Recorded by | Soft to slam | Audible length (medium) | Hear it |
- Selectric | Typewriter | secretmojo | 12.6 dB | 99 ms | |
- Olivetti | Typewriter | keithpeter | 15.2 dB | 97 ms | |
- MX Blue | Clicky | EricsSoundschmiede | 12.0 dB | 58 ms | |

### Who it suits

Pick Selectric if you want the steady, office-typewriter rhythm and a bell at the end of every paragraph.

Pick something else if you want a typewriter that reacts strongly to your touch (Olivetti) or something softer-sounding for shared spaces.

### IBM Selectric II: questions

Is the bell on Return from the Selectric?
No. The uploader's Selectric has a broken bell, so Return plays a separate CC0 recording of an antique typewriter's margin bell and carriage return by knufds, trimmed to 2.5 seconds.

Does a real Selectric sound louder when you type harder?
Not much. A motor drives the typeball, so strikes land with similar force. Keyslam still sorts this recording's strikes into four bands by their natural loudness; on a MacBook you can switch off force sensing and pick one strength for a more even sound.

Why does the Selectric pack have no key-up sound?
A typewriter doesn't make a clean, separate key-up click in this recording, so the typewriter packs are cut with key-up detection off and every strike is treated as a press.

### The Lettera 22

Olivetti, the Italian office-machine company, launched the Lettera 22 in 1950. Marcello Nizzoli designed it, and it won a Compasso d'Oro design award in 1954, the prize's first year. It's a portable manual, light enough to carry, and it was widely used by reporters and writers.

Each key swings a metal typebar up against the ribbon and the platen. The carriage moves one space with every strike, a bell rings a few characters before the right margin, and you push the carriage back with a lever. Your finger drives the typebar, so a light touch is soft and a hard strike is loud, which makes a manual a natural match for force sensing.

### Measured from the app's pack files

What the Olivetti Lettera 22 pack contains, band by band. Peak is the median take's loudest sample; audible length is how long it stays within 30 dB of that peak. Soft to slam spans 15.2 dB. How the bands are made.

- Medium | 38th–62nd | 6 | uses regular takes | −13.6 dBFS | 97 ms |
- Hard | 70th–88th | 6 | uses regular takes | −2.6 dBFS | 61 ms |
- Slam | 92nd–100th | 6 | uses regular takes | −0.8 dBFS | 59 ms |

### What this recording adds

The uploader recorded the whole routine: paper going in, about 50 words of typing with a small bell at the end of each line, the platen returning and the paper coming out. It's a 16-bit, 44.1 kHz mono WAV from June 2011, the oldest recording behind any Keyslam pack, made with a Hitachi HMP606 dynamic mic, a Maycom MicTube preamp and a Samsung NC10 netbook running Audacity. Keyslam uses seconds 6 to 100 of the 1:46 file.

The strikes vary a lot, as a manual should. Its soft takes last longer than most: a median of 242 ms, against 81 ms across the other packs' soft bands.

Return plays “Typewriter ding_near_mono.wav” by _stubb, a clean “typewriter ding at the end of a line”, about 1 second long. It's a bell only, with no carriage slide. Space and Delete use the regular strikes, and there are no key-up sounds, since a typewriter's keys don't make a separate release click in this recording.

The two typewriters, back to back, plus a clicky keyboard for scale.
- Selectric: the electric IBM. A motor sets the strike force, so it's steadier; Return adds a carriage return after the bell.
- MX Blue: the clicky keyboard switch, for comparison with a real typebar.

Does the Olivetti pack have a carriage return sound?

# Best Keyboard Sound App for Mac (2026): 18 Apps Compared
URL: https://keyslam.com/compare/
Updated: 2026-11-04

Comparison · checked November 2, 2026
## The best keyboard sound app for Mac, compared by what you need

18 Mac keyboard sound apps side by side: price, trial, which Macs they run on, whether the sound follows your typing force, and what each one sends online. Facts about other apps come from their makers' own pages, with quotes and sources at the end.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: it depends on your Mac. If you want the sound to follow how hard you type, three of the 18 apps here read the MacBook motion sensor: Haptyk ($8, MacBooks with the sensor only), Keyslam ($3.99; macOS 13 or later, and it also runs on Macs without the sensor) and the free Clank Keys (Apple silicon, not notarized). If you'd rather buy on the Mac App Store, Klack, Thock (App Store) and Keeby are $4.99 and TypeLouder is $2.99. Free and open source: Mechvibes, Thock (open source) and Keyboard Sounds Pro, plus KeyEcho, which is free with paid packs. The two Thocks are unrelated apps; see which Thock app for Mac is which.
We make Keyslam. Every fact about another app on this page comes from the maker's own site, its App Store or Setapp listing, its GitHub page or Homebrew, checked November 2, 2026, and the numbered notes quote it word for word. Where another app suits you better, we say so. Spot a mistake? Tell us and we'll fix it and log it below.

### Pick by what matters to you

- Mac App Store | Klack, Thock (App Store), Keeby and FunKey ($4.99), TypeLouder ($2.99) | Klack needs macOS 15 and TypeLouder 15.5. Klack's App Store and website versions are separate purchases. How Keyslam compares with Klack. |

### Which Mac keyboard sound apps react to how hard you type?

Several Mac apps react to typing force: Haptyk ($8, MacBooks with the sensor only), Keyslam ($3.99) and Clank Keys (free) read the MacBook accelerometer, and TapNoise varies volume from an estimate of typing movement. Thock (App Store) calls its packs “velocity aware” without saying how. The other 13 apps in this comparison don't advertise anything like it.

Haptyk's home page still presents it as the one app where “the sound follows how hard you press”1. Clank Keys does the same for free, and has since September 13, 2026, when its first public build came out2.

- App | What it reads | What changes with force | Runs without the sensor? | Price (US) |
- Keyslam | The accelerometer, about 800 readings a second | Picks and blends real strikes from four bands, sorted by natural loudness from one recording | Yes, at a strength you pick | $3.99 |
- Haptyk | The MacBook accelerometer | “4 levels, soft to slam”3 | No: Macs without the sensor get an “Incompatible Mac” notice4 | $8 |
- Clank Keys | The MacBook accelerometer | “plays a real switch recording that matches how hard you hit the key”5 | Yes, “varied by typing rhythm”6; Apple silicon only | Free |
- TapNoise | A movement estimate | Volume. Its blog: “an estimate from body movement, not a force sensor”7 | Yes; the pressure features need a sensor MacBook8 | $14.99 ($5.99 launch price) |
- Thock (App Store) | Not described | Its site calls the packs “velocity aware”9 without saying how | Yes | $4.99 |

Two caveats apply to the three apps that read the sensor. Force sensing needs a MacBook with Apple's motion sensor: MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, and MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later. See which MacBooks have an accelerometer for the full model list. And Haptyk's refund page says the sensor interface “is not officially supported by Apple and may change or become unavailable in future macOS updates”10. Keyslam reads the same sensor through IOKit, so that caution applies to it too. How Keyslam turns a jolt into a band is on the force sensing page.

### Will it run on my Mac?

Two things decide it: whether your Mac has the motion sensor, and which macOS it runs. “Apple silicon, no sensor” means the M1 MacBook Air, the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, and every iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio and Mac Pro with Apple silicon. Where a maker lists only a macOS version, we show the app as running on any Mac with that version.

- Your Mac | Follows typing force | Plays sounds | Won't run | Maker doesn't say |
- MacBook with the sensor | Keyslam, Haptyk, Clank Keys; TapNoise varies volume from a movement estimate | All the others | None | None |
- Apple silicon, no sensor | None | Keyslam (strength you pick), Clank Keys (varied by rhythm), Mechvibes (experimental build) and all the other apps here | Haptyk | None |
- Intel Mac | None | Keyslam, TapNoise, Klakk, KeyEcho and Keyboard Sounds Pro | Haptyk, Clank Keys and Mechvibes (GitHub issue 128 says an Intel build of Mechvibes is merged for the next release) | Klack, Thock (App Store), Keeby, TypeLouder, FunKey, CupertinoClicks, Kachunk, Tacque, KeyClicker and Thock (open source) |

Haptyk: “The M1 MacBook Air, the 13″ M1 MacBook Pro, Intel Macs and desktop Macs do not have it”11. Mechvibes: “Intel Macs are not supported yet”12. Clank Keys: “macOS 13 or later, Apple Silicon (M1 or newer)”13.

### Where the sounds come from

Keyslam didn't record its own sounds: its packs are cut from CC0 recordings by Freesound users _stubb, EricsSoundschmiede, Fractal_, grcekh, handygaber, IRF1010N, keithpeter, khenshom, knufds, majod, SamsterBirdies, secretmojo, stu556, Techrul, ujonathan and zrrion, each credited by name. Haptyk's and Clank Keys' sounds come from open-source libraries. This table uses each maker's own words about where its sounds come from.

- App | Where the sounds come from | What you get |
- Keyslam | Named boards, each cut from one credited CC0 Freesound typing recording (the typewriters add a recorded bell) | 13 keyboards and 2 typewriters, key-up sounds on the keyboards, custom packs |
- Haptyk | Open-source libraries: “The recordings come from the Mechvibes and ClickClack open-source sound libraries (MIT licence)”24 | 16 packs, key-up sounds |
- Clank Keys | “Switch recordings from the Mechvibes project, MIT licence”25 | Mechvibes switch sets |
- TapNoise | Its notices page: for five themes, “The source files were generated with ElevenLabs”26; “8-bit and Laser are synthesised”27 | 20 sounds (10 keyboards, 10 fun); no custom packs28 |
- Klack | Recorded: “Each switch set consist of over 100 audio files that need to be recorded and mastered individually”29 | 7 switch sets, key-up sounds, randomized pitch |
- Thock (App Store) | “multi-sampled” Cherry MX and Gateron packs9 | 22 packs, key-down and key-up |
- Keeby | “Recorded from real mechanical switches”30 | 12 switch profiles, notch visualizer |
- TypeLouder | “Real keyboard recordings”31; four packs have recorded key-ups, the rest derive one from the press32 | 8 packs |
- FunKey | “premium sound profiles inspired by real mechanical keyboards”33 | 25+ profiles |
- CupertinoClicks | Not stated | 30 keyboard and mouse presets |
- Kachunk | Not stated | Underwood and Olivetti typewriters, 24 switch packs |
- Klakk | Not stated | 14 packs |
- Tacque | “Six synthesized sound packs”34 | 6 packs, per-key pitch variation |
- KeyClicker | Not stated | Keyboard and typewriter sounds |
- KeyEcho | Sampled per key: “each key has its own press and release”35 | 71 packs (18 free) |
- Mechvibes | Made by its community | 985 pack pages on mechvibes.com, a pack editor |
- Thock (open source) | Not stated | Built-in, custom (JSON) and community packs |
- Keyboard Sounds Pro | Not stated | 20 profiles (13 keyboard, 7 mouse), custom profiles |
Keyslam's packs, recordists and Freesound links: all 15 sound packs.

### What goes online, and how it installs

- App | What the app sends, in the maker's words | How it installs |
- Keyslam | Nothing: the app makes no network connections. The license key is Ed25519-signed and checked offline, and the trial date stays in your Keychain. | Direct download, notarized by Apple |
- Haptyk | Usage statistics “when the app launches, every 5 minutes while running, and when you quit”36; the trial email is kept with a machine fingerprint37 | Notarized DMG from haptyk.com38 |
- Clank Keys | “the app contains no networking code”39 | GitHub, closed source; “signed by its maker, not notarised by Apple”40, so the first launch needs a Terminal command41 |
- TapNoise | “It goes online only to check your license with Dodo Payments, and once a day to look for an update.”42 | Direct; “signed by its maker but not notarized by Apple”43 |
- Klack | “No data or personal information is collected by Klack.”44 | Mac App Store, or a standalone that's sold separately: “Buying one does not unlock the other.”45 |
- Thock (App Store) | “The app itself does not collect, store, or transmit personal data.”46 | Mac App Store |
- Keeby | App Store label: Data Not Collected. The direct edition needs internet “for activation and periodic license checks”47 | Mac App Store, or direct (Polar) |
- TypeLouder | “The app operates entirely offline”, with no network permission48 | Mac App Store |
- FunKey | App Store label: Data Not Collected | App Store |
- CupertinoClicks | Not stated | Direct download |
- Kachunk | “zero telemetry”49, works offline50 | Notarized direct download, or the Mac App Store |
- Klakk | “Activation and usage telemetry are separate network features described in the privacy policy. This is not a claim of zero network activity.”51 | Notarized DMG direct, or the Mac App Store |
- Tacque | “nothing is recorded, stored, or sent anywhere”52 | Mac App Store, Setapp |
- KeyClicker | App Store label: Data Not Collected | Mac App Store; newest version on GitHub |
- KeyEcho | “The open-source app sends no usage analytics or crash reports.”53 | Notarized DMG or Homebrew |
- Mechvibes | “one anonymous ping per launch”54 through Aptabase, which you can switch off, and a daily GitHub update check | Experimental Apple silicon DMG, “NOT notarized”55; permissions re-added after each update56; the Homebrew cask is disabled57 |
- Thock (open source) | Not stated | Homebrew or GitHub |
- Keyboard Sounds Pro | Not stated | Universal DMG on GitHub |
“Data Not Collected” is the developer's own answer on the App Store privacy label. Not notarized means macOS blocks the first launch until you allow it. Every keyboard sound app needs permission to see which keys you press; what Input Monitoring lets an app see.

### How we check, and what we've corrected

On November 2, 2026 we read each app's website, pricing, FAQ, privacy and refund pages, its Mac App Store listing, GitHub repo or update feed, and asked archive.org to save a copy of each page we quote (for a few pages it couldn't). Where a maker doesn't say something, the table says “Not stated” instead of guessing.

For the Mac App Store, we searched with 12 terms and read the description of every keyboard-sound listing that came back. None mentions an accelerometer, a motion sensor, velocity or typing force. (Thock's website, not its listing, calls its packs “velocity aware”.) Keyslam is a direct download, not an App Store app. We haven't tested whether Apple would approve an App Store version that reads the motion sensor, so we don't claim it couldn't be done.

We recheck all of them monthly, TapNoise after its launch pricing ends on November 15, 2026, and Haptyk after each release in its update feed. When something changes, it goes in this log.

- Date | Topic | What we said | What's right |
- 2026-11-02 | Who reads the sensor | This page said that, of the apps we checked, Keyslam and Haptyk use the MacBook motion sensor and TapNoise “advertises soft and hard responses”. | Clank Keys, a free app first released on September 13, 2026, also reads the accelerometer. TapNoise's own blog calls its pressure feature an estimate from body movement, not a force sensor. |
- 2026-11-02 | Lowest price | We said Keyslam had the lowest price of the apps that advertise force-sensitive sound. | Clank Keys is free. Of the two paid apps that read the sensor, Keyslam ($3.99) costs less than Haptyk ($8). |
- 2026-11-02 | Mac App Store | Our FAQ claimed that App Store sandboxing stops apps reading the motion sensor. | We hadn't verified that, so it's gone. What we did check: none of the Mac App Store keyboard-sound listings we read describes force sensing. |
- 2026-11-02 | Keyslam's strengths | Our own row said each board had “4 strengths”, which read as four separate recordings. | Each pack's strikes are cut from one real recording. They are sorted by natural loudness into soft, medium, hard and slam bands (slam is the hardest ~8%), and each band is leveled. |
- 2026-11-02 | Klack | We listed Klack as running on “macOS”, with no trial “on the App Store”. | The App Store version needs macOS 15. Klack has no trial at all; its FAQ points to previews on its site, a 14-day refund and up to 5 devices. |
- 2026-11-02 | Haptyk | We wrote that Haptyk's “anonymous usage counts leave the Mac”. | Now quoted from its privacy policy: usage statistics go out at launch, every 5 minutes while it runs, and at quit. |
- 2026-11-02 | Mechvibes | We listed Mechvibes as a macOS, Windows and Linux app, with no caveats. | The Mac build of Mechvibes 3 (v3.4.0) is experimental, Apple silicon only and not notarized. |
- 2026-11-02 | Coverage | The table had 9 apps. | It now has all the apps in our research, with Thock split into the App Store app and the unrelated open-source one. |

Found something out of date or unfair? Send a correction. Makers of these apps are welcome to write in too.

### Comparison questions

What is the best keyboard sound app for Mac?
It depends on your Mac. For sound that follows how hard you type: Keyslam ($3.99; macOS 13 or later, and it also runs on Macs without the sensor) or Haptyk ($8, MacBooks with the motion sensor only); Clank Keys does it free on Apple silicon MacBooks with the sensor, but isn't notarized. To buy on the Mac App Store: Klack ($4.99, macOS 15 or later). Free and open source: Mechvibes, Thock (open source) or Keyboard Sounds Pro, and KeyEcho is free with paid packs. We make Keyslam, so check the sources on this page.

Are Klack and Klakk the same app?
No. Klakk's own site says “Klakk (K-l-a-k-k) and Klack (K-l-a-c-k) are separate apps from different developers.” Klack is Henrik Ruscon's $4.99 Mac App Store app. Klakk sells $4.49 Mac and Windows editions on tryklakk.com, with a 3-day trial, and a free download with paid upgrades on the App Store.

Why isn't Keyslam on the Mac App Store?
Keyslam is sold directly from its own website, not through the Mac App Store. We haven't tested whether Apple would approve an App Store version that reads the MacBook motion sensor, so we don't claim it's impossible. None of the Mac App Store keyboard-sound listings we read on November 2, 2026 describes force sensing.

Which keyboard sound apps send data from my Mac?
Going by their own pages: Haptyk sends usage statistics at launch, every 5 minutes and at quit. Mechvibes sends one anonymous ping per launch (you can switch it off) and checks GitHub daily. Klakk has activation and usage telemetry. TapNoise goes online to check its license and once a day for updates, and Keeby's direct edition checks its license periodically. Clank Keys says it has no networking code, TypeLouder says it works entirely offline, and Keyslam makes no network connections.

How do you keep this comparison accurate?
We quote each maker's own page, save an archive.org copy where archive.org can make one, and recheck monthly: TapNoise after its launch pricing ends on November 15, 2026, Haptyk after each release. Every change goes in the corrections log on this page. If you spot an error, tell us.

# Klack Alternative for Mac: macOS 13+, Free Trial | Keyslam
URL: https://keyslam.com/alternatives/klack/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Klack alternative · specs checked November 2, 2026
## Klack alternative for Mac that runs on macOS 13, with a free trial

Klack is a $4.99 Mac App Store app with seven recorded switch sets. Its App Store version needs macOS 15, and it has no trial. Keyslam runs on macOS 13 Ventura and later, costs $3.99 once and lets you try everything for 7 days.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: If Klack won't install on your Mac, or you'd like to try before you pay, Keyslam covers both.
It runs on macOS 13 Ventura and later (Klack's App Store version needs macOS 15), has a 7-day free trial (Klack has none),
costs $3.99 once (Klack is $4.99), and on MacBooks with Apple's motion sensor the sound follows how hard you type.
Klack is still the better pick if you want to buy through the Mac App Store.

one line at a time, with the exact words, a link and an archived copy.

- Refunds | 14 days from purchase; App Store refunds go through Apple | “Yes, you may request a full refund within 14 days of your original purchase. For App Store refunds, please contact Apple’s support directly.” tryklack.com FAQ (archived) |
- On/off shortcut | Yes, since version 1.2. We couldn't confirm its default keys. | “1.2 A shortcut to toggle Klack and the option to hide the menu bar icon.” Klack changelog (archived) |
- Auto-sleep | Sleep triggers for screen sharing, Focus, media and calendar | “Sleep triggers for screen sharing, focus, media, and calendar” Klack changelog (archived) |
- Data | None collected, per its FAQ | “No data or personal information is collected by Klack.” tryklack.com FAQ (archived) |
- Developer | Henrik Ruscon | “Developer Henrik Ruscon” Mac App Store listing (archived) |
- AI crawlers | Blocked in robots.txt, including ClaudeBot, GPTBot and PerplexityBot | “User-agent: ClaudeBot Disallow: /” tryklack.com/robots.txt (archived) |

### Where Keyslam differs, in order

#### 1. macOS 13 vs macOS 15

Klack's App Store version needs macOS 15 Sequoia. Keyslam needs macOS 13 Ventura. Apple's compatibility lists stop the 2017 MacBook Pro and iMac at Ventura and the 2018 and 2019 MacBook Air at Sonoma, so Klack's App Store version won't install on those Macs and Keyslam will. Which Macs stop at Ventura or Sonoma.

#### 2. A 7-day trial vs none

Everything is unlocked during the 7-day free trial, with no account, email or card. Klack's FAQ answers “No” to trying before you buy and points you to its preview buttons instead.

#### 3. $3.99 vs $4.99

One payment of $3.99, lifetime, with free updates. The personal license covers all the Macs you own; Klack's covers up to 5 devices.

#### 4. Force sensing

On MacBooks with the motion sensor (M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, and M2 and later) Keyslam reads the accelerometer about 800 times a second and picks real strikes from four strength bands. Klack doesn't advertise anything like it. None of the 42 Mac App Store keyboard-sound apps we checked offers force sensing; Keyslam is sold directly, not through the App Store.

### When Klack is the better choice

- You want the Mac App Store. Klack installs and updates through it, and Apple handles App Store refunds. Keyslam is a direct download.

- You like one of its seven switch sets. NovelKeys Cream, Gateron Milky Yellow and the rest are switches Keyslam doesn't have. Keyslam's packs are different hardware: MX Blue, MX Brown, MX Red, MX Black, Gateron Red, Topre, Leopold, WhiteFox, Rainy 75, Unicomp, Model F, Vintage Technics, Laptop, Selectric, Olivetti.

- You want it to go quiet by itself in more situations. Klack's sleep triggers cover screen sharing, Focus, media and calendar events. Keyslam pauses on its own only while an app is using the microphone.

If you're on macOS 15 and none of the four differences above matters to you, Klack is a fine choice.

### Hear a few switch types first

Klack lets you preview its switches on tryklack.com. You can do the same here. Vintage Technics is a board with Gateron Yellow switches,
the closest Keyslam has to Klack's Gateron Milky Yellow set; the others cover linear, tactile, Topre and clicky.

### Klack questions

Is Klack free?
No. Klack is $4.99 on the Mac App Store and has no free trial; its FAQ suggests previewing the switches on its site, and it offers a full refund within 14 days (App Store purchases go through Apple). For apps that cost nothing, see our roundup of free keyboard sound apps for Mac.

Is Klack available for Windows?
We found no Windows version. Its App Store listing says “Only for Mac”, and tryklack.com's buy button is for Mac. Klakk, a different app from a different developer, sells Mac and Windows editions for $4.49 each.

Klack vs Klakk: what's the difference?
They are two different apps with near-identical names. Klakk's own site says: “Klakk (K-l-a-k-k) and Klack (K-l-a-c-k) are separate apps from different developers.” Klack is Henrik Ruscon's app, sold for Mac only, and its App Store version needs macOS 15. Klakk runs on Mac and Windows; its Mac website edition needs macOS 14 and comes with a 3-day trial.

Klack or Keyslam: which should I get?
Get Klack if you want the Mac App Store, one of its seven switch sets or its sleep triggers, and your Mac runs macOS 15. Get Keyslam if you're on macOS 13 or 14, want 7 days to try it, or want the sound to follow how hard you type on a MacBook with the motion sensor.

Runs on macOS 13 Ventura and later, Apple silicon or Intel. 15 real keyboards and typewriters.

### What each app sends over the network

Haptyk's privacy policy lists what its app reports: “Device class information shared by millions of users (Mac model, chip type, macOS version, region) App configuration (version, selected sound pack, volume level, enabled features, free/pro status) Aggregate counters (total keystrokes, session count, how often you open settings or switch packs)” It adds: “This data is sent when the app launches, every 5 minutes while running, and when you quit.” The policy describes this as anonymous usage data,
and about the trial email it says: “Your email is stored only on our server alongside a machine fingerprint and is never sold or shared.” (Haptyk privacy policy (archived))

Keyslam makes no network connections at all; there is no networking code in the app. The license key is Ed25519-signed and verified on your Mac, the trial date
stays in your Keychain, and buying happens in your browser on Stripe's checkout page. Input Monitoring tells Keyslam which key went down, and nothing you type
is stored or sent. Privacy details.

### The sensor both apps rely on

Three Mac apps we checked read the MacBook accelerometer to follow typing force: Haptyk, Keyslam and Clank Keys (free; its GitHub page (archived)).
TapNoise's pressure features also need one of those MacBooks, though its blog calls them an estimate from body movement (how Keyslam compares with TapNoise). They all depend on the same sensor, which Apple doesn't document for apps. Haptyk's refund page says it plainly: “This interface is not officially supported by Apple and may change or become unavailable in future macOS updates.” Haptyk refund policy (archived)

That applies to Keyslam too. If a macOS update ever closed the sensor off, Keyslam would keep playing every sound at a strength you pick, the way it already
does on Macs without the sensor. How Keyslam's force sensing works.

### Pick Haptyk if

- You want more packs. Haptyk has 16; Keyslam has 15.

- You like its switch recordings. Its packs come from the Mechvibes and ClickClack libraries, so if you already know and like those sounds, Haptyk plays them with force sensing.

Pick Keyslam if your Mac isn't on Haptyk's list (and runs macOS 13 or later), if you'd rather not hand over an email to try it, if you want an app that never goes online,
or if you want more than 3 days to decide.

Searching for “Haptik”? The Mac keyboard sound app is spelled Haptyk.

### Haptyk questions

What is Haptyk Pro?
Haptyk's paid license: $8 one time, for up to 3 devices you own. Its terms say the 3-day trial starts when you verify your email, and after 3 days sound playback is disabled until you buy Pro. Keyslam has no separate Pro tier: $3.99 once unlocks everything, on all the Macs you own.

Why does Haptyk say “Incompatible Mac”?
Haptyk needs the motion sensor in newer Apple silicon MacBooks. Its site says the M1 MacBook Air, the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, Intel Macs and desktop Macs don't have it, and the app tells you at launch, before asking for an email. Keyslam runs on those Macs with macOS 13 or later, at a strength you pick; see keyboard sounds on Macs without a motion sensor.

Does Haptyk collect data?
Its privacy policy says the app sends usage statistics at launch, every 5 minutes while running and at quit: Mac model, chip, macOS version, region, app settings and keystroke and session counts. The trial email is stored on its server with a machine fingerprint. Keyslam makes no network connections.

Is it spelled Haptik or Haptyk?
Haptyk, with a y. It's made by Oli Bourbonnais and sold at haptyk.com.

## TapNoise alternative with a free trial and a $3.99 price

TapNoise is a playful Mac app with 20 sounds and a desktop companion. Its regular price is $14.99 for one Mac, and it has no trial. Keyslam is $3.99 once for all your Macs, with 7 days to try it.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Keyslam is a TapNoise alternative for people who want sounds cut from real keyboard recordings and a chance to try it first.
It has a 7-day free trial (TapNoise removed its trial in version 0.2.5 on October 11, 2026), costs $3.99 once for all the Macs you own
(TapNoise's regular prices are $14.99 for 1 Mac and $20.99 for 2), runs on macOS 13 Ventura (TapNoise needs macOS 14), loads your own sound packs, and plays
real strikes from named CC0 recordings. TapNoise is the better pick for Tappy, its coding-agent sounds and its fun sounds.

Keyslam: $3.99 USD once, lifetime, with free updates and all future packs.

### How each app reacts to how you type

TapNoise changes volume with an estimate of your typing movement. Its pressure features need a MacBook with the motion sensor, much like Keyslam's force sensing:
“MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max, and later MacBook Air with M2, and later” (system requirements (archived)). Its own blog is upfront about the method: “It is an estimate from body movement, not a force sensor measuring each individual switch.” (TapNoise blog (archived))

Keyslam reads the MacBook accelerometer about 800 times a second and compares each keystroke's jolt with how you usually type. It then picks
and blends real strikes from four strength bands. Each pack's strikes are cut from one real typing recording and sorted by natural loudness into soft
(about the 8th to 30th percentile), medium (38th to 62nd), hard (70th to 88th) and slam (the hardest ~8%), and each band is leveled to a consistent target.
So a hard press plays a different real strike, not a louder copy of a soft one. Force sensing in detail.

Neither approach is a per-key force sensor; a MacBook doesn't have one. On a Mac without the motion sensor, Keyslam plays every sound at a strength you pick.

### Where the sounds come from

TapNoise has 20 sounds, “10 keyboards and 10 fun sounds.” Its notices page says five of the themes, plus its slap and MacBook sounds, came from an AI audio
generator: “Thock, Creamy, Clicky, Typewriter and Bubble, plus the shared slap and MacBook sounds: the lid chimes, hinge creak, and charger and USB sounds. The source files were generated with ElevenLabs.” And: “8-bit and Laser are synthesised by TapNoise.” (TapNoise notices (archived))

Keyslam's 15 packs are other people's recordings, released as CC0 on Freesound. What Keyslam adds is the cutting, sorting and leveling. Every recordist is credited here:

- Pack | Type | Takes | Freesound recordings (CC0) |

- Notarization: “TapNoise is signed by its maker but not notarized by Apple.” (TapNoise help (archived)), so the first launch needs Open Anyway.

Which Macs stop at Ventura.

- Checkout: “Dodo Payments sells the license as merchant of record” (TapNoise notices (archived)). Keyslam sells through Stripe Checkout; the seller is Venture Deals, Co.

No. Its site says it “needs a license key from the first launch”. Version 0.2.4 added a 3-day trial on October 10, 2026, and 0.2.5 removed it the next day. You can still play its sound demos in the browser, and it refunds within 7 days.

Is TapNoise notarized?
No. Its help page says it is “signed by its maker but not notarized by Apple”, so macOS blocks the first launch until you allow it with Open Anyway.

Can I add my own sounds to TapNoise?
Not according to its own comparison table, which answers “No” for “Your own sound packs”. Keyslam loads custom packs: a folder of WAV, AIFF or FLAC files with a pack.json.
