# Mechvibes Alternative for Mac: Safety, Permissions, vs Klack
URL: https://keyslam.com/alternatives/mechvibes/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Mechvibes alternative
## Mechvibes on a Mac: is it safe, and what's the alternative?

Mechvibes is free, open source and full of community sounds. Its Mac build is also experimental. Here's what it asks of your Mac, in its own words, and how Keyslam and Klack compare. Checked November 2, 2026.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Mechvibes is a good free pick if you have an Apple silicon Mac and don't mind some setup. Version 3.4.0 (November 1, 2026) is free and MIT-licensed, with 985 community sound-pack pages on mechvibes.com. Its Mac build is marked experimental and isn't notarized by Apple. You have to re-grant two permissions after every update, and it sends one anonymous usage ping each time it launches unless you switch that off. If you want an app made only for the Mac that never goes online, runs on Intel Macs too and follows how hard you type on a MacBook, Keyslam costs $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial. It's available to download.

### Mechvibes 3 on macOS, line by line

What Mechvibes says about its own Mac build, in its own words, and what each line means when you install it. Checked November 2, 2026.

- What we checked | What Mechvibes says | What it means on your Mac | Source |
- Version | Mechvibes 3, v3.4.0, released November 1, 2026. Written in Rust. | This is the current app. Mechvibes 2 (Electron) is no longer developed. | GitHub release v3.4.0 |
- Mac download | macOS Apple Silicon (experimental) Download dmg • v3.4.0 • 52.0 MB | There's no Intel build yet. Issue 128 says one is merged for the next release. | Mechvibes download page |
- Apple notarization | It carries only an ad-hoc signature and is NOT notarized. | macOS blocks the first launch. You approve it yourself in System Settings › Privacy & Security. | macOS README for v3.4.0 |
- Testing on a Mac | This build is produced by CI and has never been run on a real Mac by the maintainer. | Mac-only bugs can slip through. Reports on GitHub help. | macOS README for v3.4.0 |
- Permissions | Accessibility and Input Monitoring | Input Monitoring lets an app see your key presses. Accessibility is broader: it lets an app control your Mac. | macOS README for v3.4.0 |
- After each update | You have to remove and re-add both entries after replacing the app with a newer build | Every update means a trip to System Settings, or the sounds stop. | macOS README for v3.4.0 |
- Usage ping | Mechvibes sends one anonymous ping per launch to track rough usage. It runs through Aptabase. | You can switch it off in Mechvibes' Settings. | Mechvibes README on GitHub |
- Update check | Mechvibes also checks GitHub for a new version once a day. | One more connection out, once a day. | Mechvibes README on GitHub |
- Sound packs | 985 community pack pages, plus a pack editor | Lots of choice, all made by the community. | mechvibes.com sitemap |
- Installing packs | The Install in Mechvibes button in the library works on Windows and Linux. On a Mac, click Download zip on a pack's page | On a Mac, you download each pack as a ZIP and import it yourself. | Mechvibes' Mac troubleshooting post |
- Homebrew | The mechvibes cask (2.3.4) has been disabled since September 1, 2026: "disable_reason":"fails_gatekeeper_check" | brew install --cask mechvibes won't install it. Use the download page. | Homebrew cask data |
- Price | completely free to use, including all sound packs. It's open-source software released under the MIT License | Free, and you can read the code. | mechvibes.com |
Quotes are copied word for word from each source on November 2, 2026. Full links, with archived copies, are at the end of this page.

### Is Mechvibes safe?

Mechvibes' code is public under the MIT license, so anyone can read what it does with your key presses. We didn't audit it. What's different on a Mac is how much of Apple's usual checking is missing, so here are three things to know before you give it access.

- Apple hasn't checked this build. It's ad-hoc signed and not notarized, so Gatekeeper can't vouch for the copy you download. Get it only from mechvibes.com/download or the GitHub releases page, never from a mirror.

- It asks for two permissions. Input Monitoring lets an app see your keyboard, mouse and trackpad even when you’re using other apps (Apple). Accessibility lets an app control your Mac through accessibility features (Apple), which reaches further. A keyboard sound app needs at least the first.

- It goes online. Its README describes one anonymous Aptabase ping per launch to track rough usage, which you can switch off in Settings, plus a daily update check on GitHub.

If those trade-offs are fine with you, Mechvibes is a reasonable free choice. To test any keyboard sound app yourself, with a firewall, in a few minutes, see is Input Monitoring safe on a Mac.

For comparison, Keyslam asks for Input Monitoring only. Its key tap is listen-only, so it can't change or block a keystroke. It makes no network connections; the license key is Ed25519-signed and checked on your Mac. Its download is Developer ID-signed and notarized by Apple.

### Mechvibes vs Klack vs Keyslam

- | Mechvibes 3.4.0 | Klack | Keyslam |
- Price | Free (MIT open source) | $4.99 on the Mac App Store; tryklack.com also sells a separate standalone version | $3.99 once, lifetime |
- Free trial | Not needed, it's free | None; you can preview each switch on its website | 7 days, no account or card |
- Where you get it | mechvibes.com or GitHub | Mac App Store, or a separate standalone version from tryklack.com | Direct download (live) |
- Apple's check | Not notarized (ad-hoc signed) | App Store version reviewed by Apple | Developer ID-signed and notarized by Apple |
- macOS | Apple silicon only for now (experimental) | macOS 15.0 or later (App Store version) | macOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel |
- Also runs on | Windows and Linux | Mac only | Mac only |
- Sounds | 985 community packs and a pack editor | 7 recorded switch sets, with key-up sounds and spatial audio | 15 real keyboards and typewriters from CC0 recordings, four strength bands each, plus your own packs |
- Follows how hard you type | Not advertised | Not advertised | Yes, on MacBooks with the motion sensor |
- Goes online | One anonymous ping per launch (can be switched off), daily update check | Its FAQ: No data or personal information is collected by Klack. App Store label: Data Not Collected | Never. The license is verified offline |
- On/off shortcut | Not stated in the sources we checked | Yes, since version 1.2 | ⌃⌥⌘K by default (changeable) |
- Goes quiet by itself | Not stated in the sources we checked | Sleep triggers for screen sharing, Focus, media and calendar | While any app is using the microphone, such as on a call |
- One purchase covers | No license needed | Up to 5 devices | All the Macs you own |
- Refund | Not applicable | 14 days; App Store refunds go through Apple | 14 days |
Mechvibes and Klack details from their own sites, READMEs and App Store listing, checked November 2, 2026: Mechvibes download page, macOS README for v3.4.0, Klack FAQ, Klack changelog, Klack on the Mac App Store, tryklack.com. Keyslam details from our fact sheet and the app source code.

### Mechvibes or Klack: which one fits?

- Pick Mechvibes if you want it free, if you also type on Windows or Linux, or if you want a huge choice of community packs and an editor to make your own. You'll need an Apple silicon Mac for now, and a few minutes in System Settings after each update.

- Pick Klack if you're on macOS 15 or later and want to buy, install and update through the Mac App Store. It has 7 recorded switch sets and a shortcut to turn it on and off. Note that the App Store and tryklack.com versions are sold separately: buying one doesn't unlock the other.

- Pick Keyslam if you want the sound to change with how hard you type on a MacBook, if you're on an Intel Mac or on macOS 13 or 14, or if you want an app that makes no network connections at all, with no launch ping or update check.

### How is Keyslam different from Mechvibes?

Fewer sounds, more done to each one. Keyslam has 15 packs to Mechvibes' 985. Each one's keystrikes come from a single real typing recording released as CC0 on Freesound (the typewriters add a second recording for the bell). Every strike is detected and paired with its key-up, then the strikes are sorted by natural loudness into four bands: soft, medium, hard and slam, the hardest ~8%. Each band is leveled, and every pack is set to the same loudness (−28 LUFS), so switching packs changes the tone, not the volume. 13 of the 15 packs have key-up sounds.

It feels how hard you type. On MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, and on MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later, Keyslam reads the built-in motion sensor about 800 times a second and picks real strikes from the matching band. On other Macs you pick the strength.

It's made only for the Mac. It's written in Swift with a C audio core and a buffer of about 5 ms, and it needs macOS 13 Ventura or later on Apple silicon or Intel. After 3 idle minutes the audio and the motion sensor switch off.

Your own sounds work too, in a different format. Keyslam loads WAV, AIFF or FLAC files listed in a small pack.json. Mechvibes packs don't load directly; the pack format and how to convert one are on the sounds page.

### When Mechvibes is the better choice

Mechvibes costs nothing, its code is open, and its library is many times bigger than Keyslam's. If you use Windows or Linux as well as a Mac, it's the same app on all three. If you love tinkering with packs, its editor is built for that. Keyslam can't match any of those. It's a paid app that runs on Macs alone, with a small, curated set of boards.

Already using Mechvibes and it's acting up? Fixes for Mechvibes not working on a Mac cover the Gatekeeper prompt, lost permissions, no sound and pack ZIPs.

### Mechvibes questions

Can I turn off Mechvibes' usage ping?
Yes. Its README says the one anonymous ping per launch is handled by Aptabase and can be switched off in Settings. Mechvibes still checks GitHub for a new version once a day. Source: the Mechvibes README.

Should I still use Mechvibes 2 on a Mac?
Probably not. Mechvibes' download page says Using Mechvibes 2? It is no longer developed. Its Electron repo was archived on October 30, 2026, and the Homebrew cask (2.3.4) was disabled on September 1, 2026 because it fails Homebrew's Gatekeeper check. Mechvibes 3 is the current app.

Does Keyslam need Accessibility permission like Mechvibes?
No. Keyslam asks for Input Monitoring only, which is enough to know which key went down. It doesn't ask for Accessibility, the microphone or Full Disk Access, and it never stores or sends what you type.

How many sound packs does Mechvibes have?
We counted 985 pack pages in the mechvibes.com sitemap on November 2, 2026. They're made by the community, and the site says all of them are free.

# How to Make Your MacBook Sound Like a Mechanical Keyboard
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/make-macbook-sound-like-mechanical-keyboard/
Updated: 2026-11-02

How-to · about 2 minutes
## How to make your MacBook sound like a mechanical keyboard

MacBook keys are built to be quiet. A keyboard sound app plays a recording of a real mechanical board each time a key goes down, in whatever app you type in. Here's the full setup, the free options, and the parts no app can change.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: install a keyboard sound app, switch it on in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Input Monitoring, and pick a keyboard. From then on, each key you press plays that board's sound in whatever app you're typing in. Keyslam ($3.99 once after a 7-day free trial) uses real recordings and, on MacBooks with the motion sensor, follows how hard you type. Mechvibes and KeyEcho are free.

### What you need

MacAny Mac with macOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel
TimeAbout 2 minutes
PermissionInput Monitoring, one switch
Disk spaceAbout 16 MB installed (10.9 MB download), all packs included
Force sensingMacBook Pro with M1 Pro/M1 Max or later; MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 or later
Cost$3.99 once after a 7-day trial, or a free app

### How do I add keyboard sounds to a Mac?

macOS can't do it on its own, so you add an app that listens for key presses and plays a sound for each one. It needs one permission, Input Monitoring, because it has to notice keys you press in other apps. The sound comes out of your speakers or headphones. The keyboard itself doesn't change.

### Step by step: set up Keyslam on a MacBook

- Get the app. Download Keyslam, our keyboard sound app for Mac, as a notarized .dmg for Apple silicon and Intel. Open it and drag Keyslam to your Applications folder.
- Open it. There's no window and no Dock icon. A keyboard icon appears in the menu bar at the top of the screen. Click it to open the menu.
- Allow Input Monitoring. The menu shows an orange card: “Keyslam needs Input Monitoring”. Click Open Settings. It opens System Settings › Privacy & Security › Input Monitoring, where you turn Keyslam on. If macOS wants the app restarted, a Relaunch Keyslam button appears in the same card.
- Pick a keyboard. The Sound grid lists all 15 boards. Click one and it plays a short phrase right away. Preview plays it again. Every pack is leveled to the same loudness (−28 LUFS), so one board isn't suddenly louder than another.
- Set strength and volume. On a MacBook with the motion sensor, Feel how hard you type is on. A four-part meter lights up soft, medium, hard or slam as you type. Slide Sensitivity right to reach hard and slam with less force, or left to save them for real hits. On other Macs, or with force sensing off, choose Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam as a fixed strength. Then set the volume slider.
- Fine-tune it. The checkboxes at the bottom of the menu finish the job, among them Key release sounds (the key coming back up), Stereo by key position (Q a little left, P a little right) and Open at login, so the sound is there after a restart.

Something not working after step 3? Fix a keyboard sound app that makes no sound.

### How do I change the keyboard sound on a MacBook Air or Pro?

You can't change the sound the built-in keys make, because macOS has no setting for it. What you can change is the sound played with each key. In Keyslam, click the menu bar icon and pick a different board in the Sound grid. The change is instant, and it works the same on MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.

### Which board to pick

Start with the feeling you want, then press Play. These are the 15 packs in the app.

- If you want | Try | Why | Hear it |
- A loud click you can't miss | MX Blue | A click jacket snaps on the way down and again on the way up. | |
- Feedback without a click | MX Brown | A small bump and a muted, rounded clack instead of a sharp click. | |
- Smooth and quick | MX Red | A light linear press on a Corsair K95. Mostly the bottom-out. | |
- A heavier linear | MX Black | Cherry MX Blacks on a Leopold FC980M PD: heavy, smooth and full-bodied. | |
- Dark and smooth | Gateron Red | Gateron Red linears on a GMMK TKL, with a little hollow ring from the case. | |
- The deep thock people chase | Topre | Recorded on a Happy Hacking Keyboard. The rubber dome damps each hit. | |
- Close-up detail | Leopold | An FC660M with MX Browns and thick PBT caps, miked close. | |
- A lively board that rings | WhiteFox | Hako Violet tactile switches, with more room sound after each key. | |
- A creamy thock | Rainy 75 | A Rainy 75 its uploader tagged “creamy” and “thocky”. The switches aren't named. | |
- The buckling-spring clack | Unicomp | A Unicomp keyboard, the Model M design: a big, springy click-clack. | |
- Vintage IBM | Model F | An early-1980s IBM Model F XT: buckling springs with a loud, deep clack. | |
- Chunky and retro | Vintage Technics | An old Technics case with waxed Gateron Yellows. | |
- Something subtle | Laptop | A 2018 MacBook Pro's butterfly keys, miked close: short, soft taps. | |
- An office typewriter | Selectric | IBM Selectric II typeball strikes, with a recorded bell and carriage return on Return. | |
- A manual typewriter | Olivetti | Olivetti Lettera 22 typebars: snappy strikes, with a bell on Return. | |

### Can a laptop keyboard sound mechanical?

The sound, yes. The feel, no. An app can't add key travel, a heavier spring or a tactile bump. What it can do is make each keystroke sound like a real board, and the details decide whether it convinces you or sounds like a loop.

Each Keyslam pack is cut from a real typing recording. Every strike is detected, then the strikes are sorted by natural loudness into four bands, and each band is leveled to a consistent target. On the keyboard packs each strike is paired with its key-up, and Space, Return and Delete get their own takes; the two typewriters play a separately recorded bell on Return. Every key keeps its own take and pitch, and stereo placement follows the key's position.

### The four strength bands

Where each band's strikes come from in the original recording, ranked by loudness:

- Band | Loudness percentile | Sounds like |
- Soft | 8th to 30th | A light tap |
- Medium | 38th to 62nd | An everyday keystroke |
- Hard | 70th to 88th | A firm press |
- Slam | The hardest ~8% | Your firmest hits |

On MacBooks with the motion sensor, Keyslam reads the accelerometer about 800 times a second, compares each keystroke's jolt with how you usually type, and picks and blends strikes from these bands. How force sensing picks a band.

### Does macOS have built-in typing sounds?

Not for everyday typing. The only built-in key click is part of Slow Keys, an accessibility feature that also makes every key wait before it types. Where Mac typing sounds come from, and how to turn them on or off.

### Free ways to get mechanical keyboard sounds on a Mac

You don't have to pay. Two open-source apps play sounds system-wide for free, and two browser options cost nothing but stay inside the browser.

- Option | Cost | Plays outside the browser | Follows typing force |
- Keyslam app | $3.99 once after a 7-day trial | Yes, in any Mac app | Yes, on MacBooks with the motion sensor |
- Mechvibes | Free, open source | Yes | Not advertised |
- KeyEcho | Free, open source; paid packs optional | Yes | Not advertised |
- Opera GX keyboard sounds | Free with the browser | No, only in Opera GX | Not advertised |
- Keyslam simulator | Free in any browser | No, only on that page | You pick the strength |

Prices and features from each app's own site (mechvibes.com; GitHub; macOS README; keyecho.app; KeyEcho llms.txt; GitHub; opera.com), checked November 2, 2026. Full details in every Mac keyboard sound app, compared.

A free app is the better pick if you don't want to spend anything, you want open-source code you can read, or you only want sounds now and then. Mechvibes or KeyEcho will do the job. See the free keyboard sound apps for Mac for what free means with each one.

Keyslam is worth $3.99 if you want the sound to follow how hard you type on a MacBook, recordings of named boards with credited CC0 sources, and an app that makes no network connections.

### Caveats before you start

- The feel stays the same. Only the sound changes. Travel and resistance are still MacBook keys.

- Bluetooth adds delay. Keyslam starts the sound as the key goes down, with an audio buffer of about 5 ms. Bluetooth headphones add their own delay on top, so wired headphones or the built-in speakers feel tightest.

- Force sensing needs the sensor. The M1 MacBook Air, the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, Intel Macs and desktops play at the strength you pick. Check which MacBooks have an accelerometer.

- External keyboards work. The sensor feels the MacBook's case, so keys on an external board play at your usual strength.

- Password fields stay silent. macOS doesn't deliver those keystrokes to any app.

- Calls. On speakers, your microphone can pick the sound up. Wear headphones, or flip the switch at the top of Keyslam's menu off before the call.

- Battery. After 3 minutes without typing, the audio and the motion sensor switch off.

### Questions about MacBook keyboard sounds

Do I need to keep the app running?
Yes. The sound comes from the app, so it stops when you quit. Keyslam lives in the menu bar with no Dock icon, and the Open at login checkbox starts it after every restart.

Can I make the MacBook's own keys louder or clickier?
No. MacBook keys are a low-travel design and macOS has no setting that changes how they sound. You can add a sound with an app, or plug in a real mechanical keyboard over USB or Bluetooth.

Should I buy a mechanical keyboard instead?
If you want the feel as well as the sound, yes. Only a real board changes how the keys move. A sound app costs less, adds nothing to your bag and works on the MacBook keyboard in your lap. You can also use both: Keyslam plays for external keyboards too.

### On your phone? Keyslam runs on your Mac

Open https://keyslam.com/download/ on your Mac to download it (macOS 13 or later, free 7-day trial).

# Mechanical Keyboard Sound Types: Clicky vs Tactile vs Linear
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/mechanical-keyboard-sound-types/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Guide
## Mechanical keyboard sound types, explained

Clicky, tactile and linear switches, buckling springs, Topre domes, laptop keys and typewriters all make sound in different ways. Here's the mechanism behind each one, with a real recording to play as you read.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: mechanical switches come in three sound types. Clicky switches, like Cherry MX Blue, have a part that snaps and clicks as the key actuates. Tactile switches, like MX Brown, have a bump you feel but barely hear. Linear switches, like MX Red, slide straight down, so you mostly hear the keycap bottoming out. Buckling springs, Topre, laptop and typewriter keys work differently again. After the switch, the keycaps, plate, case and desk decide most of the sound.

### What you hear in one keystroke

Slow a single keystroke down and it has up to four parts. Every sound type below is a different mix of them.

- The click. Only clicky switches have it: a jacket or bar inside the switch snaps as the key actuates, partway down and before the bottom.
- The bottom-out. The stem hits the bottom of its housing and the keycap's energy goes into the plate and case. This is the main sound of every mechanical board.
- The ring. What the case, plate, springs and desk do after the hit. A hollow case rings; a heavy or foam-filled one goes quiet fast. Springs can add a metallic ping.
- The return. When you let go, the spring pushes the stem back up and it taps the top of the housing. Clicky switches click again.

### Clicky: a click before the bottom

A clicky switch adds a dedicated noise-maker. In Cherry MX Blue it's a click jacket, a plastic sleeve on the stem that catches and then snaps down at the actuation point, 2.2 mm into its 4 mm of travel. Some other brands use a thin click bar instead. Either way you get a crisp, high click on every press and a smaller one on release. That usually makes clicky switches the loudest of the three switch families.

Hear it next to the other two Cherry switches in Cherry MX Blue vs Brown vs Red.

### Buckling spring: a spring that snaps

IBM's Model F and Model M keyboards make their click a different way. Under each key sits a long coiled spring; pressed far enough, it buckles, and that sudden snap is both the click you hear and the moment the key registers. The spring keeps ringing a little after the snap, which is why these boards sound loud and springy rather than just sharp. Our Unicomp pack is a buckling-spring keyboard by Unicomp, which carries on the Model M design; the Model F pack is an early-1980s IBM Model F XT.

### Tactile: a bump you feel

A tactile switch has a bump on the stem's legs that you push past at actuation, but nothing that clicks. MX Brown's bump peaks at 55 cN. Some enthusiast tactiles, like the Hako Violet switches in the WhiteFox pack, have a much more pronounced bump. Because the sound is mostly bottom-out and return, the keyboard around the switch matters a lot: our Leopold and MX Brown packs use the same switch and sound clearly different, partly because the Leopold has a mix of PBT and GMK keycaps and was miked from a wrist rest, right in front of the keys.

### Linear: smooth all the way down

A linear switch has no bump and no click, just a spring and a straight slide. MX Red actuates at 45 cN. With nothing happening mid-press, linear boards can be very quiet when you type lightly, and almost all of their sound comes from the bottom-out when you don't. Lubed or waxed linears sound smoother and softer, which is where the word creamy comes from. Our Vintage Technics pack is a modded board with waxed Gateron Yellow linears; the MX Red pack is a Corsair K95. MX Black is a Leopold FC980M PD with Cherry's heavier Black linears, and Gateron Red a GMMK TKL with Gateron Red switches.

### Topre: a dome and a spring

Topre isn't a mechanical switch in the strict sense. Under each key sits a rubber dome with a conical spring inside, and the keystroke is detected electro-capacitively, with no metal contacts touching. The dome cushions the bottom-out, so instead of a clack you get the low, rounded sound enthusiasts call thock. Our pack is a Happy Hacking Keyboard.

### Laptop keys: short and soft

Laptop keys aren't mechanical switches either. The 2018 MacBook Pro in our Laptop pack uses Apple's butterfly mechanism: a very short press onto a dome switch under a thin keycap. Short travel and little moving mass make a quick, soft tap with almost no ring. Current MacBooks have gone back to a scissor mechanism.

### Typewriters: a strike, not a switch

A typewriter key does mechanical work. On a manual like the Olivetti Lettera 22, your finger swings a typebar into the platen, so a light press and a hard press sound very different. On an electric IBM Selectric II, a motor rotates and tilts a typeball into the paper, so the machine, not your finger, sets the force. Both are louder and ring longer than a computer keyboard, and in Keyslam Return comes with a bell. More in typewriter sounds for Mac.

### Beyond the switch: what changes the sound

Put one switch into five keyboards and you get five sounds. These are the parts that push a board toward a deeper thock or a brighter clack.

- Part | Deeper, more muted when… | Brighter, more clacky when… |
- Keycaps | Thick PBT | Thin ABS |
- Plate | Polycarbonate, FR4 or POM, or no plate | Aluminum, steel or brass |
- Mount | Gasket or soft top mount | Tray mount screwed to the case |
- Case | Heavy, or filled with foam | Hollow plastic |
- Stabilizers | Lubed and tuned | Dry, so Space and Return rattle |
- Your typing | Light presses that stop short of the bottom | Hard bottom-outs |
- Desk | Desk mat or a soft surface | Bare wood or glass |

General tendencies from how boards are built, not rules: a heavy hitter can make any board clack.

### Every board on this page, measured

Each pack is cut from one real typing recording. Every strike is detected and paired with its key-up; the strikes are sorted by natural loudness into four bands (soft is roughly the 8th to 30th percentile, medium the 38th to 62nd, hard the 70th to 88th, and slam the hardest ~8%), and each band is leveled to a consistent target. Every pack then plays at the same loudness, −28 LUFS.

- Board | Family | Strikes per band (soft · medium · hard · slam) | Key-up takes | Soft to slam | Hear it |
- MX Blue | Clicky | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 6 | 11.5 dB | |
- MX Brown | Tactile | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 4 | 10.9 dB | |
- MX Red | Linear | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 6 | 10.2 dB | |
- MX Black | Linear | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 4 | 11.2 dB | |
- Gateron Red | Linear | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 6 | 11.7 dB | |
- Topre | Electro-capacitive | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 3 | 10.5 dB | |
- Leopold | Tactile | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 4 | 9.9 dB | |
- WhiteFox | Tactile | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 5 | 10.6 dB | |
- Rainy 75 | Mechanical | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 5 | 11.4 dB | |
- Unicomp | Buckling spring | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 6 | 9.4 dB | |
- Model F | Buckling spring | 6 · 6 · 6 · 5 | 5 | 10.3 dB | |
- Vintage Technics | Linear, modded | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 6 | 11.6 dB | |
- Laptop | Butterfly | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | 5 | 11.5 dB | |
- Selectric | Typewriter | 6 · 1 · 6 · 6 | None | 12.4 dB | |
- Olivetti | Typewriter | 6 · 6 · 6 · 6 | None | 14.3 dB | |

Soft to slam: how much louder the slam band plays than the soft band, from the median level of the first 40 ms of each regular-key strike. Leveling pulls each band toward a fixed target, so most boards land at 10 to 12 dB; the manual Olivetti keeps the most of its natural spread. The Selectric recording gave only one clean medium strike, so its medium presses blend that strike with its neighbors. Measured November 2, 2026.

### Sound types: questions

What does a mechanical keyboard sound like?
A short, percussive clack each time a key bottoms out, plus a lighter tap when it springs back up. Clicky switches add a sharp click on top. Depending on the keycaps and case it can be deep and muted or bright and sharp. Play all 15 real boards in the table above to hear the range.

What is a keyboard sound profile?
Enthusiast shorthand for how a whole board sounds: its pitch (deep or bright), its texture (smooth, scratchy or rattly) and how long each key rings. It comes from the switch, keycaps, plate, mount, case and stabilizers together, which is why two boards with the same switch can have different sound profiles.

Is a MacBook keyboard mechanical?
No. MacBook keys press a small dome switch through a butterfly mechanism (on many 2015 to 2019 models) or a scissor mechanism (current models). There are no individual mechanical switches, which is why MacBooks are so quiet. Apps like Keyslam add the sound of a mechanical board through your speakers or headphones.

Do keycaps or switches change the sound more?
Between two switches that don't click, the keycaps, plate and case usually change the sound more than the switch does. The exception is clicky switches: a click jacket or click bar adds a sound nothing else removes. Compare the MX Brown and Leopold packs above: same switch, different board.

# Thocky vs Clacky vs Creamy Keyboards: Hear Each Sound
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/thocky-vs-clacky-keyboard-sound/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Guide
## Thocky vs clacky vs creamy: what the sound words mean

Keyboard people describe sound with a small, made-up vocabulary. Here's what each word means, what causes it, and a real board to play for each one.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: thocky means deep and muted, a low, rounded “thock”. Clacky means higher, sharper and brighter. Creamy means smooth and soft-edged, with no scratch or rattle, usually from well-lubed linear switches. Poppy is short, crisp and a little higher, like a pop. The words describe pitch and texture, not volume, and the keycaps, plate, case and lube shape them as much as the switch does.

### The sound words, side by side

- Word | What you hear | Usually comes from | Closest board here |
- Thocky | Low, rounded and muted, with a short ring | Thick PBT caps, a dense or foam-filled case, a softer plate, damped switches | Topre, Rainy 75
|
- Clacky | Higher, sharper and brighter, with more ring | Thin ABS caps, a metal plate, a hollow case, hard bottom-outs | MX Red, WhiteFox
|
- Creamy | Smooth and soft-edged: no scratch, ping or rattle | Lubed linear switches, tuned stabilizers, foam | Rainy 75, Vintage Technics
|
- Poppy | Short, crisp and a little higher; a quick pop, then quiet | Long-pole linear switches, the tape mod | No textbook match yet; nearest is the crisp Leopold
|
- Clicky | A sharp, separate click before the bottom | A click jacket or click bar inside the switch, or a buckling spring | MX Blue, Unicomp
|

Board matches are our picks, not a standard; people use these words loosely. The Rainy 75's uploader tagged it “creamy” and “thocky” on Freesound. Each board is a real CC0 recording, leveled to the same loudness.

#### Play two in a row

Same phrase, same medium strength, two boards back to back.

### What does thocky mean?

Thock is onomatopoeia: the word sounds like the noise. A thocky keyboard has most of its sound in the low and low-mid frequencies, a soft attack and a short decay, closer to a wooden block than a plastic tap. People use it as praise, and it's the sound many custom-keyboard builders chase. The Topre pack is the classic example: its rubber domes cushion every bottom-out, which is why it's our first pick for ASMR keyboard sounds on a Mac. For a mechanical board described the same way, the Rainy 75 pack is one its uploader tagged “thocky”. (Searching for the Thock app instead? Two different Mac apps share that name; here's which Thock app for Mac is which.)

### What makes a keyboard sound thocky?

- Dense keycaps. Thick PBT caps absorb more of the hit and push the pitch down.

- A softer plate or mount. Polycarbonate or FR4 plates and gasket mounts flex a little, which takes the edge off the high frequencies.

- A heavy or foam-filled case. Less empty space means less hollow ring.

- Damping in the switch. Topre domes and silent switches soften the bottom-out.

- A lighter touch. Hard bottom-outs add brightness to any board.

### What makes a keyboard sound clacky?

The opposite recipe: thin ABS keycaps, a stiff aluminum or brass plate, a hollow plastic case and hard bottom-outs. Clacky isn't worse, just brighter, and plenty of people prefer it because it sounds fast and gives clear feedback. The MX Red pack, recorded on a Corsair K95, is a clacky board; the WhiteFox is punchier, with a longer ring.

### What does creamy mean?

Creamy describes texture more than pitch. On a creamy board each press glides, the bottom-out is soft-edged, and there's no scratch from dry switches, ping from springs or rattle from stabilizers. It usually means lubed linear switches in a well-damped board. Creamy and thocky often go together, but they aren't the same thing. Our closest matches are the Rainy 75 pack, which its uploader tagged both “creamy” and “thocky” (the switches aren't named), and the Vintage Technics pack, an old Technics-branded board with wax-lubed Gateron Yellow linears.

### How to make your keyboard sound creamy

- Lube the switches. A thin coat of switch lubricant on the stem rails and inside the housing smooths the travel and takes out scratch. Linear switches gain the most.
- Tune the stabilizers. Lube the wire ends and housings under Space, Return, Shift and Backspace so the long keys stop rattling.
- Add foam. Case foam, and a thin sheet between the plate and PCB on boards that allow it, removes the hollow ring.
- Try the tape mod. A few layers of painter's tape on the back of the PCB deepen the sound and make it a little poppier.
- Finish with thicker keycaps and a desk mat. PBT caps and a soft surface take out the last of the clack.

All of that needs a mechanical keyboard you can open. On a MacBook, the closest you can get is a recording: Keyslam plays the Rainy 75, Vintage Technics or Topre board on every key you press, in all your apps. See mechanical keyboard sounds for Mac.

### Poppy and clicky, briefly

Poppy is a short, crisp, slightly higher sound that stops quickly. You hear it from long-pole linear switches, whose stems bottom out on a center pole, and from boards with the tape mod. Clicky is the sharp, separate click of switches like Cherry MX Blue, or the snap of a buckling spring like the Unicomp. It's a mechanism rather than a texture, and it tends to dominate whatever else the board does.

### Typing force changes the word

How hard you type moves any board along the scale. Light presses that stop short of the bottom sound softer and rounder; hard bottom-outs add clack. In Keyslam each board has four bands of real strikes, from soft to slam, and on MacBooks with the motion sensor the band follows how hard you hit. How force sensing works.

### Keyboard sound words: questions

Is thock the same as creamy?
No, though they often come together. Thock is about pitch: deep and muted. Creamy is about texture: smooth, with no scratch, ping or rattle. A board can be thocky and scratchy, or creamy and fairly bright.

What does a poppy keyboard sound like?
Short and crisp, a little higher than thock, with a quick pop and almost no ring. Long-pole linear switches and the tape mod are common ways to get it.

Are thocky keyboards quieter?
Usually a little, because a thocky sound has less high-frequency energy, and that's the part that carries across a room. A hard typist on a thocky board can still be loud: volume comes mostly from how hard you bottom out.

Can I make a MacBook sound thocky?
Not the physical keyboard, but you can play a thocky recording on every key. In Keyslam, pick Topre, Rainy 75 or Vintage Technics. With headphones, you're the only one who hears it.

# Is Input Monitoring Safe on Mac? Keyloggers vs Sound Apps
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/is-input-monitoring-safe-mac/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Privacy guide
## Is Input Monitoring safe on a Mac?

Keyboard sound apps need Input Monitoring to hear your key presses. Here's what that permission allows, how it differs from a keylogger, and how to check any app yourself.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Input Monitoring is as safe as the app you give it to. It lets an app see each key you press in other apps, which is exactly what a keylogger needs too. So the real question is what the app does with those keys: whether it stores them, sends them somewhere, or does neither. macOS keeps password fields out of reach, and you can switch the permission off per app at any time in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Input Monitoring.

### What Input Monitoring lets an app see

Apple's wording is short: “Some apps can monitor your keyboard, mouse, or trackpad even when you're using other apps.” You choose which ones (Apple: control access to input monitoring). That covers key presses and pointer input. It doesn't cover your screen, your files, your microphone or the network. Screen, files and microphone each have their own switch; internet access has none at all.

### Mac permissions, and which ones keyboard sounds need

- Permission (Privacy & Security) | What it lets an app do | Needed for keyboard sounds? | Keyslam asks for it? |
- Input Monitoring | See keyboard, mouse and trackpad input even while you're using other apps | Yes, to know a key went down | Yes |
- Accessibility | Access and control your Mac through accessibility features | No, though some apps use it to watch keys | No |
- Microphone | Hear what your microphone picks up | No | No |
- Full Disk Access | Read files in protected places, like Mail and Messages data | No | No |
- (none for the internet) | macOS doesn't ask before an app connects to the internet; a third-party firewall can show it | No | Makes no connections |

Permission descriptions from Apple's Mac User Guide: Input Monitoring, Accessibility. Checked November 2, 2026.

### Is a keyboard sound app a keylogger?

It uses the same door, so the worry is fair. What makes something a keylogger is what happens next: it writes your keys down or sends them somewhere. A keyboard sound app only needs to know that a key went down, and which one, so it can pick a sound. It has no reason to keep anything.

You can't read an app's code, but you can check the two things that matter. First, does its privacy policy say plainly that it never stores or sends what you type? Second, does it make network connections? An app that never connects out can't send your keys anywhere, and one that stores nothing leaves nothing behind. The network test below takes a few minutes.

### Is a keyboard sound app safe for Mac?

Most are small, single-purpose apps. Before you grant Input Monitoring, run through this list:

- Who makes it? A developer you can name and contact is a better bet than an anonymous download.

- Is it notarized, or from the Mac App Store? macOS checks apps from outside the App Store for Apple's notarization, and warns you or blocks the app when it's missing.

- Which permissions does it ask for? Input Monitoring is enough for sounds. Be wary of an app that also wants Accessibility, Full Disk Access or the microphone without saying why.

- What does its privacy policy say about keystrokes? Look for a direct sentence, not a vague one.

- Does it have analytics, and does it connect out? Read the policy, then check with a firewall.

#### Is Klack safe?

Klack is sold on the Mac App Store ($4.99 on the Mac App Store; tryklack.com also sells a separate standalone version when we checked on November 2, 2026). Mac App Store apps run in Apple's App Sandbox and show an App Privacy section on the listing, so read its Mac App Store listing before you install. Asking about an open-source app instead? See Mechvibes vs Keyslam or all the apps compared.

### Secure input: why password fields are protected

When you click into a password field, macOS turns on secure input. While it's on, apps that monitor input don't receive your keystrokes, Input Monitoring or not. Terminal lets you switch on the same protection for everything you type there, with Terminal › Secure Keyboard Entry. Apple says it “can prevent other apps on your computer or the network” from detecting what you type (Apple: Secure Keyboard Entry).

That's also why keyboard sounds go quiet in password fields. And if an app leaves secure input switched on after you've moved on, keyboard sound apps hear nothing anywhere until it lets go.

### How to enable or revoke Input Monitoring

- Open the list. Choose Apple menu › System Settings › Privacy & Security, then click Input Monitoring.
- Read every name. Each app in the list either asked for this permission or was added by hand. Look up any you don't recognize.
- Switch off what you don't use. Turn an app's switch off and it loses access to keys you press in other apps. macOS may ask for your password or Touch ID.
- Remove apps you've deleted. Select the app and click the Remove button (−) under the list.
- Turn one back on later. Flip its switch on again. Some apps need a restart to notice; Keyslam shows a Relaunch Keyslam button when it does.

A keyboard sound app usually asks for the permission the first time it opens. Keyslam's menu has an Open Settings button that jumps straight to this list, and its install steps and requirements show where that fits in setup.

### How to check whether an app sends anything

- Install a firewall that asks. LuLu is free and open source (macOS 10.15 or later). Little Snitch is a paid option. Both alert you when an app tries to connect out.
- Open the app you're testing. Leave it running and type normally for a few minutes, in a few different apps.
- Watch for alerts with its name. Any connection attempt shows up with the app's name and the server it wants to reach. You decide whether to allow it.
- Check Activity Monitor for a second opinion. Open Activity Monitor and click Network. It shows how much data your Mac is sending, and you can sort the list by process.

With Keyslam you should see nothing: it makes no network connections. Buying opens Stripe Checkout in your browser, so any connection you see then belongs to the browser, not to Keyslam. The license key you paste is checked on your Mac.

### What Keyslam does with Input Monitoring

PermissionInput Monitoring, nothing else
Event tapListen-only: it can't change, block or add a keystroke
What it usesWhich key went down or up, to pick a sound, its stereo position and its key-up sound
What it keepsNothing you type. No log of keys
NetworkNone. The license key is Ed25519-signed and verified offline
AnalyticsNone
Trial dateStored in your Mac's Keychain
Motion sensorProcessed in memory to estimate strength; never stored or sent

### Questions about Input Monitoring

Does Input Monitoring let an app see my passwords?
Not from password fields. macOS switches on secure input there and doesn't deliver those keystrokes to apps that monitor input. A password typed into an ordinary text box is different: any app with Input Monitoring can see it like any other text.

What happens if I turn Input Monitoring off for a keyboard sound app?
It can no longer hear keys in other apps, so it goes quiet. Nothing else breaks. When Keyslam opens without the permission, its menu says “Needs Input Monitoring access” and offers an Open Settings button.

Is Accessibility permission the same thing?
No. Input Monitoring lets an app watch your keyboard, mouse and trackpad. Accessibility lets an app control your Mac through accessibility features, which is broader. A keyboard sound app needs only Input Monitoring, and Keyslam asks for nothing else.

- For force sensing: MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, or MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later. Every other Mac plays all the sounds at a strength you pick. See which MacBooks have the motion sensor and keyboard sounds on Intel Macs and desktops.

Not sure about your setup? The Keyslam FAQ gives a straight yes or no for AirPods, external keyboards, calls and Intel Macs.

### How to install Keyslam

Setup takes about a minute.

- Open the .dmg and drag Keyslam onto the Applications folder next to it.

- Open Keyslam from Applications. macOS asks if you're sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet; click Open. A keyboard icon appears in the menu bar.

- Allow Input Monitoring. Click the icon, then Open Settings on the “Keyslam needs Input Monitoring” card, and turn Keyslam on under Privacy & Security › Input Monitoring. If the menu then shows Relaunch Keyslam, click it.

- Pick a board, set the volume and type. Your 7-day trial starts on this first launch, with no account or card.

- Optional: tick Open at login so the sounds are back after every restart.

### If macOS says Keyslam can't be opened

The copy from keyslam.com is notarized by Apple, so the only prompt you should see is the usual one for apps from the internet. If macOS instead says Apple can't check Keyslam for malicious software, or that it's damaged, that copy didn't come from this page or the download broke. Move it to the Trash and download it again from keyslam.com. Don't override the warning for a copy you got somewhere else.

### Updating

Keyslam doesn't check for updates by itself, because it makes no network connections. New versions are listed on the changelog and on this page. To update, quit Keyslam, download the new .dmg and drag it over the old copy. Your license, trial date and settings carry over. If macOS asks for Input Monitoring again, switch it back on.

### Uninstalling

- Quit Keyslam from its menu (the Quit button at the bottom).

- Drag Keyslam from Applications to the Trash.

- Remove it from Input Monitoring in System Settings › Privacy & Security with the minus button.

- Optional: delete ~/Library/Application Support/Keyslam if you added your own packs.

Your license stays in your Mac's login Keychain, so if you reinstall later, Keyslam is still activated.

### Download questions

Is Keyslam notarized by Apple?
Yes. The download is signed with a Developer ID and notarized and stapled by Apple, so it opens with the normal prompt for apps from the internet.

I'm on my phone. Can I get Keyslam on my Mac?
Yes. Open this page on your Mac, or email yourself the link: https://keyslam.com/download/.

# Keyslam FAQ: What It Does and Doesn't Do (Yet)
URL: https://keyslam.com/faq/
Updated: 2026-11-02

FAQ
## Keyslam questions, answered straight

What Keyslam does today, what it doesn't do yet, and the details behind each answer. Every “no” here is a real no, checked against the app.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Keyslam is a Mac-only menu-bar app (macOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel) that plays real keyboard recordings as you type. It works with any keyboard and with AirPods, needs no account or internet, and costs $3.99 once after a 7-day trial. It doesn't play mouse clicks. ⌃⌥⌘K turns the sounds off or on from any app, and they pause on their own while an app is using the microphone.

### What Keyslam does today

- Topic | Answer | What to know |
- Intel Macs and desktops | Yes | Every sound works on macOS 13 Ventura or later; you pick the strength. Keyslam on Intel Macs. |
- Force sensing | MacBooks with the sensor | MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later; MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later. Which MacBooks have it. |
- AirPods and Bluetooth | Yes, with a delay | The wireless link adds its own lag. Built-in speakers and wired headphones don't add it. Why AirPods lag, and a test. |
- External keyboards | Yes | Every keyboard plays. Force sensing feels the MacBook's case, so external keys play at your usual strength. |
- Going quiet during calls | Yes, on by default | Sounds pause while any app is using the microphone and come back when it's free. |
- Shortcut to switch sounds off | Yes: ⌃⌥⌘K | Works in any app. Pick ⌃⌥⌘S, ⌃⌥⌘M or ⌃⌥⌘T instead, or switch it off, in the menu. |
- Louder than the Mac's volume | No | Keyslam's slider is a mix level under the Mac's own volume. |
- Mouse click sounds | No | Keyboard sounds only. |
- Windows, iPhone, iPad | No | Mac only. The simulator runs in any browser. |
- Mac App Store | No | Sold directly. None of the 42 Mac App Store keyboard-sound apps we checked offers force sensing. All apps compared. |
- Internet connection | Not needed | The app makes no network connections; the license is checked offline. Privacy details. |
- Account or card for the trial | No | 7 days, everything unlocked. Rather not pay at all? See free keyboard sound apps for Mac. |
- Your own sounds | Yes | WAV, AIFF or FLAC with a pack.json. Pack format. |
- Key-up sounds, stereo, open at login | Yes | Each is a checkbox in the menu. |
- Password fields | Silent | macOS hides those keystrokes from all apps. Is Input Monitoring safe on a Mac? |
- Battery and sleep | Stays out of the way | Audio and the motion sensor switch off after 3 idle minutes. |
- All the Macs you own | Yes | One personal license, nothing counts activations. |
- Download | Yes | Version 1.0.1, notarized by Apple. Download it here. |

Checked against Keyslam 1.0.0 on November 2, 2026.

### The questions people ask most

Does Keyslam go quiet during video calls?
Yes, by default. While any app is using the microphone, as on a video call, Keyslam pauses its sounds and the menu says “Paused while the mic is in use”; they come back when the mic is free. Keyslam doesn't record or open the microphone and asks for no microphone permission; it only checks whether the input is in use. On macOS 13 with AirPods or a USB headset as the microphone it may not notice the call, so press the on/off shortcut instead. Untick Quiet during calls in the menu to keep sounds playing.

Is there a shortcut to switch the sounds off?
Yes. Press ⌃⌥⌘K (Control-Option-Command-K) in any app to turn the sounds off or back on. Next to “Turn sounds on/off with” in the menu you can pick ⌃⌥⌘S, ⌃⌥⌘M or ⌃⌥⌘T instead, or switch the shortcut off. It needs no extra permission, and if another app already uses the combination, the menu says so.

Can Keyslam play louder than my Mac's volume?
No. Keyslam's volume slider starts at about half and goes to about twice that level at the right end, but it sits under the Mac's own volume. If it's still quiet, turn the Mac up.

Does Keyslam play mouse click sounds?
No. Keyslam listens to the keyboard only, so clicks and trackpad taps stay silent. Letters, numbers, Space, Return, Delete, the modifier keys and Caps Lock all play, and most keys add a softer key-up sound when you let go (the two typewriters don't).

Can I use Keyslam on Windows, an iPhone or a Chromebook?
No. Keyslam is a Mac app for macOS 13 Ventura or later. On a Mac it plays while you type in any app, Chrome included. To hear the boards on any other device, use the free keyboard simulator in a browser.

- Who makes Keyslam and how the sounds are made: about Keyslam.

- Silent keys, permission prompts and delay: the no-sound guide.

- Anything else: contact us.

# Keyslam Privacy Policy: An App With No Network or Analytics
URL: https://keyslam.com/privacy/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Privacy
## Keyslam privacy policy

The Keyslam app makes no network connections and has no analytics. This website uses Google Analytics to count visits. This page lists everything the app and the website handle, where it goes and how long it stays.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: the Keyslam app makes no network connections at all. It uses which key went down to pick a sound, never stores or sends what you type, checks your Ed25519-signed license offline, and keeps your trial date in your Mac's Keychain. Payments go through Stripe; the seller is Venture Deals, Co.

Last updated November 2, 2026

### The Mac app

- What | Where it lives | Leaves your Mac? | Kept |
- Which key went down | Memory only, to pick a sound | No | Not stored |
- Motion sensor readings | Memory only, to judge strength | No | Not stored |
- Trial start date | Your Mac's Keychain | No | Until you delete it; it survives reinstalls |
- License key (includes the email you paid with) | Your Mac's Keychain | No | Until you choose Remove License From This Mac |
- Settings (board, volume, switches) | The app's preferences on your Mac | No | Until you delete them |
- Your own sound packs | ~/Library/Application Support/Keyslam/Packs | No | Until you delete them |

Network. The Keyslam app makes no network connections. Your license key is digitally signed (Ed25519) and checked offline on your Mac, and a periodic re-check only repeats that offline signature check. Buying opens checkout in your web browser, and activation comes back through a link that opens the app on your Mac.

Key presses. Keyslam uses macOS's Input Monitoring permission to learn which key went down and whether it was a letter, Space, Return, Delete or a modifier. Its keyboard tap is listen-only, so it can't change or block anything you type. macOS doesn't deliver keystrokes from password fields to any app. More on whether Input Monitoring is safe to allow.

Motion sensor. On MacBooks with Apple's motion sensor, accelerometer readings are processed in memory to estimate how hard each key landed. They are never stored or sent. After 3 minutes without typing, the sensor is switched off.

No analytics. The app contains no analytics, crash reporting, advertising or tracking code.

Updates. There is no built-in update check. If a future version adds one, or any other network feature, this page will be updated to say so.

### This website

Google Analytics. keyslam.com uses Google Analytics 4 to count visits and to see which pages lead people to try a sound, download the app or buy it. Google receives the page address, the referring site, your approximate location, your device and browser type, and those few events; it doesn't receive anything you type into forms. Google Analytics doesn't store your IP address. Ad features are off: no advertising cookies, no remarketing and no ad personalization. In the EU, the UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, analytics starts off and Google Analytics sends only cookieless pings until you choose Allow in the banner. See how Google uses data from sites that use its services.

Your choice. Analytics in this browser is on. Your choice is saved in this browser's local storage. Browser tracking protection and ad blockers that block Google Analytics work too.

Everything else is ours. Fonts, images and sounds are served from keyslam.com itself, and sounds you play in the browser are processed on your device.

Hosting. The site is a set of static pages hosted on GitHub Pages. Like any web host, GitHub may log basic request data such as IP addresses to run and protect the service; see GitHub's privacy statement.

Forms. The notify-me, contact and lost-key forms send what you type to our own Cloudflare Worker, not to a mailing-list or helpdesk company. We use your email only to reply to you or to send the launch link.

- Form or page | What is sent | Where it goes | Why |
- Every page (Google Analytics) | Page address, referring site, approximate location, device and browser type, and a few events: starting checkout, downloading the app, trying a sound, a completed purchase | Google | To count visits and see which pages help people find Keyslam |
- Notify-me form | Email, the page you were on, whether you want the link on your Mac, time | Our Cloudflare Worker | To send one launch email |
- Contact form | Email, topic, message, time | Our Cloudflare Worker | To reply to you |
- Lost-key form | Email and receipt number (or your card's last 4 digits); our Worker looks up that email's purchases at Stripe and checks the number | Not stored by us | To show your license key |
- Thank-you page after buying | Stripe session id, used to fetch your key | Our Worker asks Stripe; your browser keeps a copy of the key | To give you your key |
- Any form | A per-IP-address counter, to stop abuse | Our Cloudflare Worker | Expires after 2 minutes |

### Purchases

Payments are processed by Stripe. The seller is Venture Deals, Co. We receive your email address and order details to issue and support your license (your key is shown in your browser after checkout, not emailed); Stripe handles your card under its own privacy policy. After you pay, the thank-you page asks our Worker for your key using the Stripe session id, and the Worker confirms the payment with Stripe before signing the key.

Refunds: a full refund within 14 days if Keyslam doesn't work for you. Reply to your Stripe receipt or use the contact form. The trial, license and refund terms are on the pricing page.

### Questions

Ask anything about privacy through the contact page. For how the sounds are made and who makes Keyslam, see About Keyslam.

### Privacy questions

Does the Keyslam website use cookies?
Only Google Analytics cookies, to count visits, and only if analytics is on for you. In the EU, the UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland it starts off: Google Analytics then sets no cookies until you choose Allow. There are no advertising cookies. A few pages also keep small things in your browser's local storage, such as your analytics choice or a copy of your license key on the thank-you page. That stays in your browser.

Does the Keyslam app use Google Analytics?
No. Google Analytics runs only on this website. The Keyslam app has no analytics and makes no network connections.

Who sees my card details?
Stripe. You pay on Stripe's checkout page. The seller, Venture Deals, Co., can see your email address, the order details and the card's brand and last 4 digits (the lost-key form can match those 4 digits), but never your full card number.

How do I get my email deleted?
Send a message through the contact form from the address you want removed, and we'll delete your notify-me or contact entries.

## Keyboard sound app for Intel Macs, desktops and the M1 MacBook Air

Keyslam plays every one of its 15 real keyboard and typewriter recordings on any Mac with macOS 13 Ventura or later. The one feature that needs a newer MacBook is force sensing. Everywhere else, you pick the strength.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Yes. Keyslam is a keyboard sound app for Intel Macs, iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, the M1 MacBook Air
and the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, as long as the Mac runs macOS 13 Ventura or later. It's the same universal keyboard sound app for Mac on Apple silicon and Intel. All 15 sound packs,
key-up sounds and stereo placement work the same everywhere. Only force sensing needs the motion sensor in newer Apple silicon MacBooks, so on these Macs
you choose Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam in the menu bar. $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial.

### Every Mac that can run it, and what you get

“Oldest model” is the oldest Mac in each family that Apple lists for macOS 13 Ventura (Apple: macOS Ventura is compatible with these computers,
checked November 2, 2026). Which MacBooks have the sensor, with model identifiers, is in
which MacBooks have an accelerometer.

- Mac | Oldest model on macOS 13 | Sounds | Strength |

### What changes without the motion sensor

Nothing is locked. This is what the menu-bar app does on a Mac without the sensor:

- The Force section says: “Force sensing needs a MacBook with the motion sensor (M1 Pro/Max, M2 or later). Pick a fixed strength instead.”

- Below it is a Strength control with Soft, Medium, Hard and Slam. Medium is the default.

- The status line under the Keyslam name reads “MX Blue · Fixed strength” (or whichever board you picked).

- Strikes still vary a little from one keystroke to the next, and each key keeps its own take and pitch, like a real board.

- Key-up sounds, separate takes for Space, Return and Delete (except on Selectric and Olivetti), and stereo placement by key position all work as on any Mac.

- After 3 minutes without typing, the audio switches off so your Mac can sleep normally.

#### What the four strengths are

Each pack's strikes are cut from one real typing recording and sorted by natural loudness into four bands: soft (about the 8th to 30th percentile),
medium (38th to 62nd), hard (70th to 88th) and slam (the hardest ~8%). Each band is leveled to a consistent target. So picking Slam on an iMac plays the
hardest real strikes from that recording, not a louder copy of Medium.

### Hear fixed strength in your browser

This works like the Strength control Keyslam shows on a Mac without the sensor. Pick a strength, pick a board, then type in the box.
The browser plays the same recordings as the app.

SoftMediumHardSlam

Type here

### External keyboards and the Magic Keyboard

- On an iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio or Mac Pro: every keyboard you plug in or pair plays sounds, wired or Bluetooth, at the strength you pick.

- On a MacBook with the sensor: force sensing feels the MacBook's own case. A keystroke the sensor doesn't feel, such as one on a separate keyboard,
plays at your usual strength (the typical level Keyslam has learned from your typing) instead of dropping to Soft.

- What we haven't measured: whether a hard strike on a keyboard sitting on the same desk can reach the MacBook's sensor. So don't count on
force sensing with an external keyboard. To set the level yourself, switch off “Feel how hard you type” and the Strength control appears.

Some Macs stop getting macOS updates before macOS 15. Going by Apple's lists, the 2017 MacBook Pro and iMac are on
Ventura's list but not Sonoma's, and the 2018 and 2019 MacBook Air are on Sonoma's but not
Sequoia's. On those Macs the app's minimum macOS decides what installs:

- MacBook Pro (2017),
iMac (2017),

- MacBook Air (Retina, 13-inch,
2018 or 2019) | macOS 14 Sonoma | Yes | Yes | No | No (no motion sensor) |

macOS minimums: TapNoise from its system requirements (archived);

### Set it up on a Mac without the sensor

- Check your macOS. Apple menu › About This Mac. You need macOS 13 Ventura or later.

- Download Keyslam from the download page and drag it to Applications.

- Allow Input Monitoring when macOS asks. Keyslam uses it only to know which key went down.

- Pick a board and a strength from the keyboard icon in the menu bar. Medium is the starting point; Slam is the hardest ~8% of strikes.

### Intel Mac and desktop questions

Does Keyslam work on an Intel Mac?
Yes, on any Intel Mac that runs macOS 13 Ventura or later. Going by Apple's list, that reaches back to the 2017 MacBook Pro, iMac and iMac Pro, the 2018 MacBook Air and Mac mini, and the 2019 Mac Pro. It's one universal app. Intel Macs don't have the sensor Keyslam uses for force sensing, so you pick the strength.

Does Keyslam work on an iMac or Mac mini?
Yes, on macOS 13 Ventura or later, with any keyboard you connect, including the Magic Keyboard. The same goes for Mac Studio and Mac Pro. Desktop Macs have no motion sensor, so you choose Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam, and every keystroke plays real strikes from that band.

Does force sensing work with an external keyboard?
Don't count on it. Force sensing feels the MacBook's own case through its motion sensor. Keys on a separate keyboard usually don't register, so Keyslam plays them at your usual strength instead of soft. We haven't measured whether a hard strike on a nearby keyboard reaches the sensor through the desk. To choose the level yourself, switch off “Feel how hard you type” and pick a strength.

Does Keyslam work on macOS Ventura?
Yes. macOS 13 Ventura is the minimum, and Sonoma, Sequoia and later work too. That matters on Macs that stop at Ventura, like the 2017 MacBook Pro and iMac: Klack's App Store version needs macOS 15 and TapNoise needs macOS 14. More on each: a Klack alternative for macOS 13 and a TapNoise alternative with a free trial.

# Mechvibes Not Working on Mac? Fix No Sound and Gatekeeper
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/mechvibes-not-working-mac/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Troubleshooting
## Mechvibes not working on Mac: fixes for “can't be opened”, permissions and no sound

Mechvibes 3 runs on Apple silicon Macs, but its Mac build is experimental and needs some help from you. Here's every common problem and its fix, from Mechvibes' own notes and macOS. Checked November 2, 2026.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: on a Mac, Mechvibes 3 has four common sticking points. macOS blocks it because the build isn't notarized. It's missing Accessibility or Input Monitoring. An update broke those permissions: its own README says to remove and re-add both after every update. Or the sound is going to a different output. There's also no Intel build yet, and the old Homebrew cask is disabled. Find your symptom below; most fixes take a minute or two.

### First, check which Mechvibes you have

Select Mechvibes in Applications and choose File › Get Info to see its version.

- 3.x is Mechvibes 3, the current app, written in Rust. Version 3.4.0 came out on November 1, 2026. Its Mac download reads macOS Apple Silicon (experimental) (download page).

- 2.x is Mechvibes 2, the older Electron app. The download page says Using Mechvibes 2? It is no longer developed. Its repository was archived on October 30, 2026. If that's what you have, most fixes below won't help. Replace it with Mechvibes 3 from mechvibes.com/download.

### Find your symptom

- What you see | Most likely cause | Go to |
- “Mechvibes” Not Opened, or Apple could not verify it is free of malware | The build isn't notarized by Apple | Fix 1 |
- “Mechvibes” is damaged and can't be opened | macOS's quarantine flag on an ad-hoc signed download | Fix 1b |
- It opens, but typing makes no sound anywhere | Accessibility or Input Monitoring is off | Fix 2 |
- It worked until you updated it | The permissions still point at the old build | Fix 3 |
- Silent in one app or field, or after you type a password | Secure input is on | Fix 4 |
- The sound comes late | Bluetooth headphones or speakers | Fix 4 |
- It won't run on an Intel Mac | There's no Intel build yet | Fix 5 |
- brew install --cask mechvibes fails | The cask has been disabled | Fix 6 |
- “Install in Mechvibes” does nothing | One-click install isn't for Macs | Fix 7 |

### Setting up from scratch? Do it in this order

- Download the right file. Get the Apple silicon DMG (v3.4.0, 52.0 MB) from mechvibes.com/download. There's no Intel build yet.
- Drag Mechvibes to Applications. Open the DMG and drag the app into your Applications folder.
- Open it, then allow it in Privacy & Security. macOS blocks the first launch because the build isn't notarized. Fix 1 below shows how to allow it.
- Turn on Accessibility and Input Monitoring. Mechvibes needs both, in System Settings › Privacy & Security.
- Quit and reopen Mechvibes, then pick a pack. The permissions take effect on the next launch. Type in any app to test it.

### Fix 1: “Mechvibes Not Opened” or “can't be opened”

This is expected. The Mac build's README says: It carries only an ad-hoc signature and is NOT notarized. Notarization is Apple's automated check for apps downloaded outside the App Store, so without it, macOS won't open the app until you say so.

#### macOS 15 Sequoia and later

- Try to open Mechvibes once. macOS stops it. Click Done.
- Open System Settings › Privacy & Security. Scroll down to Security. You'll see a line saying Mechvibes was blocked.
- Click Open Anyway. Confirm, and enter your password or use Touch ID when macOS asks. Mechvibes opens.

Apple says the Open Anyway button is there for about an hour after you try to open the app (Apple: open an app from an unknown developer). If it's gone, try opening Mechvibes again first.

#### macOS 14 Sonoma and earlier

Control-click Mechvibes in Applications, choose Open, then click Open in the dialog. The System Settings route above works too.

#### Fix 1b: “Mechvibes is damaged and can't be opened”

On Apple silicon, macOS can show this for an ad-hoc signed app downloaded from the web, even when the file is fine, and Open Anyway may not appear. First, download it again from the official page, in case the file really did break. If the message comes back, you can clear macOS's quarantine flag for this one app:

- Check where it came from. Only do this for a copy from mechvibes.com/download or the GitHub release.
- Open Terminal and type the command below, with a space at the end. Don't press Return yet.
- Drag Mechvibes from Applications into the Terminal window. That fills in the path. Now press Return.
- Open Mechvibes again. It should start without the warning.

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine

This switches off Gatekeeper's check for that app entirely, so be sure about the source. For what you're trusting when you do this, see is Mechvibes safe?

### Fix 2: it opens, but there's no sound when you type

Mechvibes needs two switches on: Accessibility, which lets an app control your Mac through accessibility features (Apple), and Input Monitoring, which lets it see key presses while you work in other apps (Apple). Its macOS README talks about both entries, so check both.

- Open System Settings › Privacy & Security › Accessibility. Turn Mechvibes on. If it isn't in the list, click + and choose it from Applications.
- Go back and open Input Monitoring. Turn Mechvibes on there too, adding it with + if needed.
- Quit Mechvibes and open it again. Permissions take effect on the next launch. If you can't find its Quit command, select it in Activity Monitor and click the Stop button in the toolbar.

### Fix 3: it stopped working after an update

This is the one people least expect, and Mechvibes warns about it. Its README for v3.4.0 says: You have to remove and re-add both entries after replacing the app with a newer build.

- Quit Mechvibes.
- In Privacy & Security › Accessibility, select Mechvibes and click − to remove it. Turning the switch off isn't enough; remove the entry.
- Do the same in Input Monitoring.
- Open Mechvibes and add it back to both lists. Approve the prompts, or use + in each list. Then quit and reopen it once more.

The likely reason: macOS ties these permissions to an app's code signature, and an ad-hoc signature is different for every build. After an update, macOS sees a new app, even if the old entry's switch still looks on. Expect to repeat this after each update while the Mac build is ad-hoc signed.

### Fix 4: no sound, or the sound comes late

If both permissions are on and Mechvibes has been relaunched, work down this list:

- Check the output. Open Control Center › Sound, or System Settings › Sound › Output. Is the speaker or headphones you're listening on selected, and is the volume up?

- Check Mechvibes itself. Make sure a sound pack is selected and its volume isn't turned down.

- Check for secure input. macOS doesn't pass password-field keystrokes to apps that monitor input, so every keyboard sound app is silent there, by design. Terminal's Secure Keyboard Entry does the same for everything you type in Terminal. If sounds stop everywhere after you've typed a password, the app with that field may still be holding secure input; quitting it usually brings the sound back. More in what Input Monitoring can and can't see.

#### How to fix Mechvibes delay

Bluetooth headphones and speakers, AirPods included, add a delay to every sound your Mac plays, and with typing sounds you notice it. To check, switch the output to the built-in speakers or wired headphones and type again. If the delay goes away, it was the Bluetooth link. If it's there on built-in speakers too, report it (below).

#### Still silent?

The README is frank that this build has never been run on a real Mac by the maintainer, so you may have found a real bug. Open an issue on Mechvibes' GitHub with your Mac model, macOS version, and the steps you've tried. Reports from real Macs are how Mac bugs get found.

### Fix 5: Mechvibes on an Intel Mac

There's no fix yet. Mechvibes' own troubleshooting post says: Intel Macs are not supported yet ( issue #128 ). The good news is in that issue: an Intel Mac build is now merged and ships with the next release. Watch the download page for it.

Don't fall back on the old Homebrew cask (next fix). If you'd rather not wait, see keyboard sound apps that run on Intel Macs today.

### Fix 6: Homebrew won't install Mechvibes

The mechvibes cask still points at Mechvibes 2 (version 2.3.4), and Homebrew disabled it on September 1, 2026. Its cask data gives the reason as "disable_reason":"fails_gatekeeper_check". So brew install --cask mechvibes won't give you a working app. Download Mechvibes 3 from mechvibes.com/download instead.

### Fix 7: sound packs won't install

The library's one-click button isn't meant for Macs. In Mechvibes' words: The Install in Mechvibes button in the library works on Windows and Linux. On a Mac, click Download zip on a pack's page. Then import that ZIP in the Mechvibes app. To make your own pack, use the editor on mechvibes.com.
Wondering whether it's wise to override Gatekeeper and grant two permissions? That's answered in is Mechvibes safe?

### Rather not fix it?

If Mechvibes is working for you now, there's no need to switch. It's free, and nothing above is hard once you know it. If you'd rather have something that installs like an ordinary Mac app, two options:

- KeyEcho is free with optional paid packs. Its macOS builds are notarized, with separate downloads for Apple silicon and Intel. See KeyEcho's packs and prices.

- Keyslam is our app: $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial. It asks for Input Monitoring only, makes no network connections, runs on macOS 13 Ventura or later on Apple silicon or Intel, and on MacBooks with the motion sensor it follows how hard you type. It's Developer ID-signed and notarized by Apple, so Gatekeeper opens it with the normal prompt for apps from the internet; see the install steps and requirements.

Everything else, free and paid, is in the Mac keyboard sound app comparison, and the Mechvibes trade-offs are laid out in Mechvibes vs Keyslam vs Klack.

### Mechvibes on Mac: quick answers

Why is Mechvibes not working on my Mac?
Usually one of these: macOS blocked it because it isn't notarized (Fix 1), Accessibility or Input Monitoring is off (Fix 2), an update invalidated those permissions (Fix 3), or the sound is going to another output (Fix 4). On an Intel Mac, there's no build yet (Fix 5).

Does Mechvibes work on Apple silicon and Intel Macs?
Apple silicon, yes: version 3.4.0 has an Apple silicon build, marked experimental. Intel, not yet. GitHub issue 128 says an Intel build is merged and ships with the next release.

Why does Mechvibes stop working after every update?
Because macOS treats each new ad-hoc signed build as a different app. Its README says you have to remove and re-add both the Accessibility and Input Monitoring entries after replacing the app with a newer build.

How do I add custom sound packs to Mechvibes on Mac?
Open a pack's page on mechvibes.com, click Download zip, and import the ZIP in the app. The one-click Install in Mechvibes button works only on Windows and Linux. To build your own pack, use the editor on mechvibes.com.

Every Mechvibes quote on this page is copied word for word from these, checked November 2, 2026. Mechvibes changes quickly; if a fix here is out of date, tell us.
