# Thock App for Mac: Which Thock Is Which, Plus an Alternative
URL: https://keyslam.com/alternatives/thock/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Thock for Mac
## Thock for Mac: which Thock is which?

Search for Thock and you'll find two Mac apps with the same name, different makers and different prices. Here's how to tell them apart and install the one you want, checked November 2, 2026.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: there are two Mac apps called Thock, made by different people. Thock (open source) is free under the MIT license, made by Kamil Lobinski, installed from GitHub or Homebrew, and needs macOS 13.5 or later. Thock - Mechanical Keyboard is a $4.99 Mac App Store app by Alan Agon, with its site at thock.pro, and needs macOS 13.0 or later. The open-source project says it is not distributed on the App Store and is not affiliated with any app that has taken this name. Neither one says it reads the MacBook motion sensor. Keyslam does, for $3.99 once.

### The two Thocks, side by side

- | Thock (open source) | Thock - Mechanical Keyboard (App Store) |
- Made by | Kamil Lobinski | Alan Agon (App Store seller) |
- Website | thockapp.com | thock.pro |
- Price | Free, MIT license | $4.99, no trial |
- Where you get it | GitHub releases or Homebrew | Mac App Store |
- macOS | 13.5 Ventura or later | 13.0 or later |
- Latest version | 1.23.0, March 28, 2026 | 1.01, January 27, 2026 |
- Sounds | Built-in packs, custom packs in a simple JSON format, and a community pack registry in Settings | 22 Cherry MX and Gateron packs listed on its site |
- Key-up sounds | Not stated in its README or llms.txt | Yes: plays on key down and key up |
- Typing force | Not advertised | Its site calls the packs velocity aware without saying how velocity is measured |
- Extras | Mutes while music plays, spatial audio by key position, a Raycast extension and a command-line tool | A custom hotkey to pause or resume, a 15-minute snooze, Family Sharing |
- Privacy | Not stated on the pages we checked | The app itself does not collect, store, or transmit personal data. Its website uses Microsoft Clarity and Vercel Analytics |
From thockapp.com llms.txt, kamillobinski/thock on GitHub, Thock - Mechanical Keyboard on the Mac App Store, thock.pro and thock.pro privacy policy, checked November 2, 2026. We left out GitHub star counts: they change daily and the numbers we found disagreed.

### Version and price log

What we could date from each app's own release records, as of November 2, 2026.

- Date | Thock | What happened | Source |
- January 27, 2026 | App Store | Version 1.01 released. Still the current version on November 2, 2026, at $4.99. | iTunes Lookup API record |
- March 28, 2026 | Open source | Release 1.23.0. Still the latest release on November 2, 2026, with 13 more commits on its main branch since. | Thock 1.23.0 release notes |
- November 2, 2026 | Both | Checked by us. Open source: free, MIT. App Store: $4.99, Family Sharing for up to six people. | GitHub, App Store |

### How to tell which Thock you have

- Think back to how you got it. Paid $4.99 in the App Store? It's Alan Agon's Thock. Downloaded it free from GitHub, or installed it with Homebrew? It's Kamil Lobinski's open-source Thock.

- Check your App Store purchases. Open the App Store and click your name at the bottom of the sidebar. If Thock is in your purchased apps, it's the App Store one.

- Ask Homebrew. In Terminal, run brew list --cask. If thock is in the list, Homebrew installed the open-source app.

- Look at the version. Select Thock in Applications and choose File › Get Info. On November 2, 2026, 1.01 was the App Store version and 1.23.0 the latest open-source release.

### How to install each Thock

#### Thock (open source)

Install it with Homebrew, using the command from its README: brew install --cask kamillobinski/thock/thock. Or download the ZIP from the GitHub releases page. It needs macOS 13.5 Ventura or later, and like any keyboard sound app it needs a macOS privacy permission before it can see your key presses.

#### Thock - Mechanical Keyboard (App Store)

Buy it from its Mac App Store listing for $4.99. It needs macOS 13.0 or later, installs and updates through the App Store, and Family Sharing lets up to six family members use it.

### How Keyslam compares with each Thock

- It feels how hard you type. On MacBook Pro with M1 Pro or M1 Max and later, and MacBook Air and MacBook Pro with M2 and later, Keyslam reads the built-in motion sensor about 800 times a second. Each keystroke then plays a real strike from the matching soft, medium, hard or slam band. See how force sensing works.

- More than switches. Alongside the mechanical boards there are two typewriters (Selectric and Olivetti) and a MacBook keyboard (Laptop), all real recordings. App Store Thock lists Cherry MX and Gateron packs; the open-source Thock takes custom and community packs.

- macOS 13 Ventura, Apple silicon or Intel. That's the same minimum as App Store Thock, and a little lower than the open-source Thock's 13.5.

- $3.99 once, after a 7-day free trial. App Store Thock is $4.99 with no trial. The open-source Thock is free.

- No network connections at all. The license key is verified offline on your Mac. App Store Thock's privacy policy says it runs entirely on your Mac too; the open-source Thock's pages we checked don't say either way.

#### When a Thock is the better pick

The open-source Thock if you want it free, like the idea of a CLI or a Raycast extension, or want to install community packs from inside the app. App Store Thock if you'd rather buy through Apple and share with your family, or want its 22 Cherry MX and Gateron packs. Keyslam is available; until then, every board plays in the browser simulator.

### Thock questions

Is Thock free?
The open-source Thock is: it's free under the MIT license. The App Store app called Thock - Mechanical Keyboard costs $4.99, with no trial. Prices checked November 2, 2026.

Are the open-source Thock and the App Store Thock the same app?
No. They have different developers, websites and version numbers. The open-source project's llms.txt says Thock is not distributed on the App Store and is not affiliated with any app that has taken this name.

Does Thock react to how hard you type?
Neither says it reads the MacBook motion sensor. The open-source Thock doesn't advertise it. App Store Thock's site calls its packs velocity aware but doesn't say how velocity is measured. Keyslam reads the motion sensor on supported MacBooks to pick soft, medium, hard or slam strikes.

Does Thock work on macOS Ventura?
App Store Thock needs macOS 13.0 or later, so it runs on any version of Ventura. The open-source Thock needs macOS 13.5 or later, so update Ventura to 13.5 first. Keyslam needs macOS 13 or later.

# Free Keyboard Sound Apps for Mac (2026): Honest List
URL: https://keyslam.com/free-keyboard-sound-apps-mac/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Free options · checked November 2, 2026
## Free keyboard sound apps for Mac, and when a $3.99 one is worth it

9 free or free-to-start keyboard sound apps for Mac, what “free” gets you with each one, and ways to hear keyboard sounds without installing anything.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: yes. Mechvibes, Thock (the open-source one), Keyboard Sounds Pro, Clank Keys and Tacque cost nothing, and KeyEcho is free with 18 of its 71 packs. Each has a catch: Mechvibes' Mac build is experimental and Apple silicon only, Clank Keys isn't notarized, and Tacque needs macOS 15. Keyslam isn't free. It's $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial, and its browser tester costs nothing, with no time limit.

### Every free option we found, and the catch

- App | What you get free | The catch | Runs on | Follows typing force |
- Mechvibes | The app and every pack: “completely free to use, including all sound packs”1 | Experimental Mac build, ad-hoc signed and not notarized2; re-add its permissions after each update3 | Apple silicon only, for now4 | No |
- KeyEcho | The app and 18 of its 71 packs5 | The other 53 packs cost $3.99 each or $9.99 for all, with no trial6 | Apple silicon and Intel; Windows and Linux too7 | No |
- Thock (open source) | Everything, under the MIT license8 | Not the $4.99 App Store app with the same name9 | macOS 13.5 or later10 | No |
- Keyboard Sounds Pro | Everything, MIT-licensed11 | Its site still says “for Windows & Linux”12; the Mac installer is on GitHub | Universal DMG: Apple silicon and Intel13 | No |
- Clank Keys | Everything: “You pay nothing.”14 | Closed source and not notarized15; the first launch needs a Terminal command | Apple silicon, macOS 13 or later16 | Yes, on MacBooks with the sensor |
- Tacque | The app and its six packs; a $1.99 tip is optional17 | The packs are synthesized18 | macOS 15 or later19 | No |
- KeyClicker | A free tier; $1.99 buys All Access for life20 | The listing doesn't say what the free tier includes | macOS 14 or later21 | No |
- Kachunk | The Underwood 1938 typewriter and the Cream pack, “free to download and keep forever”22 | The other 24 packs: $4.99 once unlocks all 2623 | macOS 13 or later24 | No |

- Keyslam (trial) | Everything for 7 days, no account or card; the browser tester with no time limit | $3.99 once after the trial | macOS 13 or later, Apple silicon or Intel | Yes, on MacBooks with the sensor |
Checked November 2, 2026 on each app's own site, its App Store or Setapp listing, or its GitHub page. The notes below quote them word for word. Paid apps, with prices and trials, are in every Mac keyboard sound app compared.

### What “free” means with each app

#### Mechvibes 3

Mechvibes is free and MIT-licensed, and its library is free too: 985 community pack pages on mechvibes.com when we counted, plus an editor for making your own. Version 3.4.0 of Mechvibes 3, which is written in Rust, came out on November 1, 2026. On the Mac, the project is upfront about the rough edges: its macOS README says the build “has never been run on a real Mac by the maintainer”. One-click pack install works on Windows and Linux; on a Mac you download a pack's ZIP and import it. It sends one anonymous Aptabase ping per launch, which you can turn off, and checks GitHub for updates once a day. The Homebrew cask has been disabled since September 1, 2026, and Mechvibes 2 is no longer developed. Can't get it to play? See why Mechvibes isn't working on a Mac.

#### KeyEcho

KeyEcho, from WaveApp LLC, is open source under AGPL-3.0, with notarized Mac builds and a Homebrew cask. You get 18 packs free. Each of the other 53 is a $3.99 Crafted Pack, or $9.99 buys “All Sounds Forever”. There's no trial for those, but there is a 14-day refund with no reason required, and one key works on Windows, macOS and Linux. Every key has its own press and release sample, and the app sends no usage analytics or crash reports. How Keyslam compares with KeyEcho.

#### Thock (open source)

Kamil Lobinski's Thock is the free one: MIT-licensed, macOS 13.5 or later, installed with Homebrew or a ZIP from GitHub. It loads custom packs written in simple JSON, has an in-app registry of community packs, mutes itself while music plays, places each sound by key position, and comes with a Raycast extension and a command-line tool. The latest release when we checked was 1.23.0, from March 28, 2026. Its site is clear about the name: this Thock “is not distributed on the App Store and is not affiliated with any app that has taken this name”. The $4.99 Thock on the Mac App Store is a different app; the two Thock apps, side by side.

#### Keyboard Sounds Pro

Keyboard Sounds Pro, by Nathan Fiscaletti, is free and MIT-licensed. It ships 20 built-in profiles (13 keyboard, 7 mouse), lets you build your own, and has pitch shift, pan and equalizer effects. Its website title still reads “Customizable Keyboard & Mouse Sounds for Windows & Linux”, but desktop v0.3.2, released May 1, 2026, includes a universal macOS DMG, built for both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. The pages we checked don't say whether the Mac build is notarized or what, if anything, it sends online.

#### Clank Keys

Of the free apps we found, Clank Keys is the one with force-sensitive sound, on MacBooks with the motion sensor. Its README says it “Reads the accelerometer hidden inside your MacBook and plays a real switch recording that matches how hard you hit the key.” Without the sensor, it varies the sound by typing rhythm. The switch recordings come from the Mechvibes project (MIT). The trade-offs are in setup: the source isn't published (the GitHub repo holds release builds only), the app isn't notarized, and you clear macOS's quarantine flag with a Terminal command before the first launch. The README also says the app contains no networking code. It needs macOS 13 and Apple silicon. Version 1.3.0, its first public build, came out on September 13, 2026.

#### Free on the Mac App Store: Tacque, KeyClicker and Klakk

Tacque, by Luminoxe, is free with an optional $1.99 tip, needs macOS 15, and plays six synthesized packs with spatial sound and per-key pitch variation. Its Setapp listing also mentions importing custom sounds and pausing during calls and media. KeyClicker, by Chujiang Wang, is free with a $1.99 All Access Lifetime purchase, needs macOS 14, and adds typewriter sounds and an on-screen display of the shortcuts you press. Both have “Data Not Collected” privacy labels. Klakk is a free App Store download with $4.99 and $2.99 Full Version purchases; its website editions cost $4.49 after a 3-day trial. Klakk isn't Klack: they come from different developers.

#### Kachunk's free tier

Kachunk, from Trifecta Labs, is “free to download and keep forever” with two packs: the Underwood 1938 typewriter and the Cream mechanical pack. $4.99 once unlocks all 26, including an Olivetti typewriter, on every Mac you own, with a 30-day refund. Its site says it's notarized, works offline and has zero telemetry. For a free typewriter sound, start here.

### Is there a free Klack alternative?

Klack itself isn't free. It's $4.99 on the Mac App Store with no trial; its FAQ suggests previewing each switch on its website, and it offers a 14-day refund (App Store refunds go through Apple). The nearest free match on paper is Tacque: also on the Mac App Store, also spatial sound, and the same macOS 15 minimum. The difference is the sound itself: Tacque's packs are synthesized, while Klack says each of its switch sets is made of over 100 audio files, each recorded and mastered individually. KeyClicker and Kachunk are free App Store downloads with paid upgrades. Outside the App Store, Mechvibes, KeyEcho and the open-source Thock are free. Weighing paid options too? See how Keyslam compares with Klack.

### Hear keyboard sounds without installing anything

To hear what a switch sounds like, or to pick a sound before you install an app, a browser is enough. These demos are free. They only play inside that browser tab, so to hear sounds in all your apps you still need one of the apps above.

- Demo | What it plays |
- Keyslam keyboard simulator | A full on-screen Mac keyboard with all 15 boards, four strength bands and shareable links |
- Keyslam keyboard sound test | Two boards back to back, with measured loudness |
- Typing test with sound | A words-per-minute test with every key playing |
- KeyEcho sound test | The letter keys A–Z only, per its page28 |
- TypeLouder sound test | A free keyboard sound test on its website29 |
- Klack previews | A play button for each switch on its home page30 |
- TapNoise demos | Sound demos on its website31 |

### When free is enough, and when $3.99 is worth it

Free is enough if:

- You want sounds now and then, or just want to hear a switch. The browser tester above does that.

- You also use Windows or Linux. KeyEcho, Mechvibes and Keyboard Sounds Pro run on all three.

- You want to read or change the code. Mechvibes, KeyEcho, the open-source Thock and Keyboard Sounds Pro are open source.

- You have a MacBook with the motion sensor and don't mind a Terminal step. Clank Keys gives you force-sensitive sound for nothing.

Keyslam is worth $3.99 if:

- You want force-sensitive sound in an app Apple has notarized, with no Terminal step. On MacBooks with the motion sensor, Keyslam reads the accelerometer about 800 times a second and picks real strikes from four strength bands.

- You want named boards with documented sources: Cherry MX Blue, Cherry MX Brown, Cherry MX Red, Cherry MX Black (Leopold FC980M PD), Gateron Red (GMMK TKL), Topre, Leopold FC660M with MX Browns, WhiteFox (Hako Violet), Rainy 75, Unicomp buckling spring, IBM Model F XT, vintage Technics, MacBook Pro (2018) keyboard, IBM Selectric II typewriter and Olivetti Lettera 22 typewriter. Each is cut from CC0 Freesound recordings, credited to the people who made them.

- You're on an Intel Mac, a desktop or macOS 13. Keyslam runs on all of them and plays a strength you pick where there's no sensor.

- You want an app that makes no network connections, and pauses on its own while any app is using the microphone.

Paid apps compared with each other, with prices and trials: the best keyboard sound app for Mac, by what you need.

### Try Keyslam free for 7 days

Everything is unlocked for 7 days, with no account and no card. After that, sounds stop until you buy a $3.99 lifetime license, which covers all the Macs you own. If it doesn't work for you, you get a full refund within 14 days. The trial date is kept in your Mac's Keychain, not on a server. How the trial and license work.

### Free keyboard sound app questions

Is there a completely free keyboard sound app for Mac?
Yes. Mechvibes, Thock (the open-source one), Keyboard Sounds Pro and Clank Keys charge nothing for anything, and Tacque asks only for an optional $1.99 tip. KeyEcho, KeyClicker and Kachunk are free with paid extras. Mechvibes runs only on Apple silicon for now, and Clank Keys isn't notarized.

Is Mechvibes completely free on a Mac?
Yes. The app is free and MIT-licensed, and every pack is free too. On a Mac, version 3.4.0 is an experimental build for Apple silicon only and isn't notarized, so macOS blocks the first launch until you allow it, and you re-add its permissions after each update.

Is Keyslam free?
No. Keyslam is free for 7 days with everything unlocked and no account or card, then $3.99 once for a lifetime license. The browser keyboard simulator is free with no time limit.

Is Keyboard Sounds Pro safe?
We haven't audited it, so we can't vouch for it. What we can check: it's MIT-licensed with its code on GitHub, and the Mac installer comes from the project's GitHub releases. Its pages don't say whether the Mac build is notarized or what it sends online. Like any keyboard sound app, it needs your permission to see key presses, so download it only from GitHub and read what Input Monitoring lets an app see before you allow it.

Which free keyboard sound app works on Intel Macs?
KeyEcho and Keyboard Sounds Pro have Intel builds. Mechvibes 3 doesn't yet (an Intel build is merged for its next release), and Clank Keys is Apple silicon only. Keyslam runs on Intel Macs with macOS 13 or later, free for 7 days. More in keyboard sounds on Intel Macs and desktops.

### How each one reacts to a hard press

Haptyk and Keyslam read the same sensor. Newer Apple silicon MacBooks have an accelerometer under the keyboard, and both apps use each keystroke's jolt to decide how loud and how hard the strike sounds.
Haptyk describes four levels, soft to slam. Keyslam sorts each board's real strikes by natural loudness into four bands and plays a different strike for a hard press, not a louder copy of a soft one.
How Keyslam's force sensing works.

TapNoise estimates it. Its pricing page lists “Harder press, louder sound”, and its blog is upfront about the method: “It is an estimate from body movement, not a force sensor measuring each individual switch.” (TapNoise blog (archived)) That effect needs a sensor MacBook too.

The difference that matters most for buying: Haptyk won't run at all on a Mac without the sensor, while TapNoise and Keyslam play their sounds on any supported Mac.

### Which one to pick

- Pick Haptyk if you have a sensor MacBook, want 16 packs, or already like the Mechvibes and ClickClack switch sounds.

- Pick TapNoise if you want its extras: “Tappy, a little keycap on your desktop” (tapnoise.com (archived)), “Agent Sounds for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor” (pricing (archived)), and fun sounds such as slaps, lid chimes and charger clicks, and you use one or two Macs.

- Pick Keyslam if you use more than one Mac, a desktop Mac, an Intel Mac or macOS 13; if you'd like 7 days to try it before paying; if you want an app that never goes online; or if you'd rather pay $3.99 than $8 or $14.99.

We make Keyslam, so weigh this page with that in mind. Every fact about Haptyk and TapNoise links to the maker's own page and an archived copy. Spot a mistake? Tell us and we'll fix it.

### Haptyk vs TapNoise questions

Haptyk or TapNoise: which is better?
It depends on your Mac. Haptyk ($8) reads the MacBook accelerometer and has 16 packs, but runs only on Apple silicon MacBooks with the motion sensor. TapNoise ($14.99 for one Mac) runs on any Mac with macOS 14, estimates typing pressure from movement, and adds Tappy and coding-agent sounds, but has no trial. Keyslam reads the same sensor as Haptyk for $3.99, also runs on Macs without it, and has a 7-day trial.

Does TapNoise charge per Mac?
Yes. Solo covers 1 Mac for $14.99 and Duo covers 2 for $20.99, one time, plus tax. It lists no plan for 3 or more Macs, so three Macs means buying Duo and Solo ($35.98). A Keyslam license covers all the Macs you own for $3.99.

How many Macs can I use Haptyk on?
Its terms say up to 3 devices you own. Each has to be an Apple silicon MacBook with the motion sensor, since Haptyk doesn't run on Intel Macs, desktop Macs, the M1 MacBook Air or the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro.

Is Haptyk more expensive than Keyslam?
Yes: $8 against $3.99, about twice as much. Both are one-time purchases with free updates. Haptyk's license covers up to 3 devices; Keyslam's covers all the Macs you own.

Can I use one Keyslam license on my MacBook and my iMac?
Yes. It's a personal license for all the Macs you own, and nothing counts activations. The MacBook gets force sensing if it has the motion sensor; the iMac plays every sound at a strength you pick.

# Why Does My MacBook Make a Sound When I Type? 7 Fixes
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/mac-keyboard-click-sounds-on-off/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Mac keyboard sounds
## Mac keyboard sounds: where they come from, and how to turn them off or on

A Mac doesn't click when you type unless something tells it to. Here are the seven things that do, how to tell them apart in under a minute, and the switch that turns each one off.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: macOS has no everyday key-click setting for the Mac's keyboard like the iPhone's Keyboard Feedback; its only built-in key click comes with Slow Keys. If your MacBook makes a sound when you type, something added it: a keyboard sound app in the menu bar, Slow Keys click sounds, VoiceOver or Speak typing feedback, a Sticky Keys beep, the alert sound for a key the app can't use, or a browser's own keyboard sounds. Each one has its own off switch.

### Find the source in under a minute

- Press the mute key, then type. If the sound stops, it's software and the rest of this page applies. If you still hear it with the Mac muted, it's the keys themselves.
- Type in TextEdit, then in your browser. Sound only in the browser points to Opera GX's keyboard sounds or a browser extension. Sound in both points to something on the Mac.
- Look at the menu bar. A keyboard icon, or any icon you don't recognize near the clock, could be a keyboard sound app. Click it.
- Match the sound to the table below. A click, a voice and a beep each have a different cause.

### What you hear, and what's making it

- What you hear | Usually | Where to switch it off |
- A mechanical click, clack or typewriter strike on each key, in any app | A keyboard sound app | Its menu bar switch, or Quit |
- A click on each key, and letters appear only after a pause | Slow Keys with Use click key sounds | Accessibility › Keyboard › Slow Keys |
- A voice reading letters or words, with extra tones | VoiceOver typing echo | Command-F5 |
- A voice reading what you type, without VoiceOver | Speak typing feedback | Accessibility › Read & Speak |
- A beep when you press Shift, Command, Option or Control | Sticky Keys beep | Accessibility › Keyboard › Sticky Keys › ⓘ |
- An alert sound when you press a key and nothing happens | The alert sound: the key had nowhere to go | Click into the text, or Sound › Alert volume |
- Clicks only while you type in the browser | Opera GX keyboard sounds or an extension | The browser's settings |

Paths are for macOS Tahoe 26 and macOS 27, checked against Apple's Mac User Guide on November 2, 2026. On macOS 13 to 15 they're the same except where noted below.

### Sound like one of these?

If the clicks you hear sound like one of these, a keyboard sound app is probably running. Press a button to compare.

### How to turn off keyboard sounds on a Mac

#### A keyboard sound app (clicks, clacks or a typewriter)

Apps such as Keyslam, Klack, Mechvibes, KeyEcho and Haptyk play a sound for each key in any app you use. Look for its icon in the menu bar or its window; quitting the app stops the sound. To stop one opening by itself, go to System Settings › General › Login Items & Extensions (just Login Items on macOS 13 and 14), select it in the list and click the Remove button (−) below it. Apple's steps.

In Keyslam: press ⌃⌥⌘K in any app, or click the keyboard icon and flip the switch at the top right of the menu. The status line reads “Off” and the menu bar icon changes from a filled keyboard to an outline. Choose Quit to close it, and untick Open at login to keep it closed after a restart.

#### Slow Keys click sounds

Open System Settings › Accessibility › Keyboard. Turn off Slow Keys, or click the Info button (ⓘ) next to it and turn off Use click key sounds. Slow Keys also waits for an acceptance delay before each key types, so if your typing suddenly feels sluggish, this is the one. Option-Command-F5 (or three quick presses of Touch ID) opens the Accessibility Shortcuts panel, which can switch Slow Keys too. Apple: keyboard accessibility settings.

#### VoiceOver typing echo

Press Command-F5 to turn VoiceOver off, or hold Command and press Touch ID three times quickly. Apple: turn VoiceOver on or off. To keep VoiceOver but stop it reading keys, open VoiceOver Utility (VO-Fn-F8 while VoiceOver is on), choose Verbosity › Text and set While typing speak to Nothing. Apple: Verbosity Text settings.

#### Speak typing feedback

Go to System Settings › Accessibility › Read & Speak and turn off Speak typing feedback. On macOS 15 and earlier the pane is called Spoken Content. Its options choose whether the Mac echoes characters, words, selection changes or modifier keys. Apple: Read & Speak settings.

#### Sticky Keys beeps

In Accessibility › Keyboard, click the Info button next to Sticky Keys and turn off Beep when a modifier key is set. If Sticky Keys keeps coming back, turn off Press the Shift key five times to toggle Sticky Keys in the same place.

#### The alert sound

When you press a key and the app in front has nowhere to put it, macOS plays its alert sound. Click into the text and it stops. To make it quieter, open System Settings › Sound and drag Alert volume down under Sound Effects. The Play user interface sound effects switch covers other system sounds, such as dragging an item to the Trash. Apple: Sound settings.

#### Sounds only in the browser

In Opera GX, go to Settings › Mods › Keyboard Sounds and disable or mute them (Opera's instructions). In Chrome, choose More › Extensions › Manage extensions and click Remove on the typing-sound extension. More in Opera GX keyboard sounds on Mac.

### How to turn keyboard click sounds on

macOS has one built-in way to click on each key press: Slow Keys with Use click key sounds. It's designed for people who press keys by accident, so every key waits for the acceptance delay before it types. You can shorten the delay, but for everyday typing it still gets in the way. Speak typing feedback and VoiceOver speak rather than click.

- Open System Settings. Choose Apple menu › System Settings, click Accessibility in the sidebar, then Keyboard.
- Turn on Slow Keys. Then click the Info button (ⓘ) next to it.
- Turn on Use click key sounds. Apple describes it as “Have keys make a sound when pressed.” Set Acceptance delay as short as it goes.

For a real mechanical click, clack or typewriter strike without that delay, you need a keyboard sound app. Here's how to make your MacBook sound like a mechanical keyboard, step by step.

### MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro: the same answer

Every setting on this page works the same on MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, iMac, Mac mini and Mac Studio, because it's part of macOS, not the hardware. The one difference shows up with keyboard sound apps that read the motion sensor to follow how hard you type. Only some MacBooks have it: see which MacBooks have an accelerometer.

### Still hear it with everything off?

If the Mac is muted and you still hear a click, a squeak or a rattle, it's mechanical. Dust or a damaged key can make a MacBook key noisy. That's a repair question, not a setting.

### Questions about Mac typing sounds

Can I make my Mac keyboard click like an iPhone?
Not with a built-in setting. The iPhone's click is in Settings › Sounds & Haptics › Keyboard Feedback and covers its on-screen keyboard only. The closest Mac option is Slow Keys' click sounds, which come with a typing delay. A keyboard sound app, such as Keyslam, adds a click without delaying your typing.

How do I turn off keyboard sounds on my Mac?
Find the source first. Check the menu bar for a keyboard sound app, then System Settings › Accessibility › Keyboard (Slow Keys and Sticky Keys) and Accessibility › Read & Speak (Speak typing feedback). Command-F5 turns VoiceOver off. A sound with no letter appearing is the alert sound, set in Sound › Alert volume.

How do I pause Keyslam?
Press ⌃⌥⌘K (Control-Option-Command-K) in any app, or click the keyboard icon in the menu bar and flip the switch at the top right of the menu. The status line under the name reads Off and nothing plays until you turn it back on. Keyslam also pauses by itself while an app is using the microphone. Quit closes the app completely.

Why does my Mac make a sound when I press a key and nothing types?
That's the alert sound. The app in front had nowhere to put the key, usually because no text field was selected or the shortcut does nothing there. Click into the text and type again.

### Want a click on purpose?

Keyslam plays real keyboard and typewriter recordings for each key you press. $3.99 once after a 7-day free trial.
Download for Mac$3.99 lifetime

# Opera GX Keyboard Sounds on Mac (Outside the Browser Too)
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/opera-gx-keyboard-sounds-mac/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Browser keyboard sounds
## Opera GX keyboard sounds on Mac, inside and outside the browser

Opera GX can play a sound for each key you type, and Opera GX runs on a Mac. The sounds stop at the edge of the browser window, though. Here's how to set it up, why it stops, and what to use when you want sounds everywhere.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Opera GX's keyboard sounds are a browser feature, set under Settings › Mods › Keyboard Sounds. On a Mac they play while you type in Opera GX and stop when you switch to another app. Typing-sound extensions for Chrome work the same way. For sounds in Pages, Slack, Terminal and the rest of macOS, use a Mac app with Input Monitoring permission, such as Keyslam.

### What Opera GX's keyboard sounds are

Opera describes them as built into GX. There are preloaded sounds under Settings › Mods, more packs in the GX Store, and an option to import your own audio files and adjust volume, intensity and effects (Opera's keyboard sounds page, checked November 2, 2026). Opera GX runs on macOS; Opera's download page lists a Universal installer.

### Turn them on, change them or turn them off on a Mac

- Open Opera GX's settings. Press Command-comma (⌘,) in Opera GX.
- Go to Mods, then Keyboard Sounds. Opera keeps its preloaded sounds there.
- Pick a sound and set the volume. Choose a preloaded sound or a pack from the GX Store. Opera says you can also import your own audio files and adjust volume, intensity and effects.
- To turn them off, come back here. Settings › Mods › Keyboard Sounds, then disable or mute them.

### Why they go quiet outside the browser

On a Mac, an app gets your key presses only while one of its windows is in front. The main exception is an app you've allowed in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Input Monitoring, which can notice keys you press in other apps. Opera's page describes no system-wide mode for GX keyboard sounds, so they follow the browser: switch to Notes or Xcode and they stop.

Extensions are narrower still. They run inside web pages, so they can't hear keys in other apps, and they usually stay silent in the browser's own address bar and settings pages too. Extensions you'll find by searching for “keyboard sounds Chrome extension” or “typing sounds extension” work this way: sounds for your tabs, not the rest of the Mac.

### Browser sounds vs a Mac app

- | Opera GX keyboard sounds | Typing-sound extension | Keyslam (Mac app) |
- Where it plays | While you type in Opera GX | On web pages in that browser | In any Mac app |
- What you grant | Nothing extra; it comes with the browser | Site access in the browser | Input Monitoring in macOS |
- What it can see | Keys typed in Opera GX | The pages it runs on, including what you type there | Which key went down; nothing from password fields |
- Price | Free | Varies | $3.99 once after a 7-day trial |
- Sounds | Preloaded, GX Store packs, your own audio files | Depends on the extension | 15 real keyboards and typewriters, CC0 recordings |
- Follows how hard you type | Not advertised | Depends on the extension | Yes, on MacBooks with the motion sensor |
- Works with the browser closed | No | No | Yes |

Opera GX details from opera.com; extension permissions from Chrome Web Store Help. Checked November 2, 2026.

### Permissions and privacy, side by side

Extensions. An extension that plays a sound on any site has to run on that site. Chrome shows this on the extension's Details page as “Allow this extension to read and change all your data on websites you visit”, and lets you limit it to specific sites (Google's instructions). That reaches page content, not just key presses.

Opera GX. Its sounds come with the browser, so there's no separate permission to grant. They know about keys typed in Opera GX, which the browser receives anyway.

A Mac app. Keyslam needs Input Monitoring. That covers more places (any app) but less content: it lets an app see key presses, not what's on the page or in your files. Keyslam stores nothing you type and makes no network connections, and its license is verified offline. More on whether Input Monitoring is safe.

### Get keyboard sounds outside the browser

The short version: install Keyslam, allow Input Monitoring, pick a board. Every step is in how to make your MacBook sound like a mechanical keyboard. Then turn off GX's own sounds at Settings › Mods › Keyboard Sounds, or you'll hear two sounds for each key while you're in the browser.

Free system-wide options exist too. Mechvibes and KeyEcho are free and open source; see the free keyboard sound apps for Mac.

### Pick a board close to your GX sound

Start from the character of the GX sound you liked, then press Play.

- If you liked | Start with |
- Bright and clicky | |
- Muted and tactile | |
- Deep and soft | |
- Quiet taps | |
- A typewriter | |

### Which should you use?

- Stay with Opera GX's sounds if you mostly type in the browser, want it free, or like GX Store packs and your own audio files.

- Use an extension if you're on Chrome and only want sounds on a few sites. Limit its site access to those sites.

- Use a Mac app if you want the sound in your editor, chat app and terminal too, recordings of named keyboards, or a sound that follows how hard you type on a MacBook.

### Questions about browser keyboard sounds

Do Opera GX keyboard sounds work outside the browser?
No. They play while you type in Opera GX and stop when another app is in front. For sounds in other Mac apps you need a keyboard sound app with Input Monitoring permission.

Is a keyboard sound extension safe?
It can be, but check its site access first. To play on any site it has to run on that site, and Chrome describes that as permission to read and change your data on websites you visit. Limit it to specific sites on its Details page, and remove extensions you no longer use.

Do Opera GX keyboard sounds work on a Mac?
Opera GX runs on macOS (Opera's download page lists a Universal installer), and Opera describes keyboard sounds as built into GX, under Settings › Mods, without naming a platform. Either way, they play only inside the browser.

# Which MacBooks Have an Accelerometer? Full Model List
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/which-macbooks-have-an-accelerometer/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Guide · MacBook hardware
## Which MacBooks have an accelerometer?

Newer MacBooks hide a motion sensor inside the case. Here is every MacBook Air and MacBook Pro model, whether it has the sensor, how to check yours in one Terminal command, and which apps use it.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro from the 2021 M1 Pro and M1 Max models on, and every MacBook Air and 13-inch
MacBook Pro with M2 or later, have an undocumented accelerometer that apps can read. The M1 MacBook Air, the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, Intel MacBooks and desktop
Macs don't. We verified it on a 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro on November 2, 2026; the other rows rely on the public sources linked under the tables.

The sensor sits inside the case and is run by the chip's Sensor Processing Unit (SPU). Apple doesn't advertise it or offer an API for it, which is why
people call it the MacBook's hidden accelerometer or hidden motion sensor.

### MacBook Pro

- Model | Identifier | Chip | Motion sensor | Basis |
- MacBook Pro (14-inch, M5 Pro or M5 Max, 2026) | Mac17,7, Mac17,9 | M5 Pro, M5 Max | Yes, tested | Tested by us on Mac17,9 (M5 Pro), Nov 2, 2026 |
- MacBook Pro (16-inch, M5 Pro or M5 Max, 2026) | Mac17,6, Mac17,8 | M5 Pro, M5 Max | Yes (reported) | spank: M2 or later |

### MacBook Neo, Intel MacBooks and desktop Macs

Model names and identifiers from Apple: Identify your MacBook Pro model and Apple: Identify your MacBook Air model. Sensor evidence from Macworld on iFixit's M2 MacBook Air teardown (July 2022), spank README, Knock and apple-silicon-accelerometer README. All checked November 2, 2026. “Reported” means at least one public source lists the model; we tested only the 14-inch M5 Pro.

### How to check your MacBook

- Find your model. Choose Apple menu › About This Mac to see the name and chip. System Information › Hardware shows the Model Identifier, such as Mac17,9.

- Or ask macOS directly. Open Terminal and paste the command below. It only reads the system's device list, so it doesn't need sudo.

- Read the answer. 1 means the accelerometer is there. 0 means macOS doesn't list it.

ioreg -r -c AppleSPUHIDDevice -d 1 | grep -c '"DeviceUsagePage"=65280,"DeviceUsage"=3}'

We tested this command on a 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro (Mac17,9) running macOS 26.6.2, where it prints 1. It looks for the same device Keyslam looks for at launch:
an AppleSPUHIDDevice on vendor usage page 0xFF00 (65280) with usage 3. Usage 9 on the same page is the gyroscope. If you'd rather browse, the
apple-silicon-accelerometer README suggests ioreg -l -w0 | grep -A5 AppleSPUHIDDevice.

### What the sensor is

- An accelerometer and a gyroscope in one small motion chip (IMU), believed from teardowns to be a Bosch BMI286, according to the apple-silicon-accelerometer README.

- Found in 2022. iFixit spotted it in the M2 MacBook Air teardown and couldn't say what Apple uses it for (Macworld).

- About 800 readings a second at its native rate. Keyslam reads it at about that rate to time and size each keystroke.

- Undocumented. Knock's site says it “relies on hardware features that are not officially documented by Apple (such as accelerometer access)”, so support can vary by model and macOS version.

- Not the Sudden Motion Sensor. Intel notebooks had a motion sensor to park hard-drive heads when dropped. Apple says SSD Macs don't use it (Apple).

### Apps that use the MacBook's hidden accelerometer

A handful of apps read the same sensor for very different jobs. Descriptions come from each project's own page, checked November 2, 2026.

- App | What it does with the sensor | Price and license | Source |
- Keyslam | Plays real keyboard and typewriter strikes that follow how hard you type | $3.99 once, 7-day free trial | How it works |
- Haptyk | Keyboard sounds that follow your typing force | $8 one-time, 3-day trial | haptyk.com |
- TapNoise | Keyboard sounds; says it “feels how hard you press through the MacBook’s motion sensor” | $14.99 once (launch price $5.99) | tapnoise.com |
- Knock | Turns taps on the MacBook's case into actions and shortcuts; Trackpad Tap Mode on any Mac | See its site | tryknock.app |
- spank | “Slap your MacBook, it yells back.” Runs from Terminal with sudo | Free, open source (MIT) | GitHub |
- apple-silicon-accelerometer | Python library and demos that read the accelerometer and gyroscope | Free, open source; needs sudo | GitHub |

Most of them do different jobs. If you want taps on the case to run shortcuts, Knock is built for that. Haptyk and TapNoise are keyboard sound apps like Keyslam,
which only uses the sensor to judge how hard each key was pressed. How Keyslam differs from each is on the Haptyk alternative page and the TapNoise alternative page.
For keyboard sound apps side by side, with prices and sources, see our comparison of Mac keyboard sound apps.

### Can two sensor apps run at the same time?

We haven't tested Keyslam alongside Knock, Haptyk, TapNoise or spank yet, so we can't promise it. Here is what we know from our own code: Keyslam opens the sensor in shared
mode, not exclusively. It also switches the sensor's reporting off when it goes idle after 3 minutes, when you switch sounds or force sensing off, and when it quits, which could pause another app's readings until
that app turns the sensor back on. We'll update this page once we've tested it.

### Is the sensor data private?

In Keyslam, yes. Readings are filtered and kept in memory, about the last 5 seconds, only to match each jolt to a keystroke. They're never written to disk or
sent anywhere, and the app makes no network connections at all.

### No sensor? You still get the sounds

Force sensing is the only feature that needs the sensor. On the M1 MacBook Air, the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, Intel Macs and desktops, every pack plays and
you choose Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam. Read keyboard sounds for Macs without the motion sensor, or see
what the MacBook typing sound app does on each model.

### Accelerometer questions

Does the M1 MacBook Air have an accelerometer?
Not one that apps can use, according to public sources: spank's README excludes the plain M1 chip, and the apple-silicon-accelerometer README lists the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro as incompatible. We haven't tested an M1 MacBook Air ourselves. Keyslam still plays every sound on it at a strength you pick; see keyboard sounds on the M1 MacBook Air and Intel Macs.

Does the MacBook Neo have an accelerometer?
Not verified. Apple announced the MacBook Neo on March 4, 2026 with the A18 Pro chip, an iPhone-class chip rather than an M-series one, and its announcement doesn't mention a motion sensor. spank's README lists A-series chips as unsupported. If you have one, run the Terminal check on this page and tell us what it prints.

Do Intel MacBooks have a motion sensor?
Yes, but a different one. Apple says all Intel-based Mac notebooks have its Sudden Motion Sensor, which was built to protect spinning hard drives, and that Macs with SSD or flash storage don't use it. It isn't the Apple silicon sensor, and Keyslam doesn't read it, so on Intel MacBooks you choose the strength.

Can an app read the MacBook accelerometer without special permission?
Keyslam does it as an ordinary app: no root, admin password, driver or kernel extension. It asks for one permission, Input Monitoring, which it needs for key presses anyway. Some open-source tools, such as spank and the apple-silicon-accelerometer library, run with sudo. Apple doesn't document the sensor for third-party apps, so this could change in a future macOS update.

### Put your MacBook's sensor to work.

Keyslam uses it to match each keyboard sound to how hard you type. $3.99 once, 7-day free trial.

# Cherry MX Blue vs Brown vs Red Sound: Hear All Three
URL: https://keyslam.com/blog/cherry-mx-blue-vs-brown-vs-red-sound/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Switch comparison
## Cherry MX Blue vs Brown vs Red: what each one sounds like

Three real recordings, matched for loudness and played back to back. Pick a strength, press play, and listen for the click, the bump and the glide.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Cherry MX Blue makes two sounds on every press: a sharp click as the key actuates, about halfway down, then the bottom-out. That makes it the loudest and brightest of the three. MX Brown has a bump you feel but no click, so it sounds like a rounder, muted clack. MX Red is linear, with no bump and no click, so you hear a quick, smooth bottom-out. Blue is the one people notice across a room; Brown and Red sound much closer to each other.

### Hear Blue, Brown and Red back to back

Every button types the same phrase, the quick brown fox: the first row varies the strength like real typing, and each row below holds one strength. Soft plays real light strikes from each recording and slam plays strikes from the hardest ~8%. All three packs are leveled to the same loudness, so you're comparing character, not volume. Headphones make the click easiest to hear.

- Strength | MX Blue | MX Brown | MX Red | Back to back |
- Natural (varies like real typing) | | | | |
- Soft | | | | |
- Medium | | | | |
- Hard | | | | |
- Slam (hardest ~8%) | | | | |

Each column is a different keyboard and recording: MX Blue from “Mechanical Keyboard 'Cherry Blue Switches'” by EricsSoundschmiede; MX Brown from “Mechanical Keyboard Cherry MX Brown” by majod; MX Red from “Keyboard clicking typing Cherry Red Mechanical” by handygaber on a Corsair K95. All CC0 on Freesound. Boards, keycaps and microphones differ, so treat this as three real keyboards, not a lab test of three switches.

#### Or type it yourself

Pick a board above, then type here

### The three switches on paper

- Switch | Type | Where the sound comes from | Actuation force | Tactile peak | Actuation point | Total travel |
- MX Blue | Clicky | Click jacket snaps on the way down and again on the way up, plus the bottom-out | 50 cN | 60 cN | 2.2 mm | 4.0 mm |
- MX Brown | Tactile | Bottom-out and top-out; the bump itself is nearly silent | 45 cN | 55 cN | 2.0 mm | 4.0 mm |
- MX Red | Linear | Bottom-out and top-out only | 45 cN | None | 2.0 mm | 4.0 mm |

Specs: Cherry MX Original data as listed in Wikipedia's list of keyboard switches, which cites Cherry's product pages. 1 cN is about 1 gram of force.

### What our three recordings measure

We measured the strikes this page plays. Every pack in Keyslam is leveled to the same loudness, −28 LUFS on a standard typing passage, so none of the three plays louder than the others. What differs is where each strike's energy sits.

- Pack | Energy below 1 kHz | 1 to 4 kHz | Above 4 kHz | Soft to slam | Key-up takes |
- MX Blue | 15% | 71% | 14% | 11.5 dB | 6 |
- MX Brown | 57% | 40% | 3% | 10.9 dB | 4 |
- MX Red | 30% | 61% | 9% | 10.2 dB | 6 |

Method: the average spectrum of the first 43 ms of each of the 24 regular-key strikes (6 per band) in each pack, 40 Hz to 16 kHz; soft to slam is the median level of each strike's first 40 ms, slam band minus soft band. Measured November 2, 2026 from the files on this page.

Read it this way: a Blue strike puts 71% of its energy between 1 and 4 kHz, close to the range where human hearing is most sensitive, so it sounds sharp and carries. The Brown recording keeps 57% of its energy below 1 kHz, which is why it sounds rounder. The Red sits between them, with 61% in the middle band.

### Cherry MX Blue vs Brown sound

Both switches have a bump. The difference is a small part called the click jacket. In a Blue, the jacket rides on the stem, catches on the way down, then snaps free with a click just as the key actuates, and resets with a softer click on the way up. A Brown has the bump without the jacket, so it only makes the two sounds every MX switch makes: the stem bottoming out in the housing, and the stem hitting the top of the housing when the spring pushes it back.

So a Blue adds two clicks to every keystroke and a Brown adds none. Pick Blue if you want every actuation confirmed out loud. Pick Brown if you want feedback you mostly feel, at a volume the people near you can live with.

### Cherry MX Blue vs Red sound

This is the widest gap of the three. A Red has no jacket and no bump: a light 45 cN spring and a straight slide to the bottom. All you hear is a quick bottom-out and a quick return. A Blue needs 50 cN to actuate, peaks at 60 cN at the bump and clicks on the way through. Reds suit fast, light typing and gaming. Blues suit people who like to hear each key register.

### Red switch vs brown switch sound

The closest pair. Neither clicks, both actuate at 45 cN and both travel 4 mm, so most of what you hear is the bottom-out, and that depends on the keyboard more than the switch. If you bottom out on every key, you'll hear little difference between them. The Brown's bump, 55 cN at its peak, can stop a light typist short of the bottom, which is quieter. In our recordings the Brown is the darker of the two, but they come from different boards and microphones, so part of that gap is the board.

### What about MX Black and Gateron Red?

Two more linear switches are in Keyslam: the MX Black pack is a Leopold FC980M PD with Cherry MX Black switches, a linear with a heavier spring than the Red; the Gateron Red pack is a GMMK TKL with Gateron Red switches. Each is a different board and microphone again, so play them next to MX Red to hear how much the board changes a linear sound.

### Which Cherry MX switch is quietest?

Of these three, Blue is the loudest because of its click. Red and Brown are close; how hard you bottom out and what the keyboard is made of matter more than the switch. Cherry also makes silent versions, such as MX Silent Red, with dampers built into the stem.

To quiet any board, try rubber O-rings under the keycaps, a desk mat and a lighter touch. If you want the sound without the noise, play a recording through headphones instead. And if all three are too much, the Laptop pack, a close-miked 2018 MacBook Pro, is a duller, subtler tap.

### Why soft and slam sound different

Each pack is cut from one real typing recording. Every strike is detected and paired with its key-up, then the strikes are sorted by natural loudness into four bands and each band is leveled to a consistent target. Soft comes from the lighter presses, slam from the hardest ~8%. On a MacBook with Apple's motion sensor, Keyslam picks the band from how hard you actually hit; on other Macs you choose it. How force sensing works.

### Each switch on its own

Cherry MX Blue sound test46 takes from EricsSoundschmiede's recording, with a typing boxCherry MX Brown sound test42 takes from majod's recording, with a typing boxCherry MX Red sound test46 takes from handygaber's recording, with a typing box

### Cherry MX sound: questions

Which is louder, Cherry MX Blue or Brown?
Blue. Its click jacket adds a sharp click on the way down and a softer one on the way up, on top of the bottom-out that both switches make. In Keyslam both packs play at the same leveled loudness, so the Blue sounds sharper rather than louder.

Are the Blue, Brown and Red packs recorded on the same keyboard?
No. Each comes from a different CC0 recording on Freesound: MX Blue by EricsSoundschmiede, MX Brown by majod and MX Red by handygaber on a Corsair K95. So the comparison also reflects each board, its keycaps and the microphone.

Do Cherry MX switches make a sound when you let go?
Yes. The spring pushes the stem back up against the top of the housing, and a Blue clicks again as its jacket resets. Keyslam plays real key-up sounds from each recording: 6, 4 and 6 takes in the Blue, Brown and Red packs.

# ASMR Keyboard Sounds on Mac: For Videos and Streams
URL: https://keyslam.com/asmr-keyboard-sounds-mac/
Updated: 2026-11-02

ASMR and creators
## ASMR keyboard sounds for Mac videos and streams

Soft Topre thock, close-miked PBT, a MacBook tap or a 1950 typewriter, on every key you press. Which boards suit ASMR typing, and how to get them into OBS or a screen recording.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Keyslam plays real keyboard and typewriter recordings through your Mac's normal sound output, so anything that records your Mac's audio records it too. In OBS Studio 30 or later on macOS 13 or later, add a macOS Audio Capture source. On macOS 27 or later, the Screenshot toolbar's screen recordings can include system audio. Before that, QuickTime Player records only a microphone, so either record your speakers with a mic or route the sound through a free loopback driver such as BlackHole. For ASMR typing, start with Topre, Leopold, Laptop or a typewriter at a fixed soft strength.

### Listen first: slow, soft typing

Each button types slowly at the soft strength, the way you might for an ASMR take. Put headphones on.

The sweep moves from left to right because each key is placed by where it sits on the keyboard, like the board in front of you.

Type slowly here

### Which boards suit ASMR typing

- Board | What it sounds like | Good for | Hear it |
- Topre | Deep, cushioned thock from a Happy Hacking Keyboard | Long, slow typing takes | |
- Leopold | Close-miked MX Browns with PBT and GMK caps; lots of detail | Close-up, crisp ASMR | |
- Laptop | A 2018 MacBook Pro's butterfly keys: short, soft taps | Quiet typing under a voice | |
- Vintage Technics | Chunky and muted, with lubed Gateron Yellow linears | Cozy, retro desk setups | |
- Rainy 75 | A dark, creamy thock; its uploader tagged it “creamy” and “thocky” | Low, soft typing takes | |
- Olivetti | A 1950 manual's typebars, with a bell on Return | Writing and storytelling videos | |
- Selectric | An electric typeball's firm strikes; a bell and carriage return on Return | An office-era sound | |
- MX Blue | Sharp clicks on every press | Click-heavy videos, if your audience likes it bright | |

Starting points, not rules; ASMR taste is personal. All 15 boards are on the keyboard sound test.

### How Keyslam's sound reaches a recording

- It's a normal app sound. Keyslam plays through your Mac's current output device, the same path as music or a video, and follows it when you switch to headphones, AirPods or a display's speakers.

- No separate output setting. Keyslam has no device picker of its own, so routing happens in macOS or in your recording app.

- In sync with your hands. The sound starts as the key goes down, with an audio buffer of about 5 ms, so it lines up with on-screen typing. Bluetooth headphones add their own delay to what you hear.

- 48 kHz inside. The audio engine renders at 48 kHz, the same rate OBS uses by default, and macOS converts it for your device.

- The same level on every board. Every pack is leveled to −28 LUFS on a standard typing passage, so switching boards between takes doesn't jump in volume.

### Record Keyslam in OBS Studio

- Use OBS Studio 30 or later. Its macOS Audio Capture source needs macOS 13 Ventura or later, the same minimum as Keyslam.
- Add the source. In Sources, click +, choose macOS Audio Capture and set it to capture desktop audio.
- Allow recording. When macOS asks, turn OBS on in System Settings › Privacy & Security › Screen & System Audio Recording (called Screen Recording on macOS 13 and 14).
- Type and watch the meter. The new source's meter in OBS's Audio Mixer should move with every key.
- Silence everything else. Desktop audio includes notifications and music, so turn on a Focus mode and pause other audio apps.

OBS can also capture a single app. Keyslam lives in the menu bar with no regular window, so if it isn't in OBS's app list, desktop audio is the reliable choice. On OBS 28 and 29, the macOS Screen Capture source records system audio instead (OBS's desktop audio guide).

### Record Keyslam with QuickTime Player

QuickTime Player's own recordings take sound from a microphone, not from what your Mac plays. On macOS 27 or later there's a simpler route: press Shift-Command-5 to open the Screenshot toolbar, click Options and choose Include System Audio before you record the screen (Apple's steps). On earlier versions, you have two options.

#### Option 1: a microphone

Play Keyslam through your speakers and record with your Mac's mic or a USB mic. You get the room and your real keys too, which some ASMR creators like. Headphones won't work for this, because the mic can't hear them.

#### Option 2: a loopback driver

- Install BlackHole, a free, open-source loopback driver.
- Create a Multi-Output Device in Audio MIDI Setup with your speakers or headphones plus BlackHole 2ch, so you hear what you record (Apple's steps).
- Choose it as your output in System Settings › Sound › Output.
- Pick BlackHole in QuickTime. Choose File › New Screen Recording or New Audio Recording, open Options and select BlackHole 2ch as the microphone.
- Switch your output back afterward. The volume keys usually don't work while a Multi-Output Device is selected, so set the level with Keyslam's own slider.

Paid routing apps such as Rogue Amoeba's Loopback do the same with per-app routing.

### Other recorders, streams and calls

Screen recorders and streaming apps with a “system audio” or “computer audio” option on macOS 13 or later capture Keyslam like any other app. On a video call, other people hear it only if your mic picks it up from your speakers or you share your computer's sound.

### Settings for clean takes

- Lock the strength. On MacBooks with the motion sensor, switch off “Feel how hard you type” and pick Soft, Medium, Hard or Slam. On other Macs the strength picker is always there. Keyslam still adds a little natural variation, and each key keeps its own take and pitch, so a long take doesn't sound like a loop.

- Or keep force sensing on for natural dynamics: light presses play soft strikes and hard ones play hard strikes.

- Stereo by key position. Leave it on for headphone ASMR, so Q sits a little left and P a little right; turn it off to keep every key centered.

- Key release sounds. On for the full up-and-down detail, off for a drier take. The typewriter packs have none either way.

- Volume. Use Keyslam's own slider to set the level against your voice or music, and watch for clipping in your recorder.

### Can I use the sounds in my videos?

Every pack is cut from recordings their authors released as CC0 on Freesound. CC0 is a public-domain dedication: anyone may use the recording for any purpose, commercial included, without asking or giving credit. Each pack's source is linked on the sound packs page, so you can check the license yourself, and crediting the recordists is a kind thing to do. If a sponsor or client needs something in writing, contact us.

Need sound files for an editor instead of live typing? See keyboard typing sound effects.

### ASMR and recording: questions

Can I record Keyslam sounds in OBS?
Yes. Keyslam plays through your Mac's normal sound output, so OBS Studio 30 or later on macOS 13 or later records it with a macOS Audio Capture source set to desktop audio.

Why doesn't QuickTime record Keyslam's sound?
QuickTime Player's own recordings take sound from a microphone, not your Mac's output. On macOS 27 or later, record the screen from the Screenshot toolbar (Shift-Command-5) and choose Include System Audio in its Options. On earlier versions, record your speakers with a mic, or route Keyslam through a loopback driver like BlackHole and choose it as QuickTime's microphone.

Can I use Keyslam sounds in monetized YouTube videos?
The recordings behind every pack were released as CC0 (public domain) on Freesound, and CC0 allows commercial use without permission or credit. Each pack's source is linked on our sound packs page so you can check it yourself.

Which keyboard sound is best for ASMR?
There's no single answer, but deep, soft sounds are the usual start: Topre for thock, Leopold for close-up detail, Laptop for quiet taps, or the Olivetti typewriter for a writer's desk. Play them slowly at the top of this page.

### MacBook keyboard sound effect

For a MacBook typing sound, use khenshom's close-up recording of a 2018 MacBook Pro above. It has multiple keystrokes and single clicks at different speeds, recorded with a shotgun mic at 24-bit, 48 kHz. It's the butterfly keyboard, not the scissor keys on current MacBooks, so it won't match a new MacBook exactly. More on that in the 2018 MacBook Pro butterfly keyboard sound test.

### Using them in a video

- Download the original from its Freesound page. Keep the page link with your project files.

- Drop it on your timeline in CapCut, Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve or iMovie.

- Cut single strikes at the start of each transient if you need one-shots. The WhiteFox and MacBook recordings include isolated keys.

- Vary the takes. Repeating one strike sounds mechanical in the wrong way; use several from the same session.

- Mix it under the voice. Key sounds are short and bright, so they cut through at a low level. The mono files (MX Red, Gateron Red, Laptop, Selectric bell, Olivetti, Olivetti bell) can be panned.

Want to type live on camera instead? Keyslam plays takes cut from these recordings as you type on a Mac; see ASMR keyboard sounds on Mac.

### Hear every pack

These buttons play Keyslam's cut of each recording, the same takes the app uses.

### Sound effect questions

Can I use these Freesound recordings in YouTube videos?
Yes. Each one is marked CC0 1.0 on Freesound, which waives copyright: you can copy, edit and publish it, including in monetized and commercial work, without asking. Keep the Freesound link as your record of the license.

Where do these recordings come from?
From Freesound, where each recordist uploaded them as CC0. They are the sources of Keyslam's 15 sound packs; Keyslam cuts them into single keystrokes and levels them for the app.

Do I have to credit the recordists?
CC0 doesn't require it. Crediting is still a kind thing to do, and the names and links are on this page if you want to.

Can I download Keyslam's sliced takes here?
No. This page links to the original recordings on Freesound. The cut and leveled takes are bundled inside the Keyslam Mac app, and you can hear them on this page with the play buttons.

# Typing Test With Sound: Free WPM Test, Real Keyboards
URL: https://keyslam.com/typing-test-with-sound/
Updated: 2026-11-02

Free typing test
## Typing test with real keyboard sounds

A free typing speed test where every key plays a real recording of one of 15 keyboards and typewriters, from a clicky Cherry MX Blue to an Olivetti Lettera 22. Pick a sound and start typing: the clock starts on your first key.
Start the test ↓Get Keyslam for Mac
Updated November 2, 2026

Sound

15 s30 s60 s

NaturalSoftMediumHardSlam

0words per minute

100%accuracy

30seconds left

Type the words here

Like MX Blue? Keyslam plays it on every key in your Mac apps.Try Keyslam free for 7 days

Press Space after each word. Wrong words turn red. Esc starts over. Your best score per length stays in this browser only.

Short answer: pick a keyboard sound, pick 15, 30 or 60 seconds, and start typing the words in the test above. The clock starts on your first key. Your score is correct characters divided by five, per minute, and accuracy is the share of your keystrokes that matched the letter expected at that point. It is free, runs in your browser and works with a phone keyboard.

### How WPM and accuracy are counted

A "word" in typing tests is five characters, spaces included, so long and short words count fairly. This test adds up the characters of every word you
typed exactly right, plus the space after it, divides by five and then by the minutes. A word with a typo scores nothing, so speed without accuracy doesn't pay.

Accuracy counts keystrokes: every character you type is checked against the letter that should be there at that moment. Fixing a typo with Delete
doesn't undo the miss, so accuracy can drop below 100% even when every word ends up right.

- Speed | Correct characters in 15 s | In 30 s | In 60 s |
- 30 WPM | 38 | 75 | 150 |
- 40 WPM | 50 | 100 | 200 |
- 50 WPM | 63 | 125 | 250 |
- 60 WPM | 75 | 150 | 300 |
- 80 WPM | 100 | 200 | 400 |
- 100 WPM | 125 | 250 | 500 |
- 120 WPM | 150 | 300 | 600 |

Characters needed for each score: WPM × 5 × seconds ÷ 60, rounded up. Shorter tests swing more with one fumbled word, so use 60 seconds to compare yourself across days.

### Which keyboard sound to type with

For a typing test with click sound, start with MX Blue: it clicks on every press, or the Unicomp buckling spring for a bigger click-clack. For a rounder sound with no click, try Topre or the MacBook butterfly
recording. For a typewriter, Return rings a bell, though this test never asks for Return.

Each button plays a short sample and selects that board for the test. Measured loudness and brightness for every board are on the
keyboard sound test page.

### How the sounds are made

Every board is cut from one real typing recording, released into the public domain (CC0) on Freesound by the person credited on its page; the typewriters add a
second recording for the bell on Return. Keyslam detects each strike, pairs it with its key-up where the recording has one, and sorts the strikes by natural loudness into four bands: soft, medium, hard and slam, the hardest ~8%. Each band is leveled to a
consistent target, and every board is leveled to the same loudness, so switching boards mid-test won't make you jump.

The Natural setting varies each press a little, the way your own typing does. Soft, Medium, Hard and Slam hold every key at one band, with only a slight variation.
The full story of the recordings is on the Keyslam about page.

### Why some people like typing with sound

Many people find that a sound on each key makes fast typing easier to follow, because every press is confirmed without looking down. Others just enjoy the
click of a board they don't own. There's no need to take anyone's word for it: run the same 60-second test with Sound on and Sound off and compare your own numbers.
If you'd like the sound outside this test, Keyslam is a keyboard sound app for Mac that plays the same boards in all your apps.

### Typing test questions

Is this typing test free?
Yes. No account, no download and no limit on attempts. Your best score per test length is kept only in this browser.

Can I take the typing test on a phone?
Yes. Tap the box and type with your phone's keyboard. Phones often don't report which key you pressed, so the page plays a sound for each character you type. Phone keyboards differ, so compare phone scores with phone scores.

Can I take the test with typewriter sounds?
Yes. Choose Selectric or Olivetti in the Sound menu. Every letter plays a real typewriter strike, recorded on the machine itself.

How is WPM calculated here?
Correct characters, including the space after each correct word, divided by five and then by the test length in minutes. A 30-second test with 150 correct characters scores 60 WPM.

Does typing with sound make me faster?
We don't make that claim. Some people type more comfortably with a click and some prefer silence. Use the Sound button to run the same test both ways and see what your own numbers say.

### Keep the sound after the test.

# About Keyslam: Who Makes It, How the Sounds Are Made
URL: https://keyslam.com/about/
Updated: 2026-11-02

About
## About Keyslam

Keyslam is a native Mac menu-bar app that plays real keyboard and typewriter recordings as you type. It is made by Samson and sold by Venture Deals, Co. Here is who we are, how every sound is made, and what the app never does.
Download for MacTry it in your browser →
Updated November 2, 2026

Short answer: Keyslam is a $3.99 macOS app, made by its founder Samson and sold by Venture Deals, Co., that plays real keyboard recordings on every keystroke. Each of its 15 packs is cut from one CC0 recording on Freesound, sorted into soft, medium, hard and slam bands of real strikes. The app makes no network connections.

### Keyslam at a glance

NameKeyslam, the Mac keyboard sound app
Made bySamson, founder
Sold byVenture Deals, Co., through Stripe Checkout
Current version1.0.1
Runs onmacOS 13 Ventura or later, Apple silicon or Intel
Price$3.99 once, 7-day free trial
Sounds15 packs cut from real CC0 recordings
NetworkNone. The app makes no connections
Websitekeyslam.com

### Who makes it

Keyslam is made by Samson, its founder. The company that sells it is Venture Deals, Co.: when you buy, checkout happens on Stripe's page in your browser, and Venture Deals, Co. is the seller on your receipt.

The idea is simple. MacBook keys are quiet, and many Apple silicon MacBooks carry a motion sensor that can feel a keystroke land. Keyslam puts the two together: real keyboard recordings, picked by how hard you actually type, in a small native keyboard sound app for Mac that stays out of your way.

Version 1.0.1 is out: a universal app, notarized by Apple. It's free to try for 7 days, then $3.99 once, and the download page has the install steps and requirements. The changelog lists what is in it.

Writing about Keyslam? The Keyslam press kit has the fact sheet, boilerplate, logo and screenshots.

### How the sounds are made

No pack is synthesized, and none is built from separate sessions at different strengths. Each one starts as a single recording of someone typing, which Keyslam's slicer (part of its source code, run when the packs are built) turns into a pack in six steps:

- Find every keystroke. The slicer looks for sharp onsets in a high-passed energy envelope of the recording.

- Pair presses with key-ups. Each press is matched with the quieter release that follows it. The two typewriter packs have no key-up sounds.

- Set aside the wide keys. Space, Return and Delete ring darker and longer on a real board, so up to about 14% of presses, the darkest and longest-ringing, are kept apart for them. The typewriters skip this step: Return rings a bell, and Space and Delete use the regular takes.

- Drop bad hits. Clipped strikes and strikes that overlap the previous key's ring are thrown out.

- Sort by natural loudness. The remaining presses are ranked by energy and split into four bands. Up to 6 takes per band are kept for regular keys and up to 4 for wide keys.

- Level everything. Each take is moved most of the way toward its band's level target. Then the whole pack is set so the same medium-strength typing passage, played through the app's engine, measures -28 LUFS (ITU-R BS.1770 integrated loudness), so switching packs keeps the volume about the same.

### The four strength bands

The bands come from where each strike falls among all the presses in that recording. Strikes in the gaps between bands aren't used.

- Band | Strikes taken from | What they are | Level target (vs medium) |
- Soft | 8th to 30th percentile | Lighter everyday taps (the faintest 8% aren't used) | 0.55× |
- Medium | 38th to 62nd percentile | Your ordinary keystroke | 1× |
- Hard | 70th to 88th percentile | Firm, deliberate presses | 1.45× |
- Slam | 92nd to 100th percentile | The hardest ~8% of strikes in the take | 2× |

From RecordingSlicer.swift in the Keyslam source. Percentiles are of press energy within one recording; levels are amplitude targets relative to the medium band.

### Hear the four bands of one recording

Pick a board and play the same short phrase from each band. Everything you hear comes from one real typing take; only the strikes that were chosen change.

Board

Pick a board, then press a band.

### How the app uses the bands

On MacBooks with Apple's motion sensor, Keyslam reads the accelerometer about 800 times a second, compares each keystroke's jolt with how you usually type, and blends the two nearest bands. On Intel Macs, desktops, the M1 MacBook Air and the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro, you pick the band yourself and every sound still works. How force sensing works.

### What Keyslam doesn't do

- No network connections. The license key is Ed25519-signed and checked offline on your Mac. The trial date sits in your Keychain.

- No analytics, no account. Nothing about your use of the app is collected.

- No recording of what you type. It uses which key went down to pick a sound, and its keyboard tap is listen-only, so it can't change or block a keystroke.

The details are in the privacy policy.

### Not to be confused with

“Keyslam” here always means the Mac keyboard sound app at keyslam.com. It isn't affiliated with any game, company or project that uses a similar name.

### About Keyslam: questions

Who makes Keyslam?
Keyslam is made by Samson, its founder. It is sold by Venture Deals, Co., and payments go through Stripe Checkout. You can reach us through the contact page.

Were the soft and slam sounds recorded separately?
No. Each pack comes from one real typing recording. Every strike in it is detected and sorted by how loud it naturally was, so soft comes from the lighter everyday taps and slam is the hardest ~8% of strikes in the same take. Each band is then leveled toward its own target.

Is Keyslam related to other projects with a similar name?
No. Keyslam, the Mac keyboard sound app at keyslam.com, isn't affiliated with any game, company or project that uses a similar name.
